operator_plays.name: Subject-To Low-Rate Mortgage Acquisition & RMLO-Underwritten Wraparound Note Spread Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Acquire property subject to existing 2.75%–4.25% mortgage debt and, where lawful, resell through an 8.5%–9.9% wraparound note originated with licensed RMLO involvement, applicable ability-to-repay review and licensed third-party servicing. Retain lawful origination economics and the net interest spread rather than operating as a landlord. RMLO involvement does not eliminate due-on-sale acceleration, seller liability, buyer default or property-related obligations.
inputs: Verified underlying loan, title, tax and insurance records with seller disclosures and counsel-reviewed due-on-sale analysis
Qualified buyer file and licensed RMLO underwriting with applicable SAFE Act, Dodd-Frank and state wraparound compliance
Legally reviewed transfer and wrap documents plus licensed third-party servicing, payment verification and default reserves
workflow: 1. Verify the underlying mortgage and title, disclose the seller's continuing debt exposure and obtain counsel-reviewed lender consent or a documented lawful acceleration-risk plan.
2. Underwrite the buyer through a licensed RMLO where required and deliver all applicable consumer, financing and wraparound disclosures.
3. Close only a lawful documented transfer with appropriate insurance and escrow arrangements, assigning property responsibilities explicitly rather than assuming none exist.
4. Service the wrap through a licensed third party, verify underlying debt and tax payments monthly and follow lawful loss-mitigation procedures if payments fail.
metrics: Collected wrap interest less underlying interest, servicing fees and credit-loss provision
Buyer delinquency rate and percentage of underlying payments verified on time
Liquidity reserves relative to acceleration, foreclosure and property carrying exposure

platform_risks.failure_mode: The underlying lender accelerates debt after a subject-to transfer
platform_risks.trigger: Enforcement of a due-on-sale clause or a related servicing or insurance default
platform_risks.impact: Immediate payoff demand, refinancing costs, foreclosure exposure and harm to the original borrower
platform_risks.detection_metric: Lender acceleration notices, unresolved servicing alerts and reserve shortfall against payoff exposure
platform_risks.fallback: Engage counsel and the servicer, pursue lender-approved assumption or refinancing and use a documented lawful sale or payoff exit if necessary

operator_plays.name: Distressed Asset Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Locate mispriced, orphaned, or administratively stranded assets—tax-sale overages, unclaimed state funds, dormant judgments, government surplus lots, or distressed micro-businesses—and capture a contingent recovery fee or acquisition spread.
inputs: Tax-sale excess proceeds ledgers
Unclaimed property & judgment dockets
Surplus auction manifests
workflow: Audit statutory fee caps, claim windows, and chain-of-title encumbrances
Execute skip-tracing or asset inspection to confirm net realizable value
Lock in contingent recovery agreements or below-intrinsic buyouts
metrics: Gross spread / contingent fee per case
Claim approval rate
Days from filing to disbursement

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory fee-cap compression or administrative hold
platform_risks.trigger: Jurisdiction updates finder fee limits, waiting periods, or filing documentation rules
platform_risks.impact: Reduced net fee margin or extended cash conversion cycle
platform_risks.detection_metric: County/state rejection notice rate and days-to-payout variance
platform_risks.fallback: Diversify across multi-state dockets and use attorney-backed filing partnerships where required

operator_plays.mechanism: Parse county probate petitions (Letters Testamentary / Letters of Administration) and daily Notice-of-Default (NOD) filings before national aggregators index them, matching out-of-state personal representatives and distressed owners to licensed probate brokers and cash buyers.
inputs: County probate court register of actions & Letters Testamentary filings
County recorder daily Notice-of-Default (NOD) & Notice-of-Trustee-Sale feeds
Skip-tracing & out-of-state personal-representative matching pipeline

Cross-match parcel equity and mortgage balances against county assessor and recorder records
Deliver empathetic estate-liquidation checklists, property-preservation referrals, or licensed brokerage introductions

platform_risks.failure_mode: State Foreclosure Consultant Act violations or unlicensed brokerage fee-splitting
platform_risks.trigger: Charging upfront fees to distressed homeowners in NOD or taking unlicensed real-estate commission splits
platform_risks.impact: Voided contracts, treble damages under state foreclosure-protection statutes, or DRE enforcement

operator_plays.name: HOA Super-Lien & Sub-Threshold Tax-Deed Statutory Redemption Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Price small HOA priority liens and tax-sale interests using jurisdiction-specific priority, notice, and redemption rules; returns depend on enforceable rights, not assumed title extinguishment.
inputs: County tax-sale and HOA lien records
Title report and statutory redemption calendar
Local counsel priority and notice opinion
workflow: 1. Screen small-balance liens against property value, senior debt, and sale eligibility
2. Have local counsel verify priority, service, redemption rights, and purchaser restrictions
3. Bid within a net-recovery ceiling and calendar every payment and notice deadline
4. Reconcile redemption proceeds or pursue counsel-supervised title resolution after rights expire
metrics: Net realized recovery after legal costs
Capital days outstanding
Notice and redemption deadline compliance rate

platform_risks.failure_mode: Sale invalidation or surviving senior lien
platform_risks.trigger: Defective notice or incorrect assumption about statutory lien priority
platform_risks.impact: Loss of expected recovery and extended title litigation
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unresolved title exceptions and notice defects per acquisition
platform_risks.fallback: Suspend bidding, seek available statutory refunds, and limit acquisitions to counsel-cleared interests

County Recorder grant/warranty deed & mortgage recording dockets

Dispatch transparent, non-governmental trigger mailers within 24–48 hours of filing with personalized QR codes pre-populating entity or parcel data

Monetize new LLCs via recurring annual labor-poster/registered-agent compliance memberships and B2B partner referrals; monetize new deeds via contingency property-tax appeal filings or high-ticket homeowner lead sales

platform_risks.failure_mode: USPS 39 U.S.C. § 3001(h)-(i) mail-stop order, State AG UDAP enforcement, or payment-processor freeze

operator_plays.name: Earnest-Money Deposit ("Gator") Escrow Lending & Joint-Venture Splits
operator_plays.mechanism: Advance $2,500–$25,000 refundable-contingency earnest-money deposits directly to title escrow under documented JV or promissory protections, with security recorded or perfected where legally appropriate. Negotiate a 15%–30% share of an earned assignment fee or a lawful fixed return; refunds depend on contractual deadlines, valid contingency exercise and escrow release terms.
inputs: Assignable purchase agreement with explicit refundable contingencies, notice procedures and deadline calendar
Verified title escrow account and executed JV or promissory documents with legally appropriate recorded or perfected protections
Borrower diligence, assignment economics and state-specific lending, brokerage, securities and usury review
workflow: 1. Verify assignment rights, counterparty identity, refundable contingencies and the enforceability of the proposed JV or lending structure.
2. Execute repayment and profit-split documents, perfect any lawful security and transmit the deposit directly to verified title escrow.
3. Track contingency and assignment deadlines, require documented progress and deliver timely cancellation notices when authorized and necessary.
4. Reconcile the closing or refund statement, recover deposited principal and collect only the contractually earned fee or lawful return.
metrics: Earned assignment-fee share or fixed return per completed deposit advance
Percentage of active deposits with verified unexpired refund rights and complete documentation
Deposit loss rate and median days from advance to cleared repayment

platform_risks.failure_mode: A supposedly refundable deposit becomes nonrefundable or disputed
platform_risks.trigger: Missed contingency notice deadline, invalid cancellation or unauthorized contract amendment
platform_risks.impact: Deposit forfeiture, delayed recovery and disputes over assignment proceeds
platform_risks.detection_metric: Deposits approaching contingency expiry without documented assignment or cancellation instructions
platform_risks.fallback: Freeze additional advances, seek timely authorized cancellation and pursue counsel-reviewed escrow release or contractual remedies

operator_plays.name: 24-to-72-Hour Escrow-Locked Transactional ("Flash") Double-Close Funding
operator_plays.mechanism: Fund the A->B acquisition only after the title agent independently verifies cleared, unconditional end-buyer B->C funds in escrow and an enforceable closing waterfall. Target a 1.0%–2.5% earned funding fee per 1–3 day turn; closing delays, fraud and legal restrictions can impair returns or principal.
inputs: Executed A->B and B->C purchase contracts, title commitment and independently verified settlement-agent credentials
Cleared end-buyer escrow funds, written disbursement conditions and a reconciled same-transaction payoff waterfall
Commercial-purpose funding agreement reviewed for applicable licensing, usury and escrow requirements
workflow: 1. Underwrite both contracts, title exceptions, end-buyer closing conditions and the settlement agent's authority and applicable bonding or insurance.
2. Independently confirm end-buyer cleared funds and irrevocable disbursement instructions using a previously verified title-agent contact channel.
3. Wire A->B funding only to approved title escrow after all release conditions are satisfied and the closing sequence is documented.
4. Reconcile B->C settlement, recover principal and earned fees, and release capital for reuse only after cleared repayment is confirmed.
metrics: Earned funding fees as a percentage of funded principal per completed turn
Median and maximum hours from funding disbursement to cleared repayment
Unrecovered principal and delayed-closing exposure as a percentage of outstanding funding

platform_risks.failure_mode: Fraudulent wire instructions or conditional end-buyer funds leave the A->B advance unrepaid
platform_risks.trigger: Last-minute beneficiary changes, failed independent callbacks or unresolved B->C release conditions
platform_risks.impact: Loss of principal, prolonged escrow disputes and interruption of capital recycling
platform_risks.detection_metric: Count of unresolved wire-verification exceptions and funded closings past contractual repayment deadlines
platform_risks.fallback: Stop disbursement, independently reverify settlement instructions and obtain counsel-directed escrow recovery before further funding

operator_plays.name: TCPA Serial-Plaintiff Docket Scraping & Real-Time Litigator-Scrub Firewall Tollbooth
operator_plays.mechanism: Offer consent-first outbound compliance screening using lawful docket-derived risk signals alongside mandatory do-not-call and revocation checks; plaintiff matching neither authorizes contact nor replaces TCPA compliance.

chapters.question_prompt: What exactly is a wraparound mortgage (wrap / AITD), how does the payment stack work on top of the seller's existing loan, and what are the core terms an operator must know?
chapters.title: Wraparound Mortgage Mechanics: How the Wrap Rides on the Underlying Loan
chapters.subtitle: Wrap notes, all-inclusive trust deeds (AITD), installment notes wrapping an existing first, wrap vs. subject-to vs. land contract vs. assumable loans, the due-on-sale landmine, and exam-level definitions
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners describe one machine: a new, larger wrap note laid over a live underlying loan, the buyer paying the wrap holder and the holder paying the original lender. The consensus edge is that the spread is earned on the full balance, not just equity: Bill Brunchick, with roughly 1,200 wrap closings, shows 6% on the equity plus a 2% rate gap on an $80,000 first at 4%, and Chris Goff models $126,000 total profit on a $350,000 wrap over a $300,000 loan at 3.5%. Street mechanics include buying on mirror wraps, selling on equity wraps, unrecorded notes with recorded AITD riders, Texas bilingual disclosures, and third-party servicers who pay the underlying lender first. Disagreement centers on acquisition: Pace Morby never buys on a wrap and prefers split-note hybrids, while Brian Gibbons says never sell on a seller-held wrap.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: The Wrap Rides on Top of a Live Loan
paragraphs: Every practitioner on the board describes the same machine: a new, larger note laid on top of a loan that stays alive underneath. Kris Haskins frames it with a $100,000 first at 6% wrapped into a $150,000 wrap, where the borrower makes one payment to the wraparound lender and that lender remits the first-mortgage payment to the original lender [kM__5b36grI @ 00:03:01]. Scott Horne of the Owner Finance Network calls the wrap a brand-new note and deed of trust subject to the underlying lien, technically a subordinate lien rather than a second, and says the cleanest way to grasp it is the flow of money: buyer pays seller, seller pays the underlying mortgage company [VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:00:36]. Tim of Tim Talks Real Estate walks the same path, adding that the buyer's single payment is usually priced a bit above the seller's old rate, the seller pockets the difference, and in most cases the bank underneath does not even know the house changed hands [Dklhw3jMfVo @ 00:02:25]. Pace Morby adds a hard definitional line: a wrap requires two notes or more, because without an existing debt there is nothing to wrap together [hTxjhDN2Cyo @ 00:07:11]. Everything downstream depends on that live underlying payment arriving on time.

The second point of agreement is why operators bother: the spread is earned on the entire balance, not only on the equity. Attorney Bill Brunchick, who says they have closed roughly 1,200 wraps through their own escrow company, lays it out on a $100,000 sale over an $80,000 underlying loan at 4%: a separate second at 6% earns 6% only on the $20,000, while an all-inclusive wrap at 6% earns 6% on the $20,000 equity plus the 2% difference on the underlying $80,000 [kM__5b36grI @ 00:10:56]. Maximilian Dier calls this flipping loans and runs a $400,000 FHA loan at 3% resold inside a $600,000 wrap at 8%, collecting a 5% spread on the $400,000 and the full 8% on the $200,000 of equity [49GchpJCUB0 @ 00:04:36]. PrepAgent's exam-prep math lands in the same place: Vivian carries an $80,000 loan at 4%, sells for $120,000 with 10% down, finances $108,000 at 7%, and earns 7% on $28,000 plus 3% on the $80,000 [-8VDqc249XY @ 00:02:29]. Edspira's Suzie example repeats the pattern, a 1.5% spread on a $35,000 loan at 7% while collecting 8.5% on the rest [OXZZS-KeaXc @ 00:05:52]. Same math, four different teachers, one conclusion: the cheap underlying debt is the asset being resold.

The consensus on prerequisites is equally tight, and it centers on the underlying lender that never signed off on the deal. Tim of Tim Talks Real Estate, in the business since 2007, calls the due-on-sale clause the landmine: almost every regular mortgage lets the lender demand the entire balance once title transfers, and a wrap almost always transfers title while that loan stays open [Dklhw3jMfVo @ 00:03:16]. Brian Gibbons of REISkills says wraps almost always violate the due-on-sale clause in the seller's underlying financing, and adds the second baseline risk: a buyer has to worry about the seller collecting the payment and never paying the first [9rVA292DHlY @ 00:01:49]. Scott Horne's answer is a loan servicer who collects from the buyer, pays the underlying mortgage company first, and releases whatever is left to the seller, a setup the industry calls its fraud preventer [VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:07:47]. Chris Goff lands on the same control point, recommending an escrow company coordinate monthly payments because paying the seller and hoping the bank gets paid carries risk [X_UODDIMvFs @ 00:06:51]. Across all four, the baseline is identical: assume the clause exists, plan for buyer default, and never let the underlying payment depend on one person's honesty.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Bill Brunchick's core street play is to buy on a mirror wrap and sell on an equity wrap. When there is little or no equity, the note to the seller mirrors the underlying loan exactly: if the first has 26 years left at 4% with a $1,200 monthly payment, the wrap note carries the same terms and the seller gets a little cash at closing [kM__5b36grI @ 00:12:11]. On the exit, the operator marks up both price and rate: on a $100,000 house over an $80,000 first at 4%, Brunchick sells at $105,000 because owner financing earns a premium, then charges about 6.25%, catching 6.25% on the $25,000 equity and 2.25% on the rest [kM__5b36grI @ 00:13:23]. Scott Horne uses the acquisition mirror wrap to solve a different problem: a seller with 25 years left at 4% on $100,000 who wants out in five years gets a wrap with identical payment and amortization plus a built-in five-year balloon [VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:02:40]. Epic Real Estate builds the wrap from parts, combining a $175,000 first at 6% and a $75,000 seller carryback at 8% into one $1,599 payment, $1,049 to the lender and $550 to the seller [5n5x76_xKLU @ 00:03:06]. Epic notes the blended rate lands closer to the 6% than the 8% because the first carries more balance.

Chris Goff publishes the cleanest full-cycle numbers. The seller owes $300,000 at 3.5%, a $1,347.13 payment with 20 years left; the wrap sells at $350,000 with $10,000 down at 5%, amortized over 30 years for a $1,878.88 payment with a 10-year balloon [X_UODDIMvFs @ 00:04:08]. That produces $531.75 a month, or $63,810 over 120 months, plus a $52,415.31 gap between the two amortized balances, for roughly $126,000 total profit including the down payment [X_UODDIMvFs @ 00:05:32]. Goff's split: the $40,000 above the first earns the full 5%, the $300,000 underneath earns only the 1.5% difference, and there are no repair, turnover, or management costs. Bill Brunchick says equity wraps work best on high-end homes: a $2,400 all-inclusive payment that only rents for $2,500 is a dead rental, but pushing taxes and insurance to the buyer, who pays PITI while the operator pays only P and I, can catch $400 to $600 a month with no landlording [kM__5b36grI @ 00:14:43]. Maximilian Dier prices for buyers the banks rejected, such as cash-business owners and people whose credit was wrecked by divorce, quoting 360-month terms at 8 to 10% with 20% down [49GchpJCUB0 @ 00:06:36]. Dier's rule for every one of those deals: never overpay, because a buyer who refinances early leaves no spread to recover the loss.

The paper stack is specific. Brunchick attaches a wraparound addendum to whatever standard purchase contract the operator already uses, with a choice between mirror wrap and equity wrap, then executes an all-inclusive wraparound promissory note that is never recorded; the recorded security instrument is a standard deed of trust with a wraparound rider, making it an AITD, or a wraparound rider to the mortgage in mortgage states [kM__5b36grI @ 00:17:27]. Brunchick is blunt that notarizing and recording a note means nothing; the recorded rider is what gives the world notice that this is a wraparound and not just a second. In Texas, Scott Horne adds the underlying lien disclosure notice and finance disclosure notice, delivered to the buyer in Spanish and English at bare minimum [VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:06:45]. When buying an existing wrap note on top of a subject-to, Horne wants a power of attorney, an authorization form, the mortgage statement, the seller's Social Security number and date of birth, and the online password [ZLt_A_LBSu0 @ 00:03:16]. Note Unlimited tracks the structure in software: two notes on the same property address, the wrap flagged with the wraparound parameter set to yes, linked under a related notes tab with amortization, cash flow and NPV views [gUg3ObEfMB0 @ 00:02:25].

callout.title: Wrap Spread Plays Operators Actually Run
callout.body: Four field moves from operators who structure, buy, and resell wraps on live underlying loans.
items: Buy on a mirror wrap when there is little or no equity, then sell on an equity wrap that marks up both price and interest rate so the spread runs on the full balance [kris haskins — kM__5b36grI @ 00:13:02].

Before paying off or selling a property bought on a balloon wrap, ask the seller to renew and extend for another three or five years; if you don't ask, you don't get [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:03:10].

Target absentee owners with property values above $300,000, at least 20% equity, and two-plus years of ownership; Goff's nationwide query returned 7,284,401 properties, and low-equity owners are more likely to deal [Chris Goff — X_UODDIMvFs @ 00:00:17].

When a wrap buyer brings a new buyer who wants to assume, buy from the seller for the same down payment and resell on a new wrap with the same terms, so the note on file belongs to a borrower you processed and the note-sale exit stays clean [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — ZLt_A_LBSu0 @ 00:05:49].

sop_steps.title: Pull a Targeted Seller List
sop_steps.action: Query absentee owners with moderate equity and two-plus years of ownership before spending on mail or skip tracing.
sop_steps.detail: Goff sets equity at 20% rather than high-equity only because owners with little equity are more likely to work with you when they cannot afford to sell with commissions [Chris Goff — X_UODDIMvFs @ 00:02:21].

sop_steps.title: Acquire and Lock Control of the Underlying Loan
sop_steps.action: Take the deed subject-to or on a mirror wrap, and collect everything needed to service the underlying debt yourself.
sop_steps.detail: Brunchick mirrors the underlying note when there is no equity and adds a little cash at closing [kris haskins — kM__5b36grI @ 00:12:31]; Horne demands the mortgage statement, seller identifiers, and the online password to control the underlying [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — ZLt_A_LBSu0 @ 00:03:32].

sop_steps.title: Underwrite the Wrap Buyer
sop_steps.action: Run consumer buyers through a residential mortgage loan originator and review the loan package before approving the sale.
sop_steps.detail: Horne checks ability to repay and debt-to-income: a 30% DTI is reasonable, while a buyer at 70% DTI simply cannot afford the house [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:06:09].

sop_steps.title: Paper, Record, and Service the Wrap
sop_steps.action: Attach the wrap addendum, sign the unrecorded all-inclusive note, record the deed of trust with the wraparound rider, and set up third-party servicing.
sop_steps.detail: Brunchick records the wraparound rider so the AITD gives notice it is a wrap, not just a second [kris haskins — kM__5b36grI @ 00:17:27]; Horne's servicer pays the underlying mortgage company first and the seller last [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:07:32].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Pace Morby draws the hardest line on the buy side: 'we never want to buy on a wrap we want to sell on a wrap' [hTxjhDN2Cyo @ 00:05:25]. Their reason is the blended rate. In Morby's car example, a $459 payment at six percent and a $200 equity payment at zero percent become one $659 payment at six percent once wrapped, so the equity slice that could have carried zero percent now bleeds interest. Morby's fix is to separate the notes and acquire on a 'hybrid': subject-to on the existing debt, plus a separate seller-finance note on the equity with its own terms [hTxjhDN2Cyo @ 00:05:40]. Attorney Bill Brunchick, who owns an escrow company that specializes in wraps and lost count of closings after about 1,200, runs the opposite playbook: buy on a mirror wrap when there is little or no equity, then sell on an equity wrap with the price and interest rate marked up [kM__5b36grI @ 00:13:02]. Brian Gibbons at REISkills sits in a third camp, calling buying on a wraparound or AITD a great idea for investors renting out or running lease options, while flatly telling operators never to sell their own property on a seller-held mortgage or wraparound because the seller will have to foreclose if the buyer defaults [9rVA292DHlY @ 00:05:09].

The second split is whose side the structure protects. Bill Brunchick prefers to buy straight subject-to and simply take the deed, but concedes that under a bare sub-to the seller is without recourse if the buyer stops paying; an all-inclusive wrap or AITD hands the seller a lien and a foreclosure path to get the property back [kM__5b36grI @ 00:11:53]. Chris Goff reports that attorneys are more likely to do a wrap than a sub-to because subject-to protects the buyer, not the seller, and a seller shopping for another property can show the wrap income. Yet Goff flips back to subject-to when seller death is the worry, because a sub-to takes the seller out of the picture and nobody needs their signature down the road [X_UODDIMvFs @ 00:07:35]. Ashland Mortgage splits it on payment: subject-to delivers the absolute lowest payment, while the wrap is more attractive to sellers who want their equity paying them every month, and Ashland treats the due-on-sale call as rarely enforced when payments stay on time [IKu9qf2jZBk @ 00:00:45]. Tim Talks Real Estate, in the business since 2007, rejects that comfort outright: treat the risk as real, and never build a plan that only works if the bank never notices [Dklhw3jMfVo @ 00:04:06].

Exit structure splits again by state and by appetite for control. Brunchick buys on a deed subject-to everywhere, then sells on an unrecorded installment land contract and keeps title until the buyer pays off, except in Texas, where the rules on installment land contracts force a wraparound deed of trust on both the buy and the sell [kM__5b36grI @ 00:18:44]. Pace Morby hits the same Texas wall from the other direction, calling executory contracts illegal there and naming Texas the only state where they cannot be done [hTxjhDN2Cyo @ 00:02:40]. On stacking, Ron LeGrand gives a one-line green light: yes, you can do a wrap over a wrap [OuQxeQu2HJA @ 00:01:32]. Scott Horne, whose Dallas lunch group started calling a wrap of a wrap 'sub 3,' refuses to let a downstream buyer simply assume an existing wrap. Horne instead buys the house from the seller for the same down payment the new buyer is paying and simultaneously sells to that buyer on a fresh wrap with the same terms, becoming the direct mortgage holder and running the buyer through loan processing [ZLt_A_LBSu0 @ 00:05:49]. Horne's logic is exit-first: if the assumption simply passes through, there is no telling whose mortgage is being sold in a future note sale or what financial information exists on that borrower.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The landmine every practitioner names is the due-on-sale clause. Tim Talks Real Estate spells out the mechanics: almost every regular mortgage carries the clause, a wrap almost always transfers the property while the original loan is still open, and the lender can demand the whole balance, not the monthly payment but the whole thing, the day they find out [Dklhw3jMfVo @ 00:03:16]. Brian Gibbons calls it the main problem with wraps and adds the buyer-side trap: the seller collects the buyer's payment and then never pays the first mortgage [9rVA292DHlY @ 00:01:49]. Gibbons handles both by putting the property in a land trust and routing the buyer's money to a third-party payee that pays the mortgage first and sends the rest to the seller. Scott Horne runs the same defense through a loan servicer: buyer pays servicer, servicer pays the underlying lender first, seller gets whatever is left. Horne calls it the industry's fraud preventer, because a later default can then only mean the buyer missed, not that the seller pocketed the money [VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:07:47]. Chris Goff wants an escrow company coordinating the monthly payment for the same reason, flagging the risk in just paying the seller and hoping the seller is making the payment [X_UODDIMvFs @ 00:06:51].

The second failure mode is the buyer simply stopping. PrepAgent's Sam-and-Bill example flips from win-win to 'not so fast': if Bill stops paying, Sam cannot pay the existing mortgage, the bank gets angry and it becomes a big issue [uHpaHL4qN84 @ 00:02:45]. Shop Rates calls buyer default the biggest risk point because the seller stays legally responsible for the original mortgage, telling sellers to choose their buyers wisely and buyers to make sure the seller is financially stable [Z_X2-JRfBYs @ 00:01:26]. Ron LeGrand puts the credit cost on the table: selling on a wrap means nobody pays off the underlying debt, so a personally guaranteed loan stays the seller's responsibility for as long as it takes the buyer to cash them out. With guaranteed debt in play, LeGrand says to be more selective on who goes in the house, or even sell at retail price right now and get that debt out of your life [OuQxeQu2HJA @ 00:05:15]. Brian Gibbons adds the closing-table bleed: title transfers and a new mortgage or trust deed gets recorded, attorney fees stack on top, and if the seller is getting no money down they may refuse to bring cash, so the investor can wind up paying all the costs just to get the deal done [9rVA292DHlY @ 00:04:50].

Then come the economics checks. Maximilian Dier says the place people get in trouble is overpaying: buy at $300,000 on a house only worth $270,000, wrap it out at $280,000 telling yourself you will make it up over time, and if the buyer refinances or pays the loan off in full, you are screwed. Dier's rule is to buy under market value with a low interest rate and build in instant equity [49GchpJCUB0 @ 00:09:19]. Bill Brunchick runs the rent-versus-wrap test on high-end homes: a $2,400 all-inclusive payment that only rents for $2,500 is not worth the risk, but pushing taxes and insurance onto a wrap buyer and raising the rate can catch a spread of $400 to $600 a month with no landlording responsibility [kM__5b36grI @ 00:14:43]. PrepAgent sets the floor: to break even, the seller must charge at least as much interest as the existing loan costs, which is why sellers negotiate the highest rate they can so the first mortgage gets paid while the deal still earns a profit [-8VDqc249XY @ 00:01:35]. Scott Horne's buyer screen is the debt-to-income check run through a residential mortgage loan originator: a 30 percent DTI is pretty reasonable, but at 70 percent the bottom line is the buyer cannot afford the house [VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:06:09].

callout.title: Four checks before a wrap closes
callout.body: Each check below comes from a trap a practitioner named or hit directly. Fail any one and the wrap does not close as structured.
items: Name the exact plan if the underlying lender calls the loan due: refinance path, reserves, and a timeline [Tim Talks Real Estate — Dklhw3jMfVo @ 00:05:31].
Route every buyer payment through a loan servicer that pays the underlying lender first and the seller last [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:07:47].
Never record the note itself; record the deed of trust or mortgage with the wraparound rider as the security instrument [kris haskins — kM__5b36grI @ 00:17:07].
Before buying into a wrap of a wrap, check whether the front-end seller is an investor who may call that loan due [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — ZLt_A_LBSu0 @ 00:07:45].

chapters.pull_quote: 'Don't build a plan that only works if the bank never notices. Build one that survives the day it does.' — Tim Talks Real Estate (Dklhw3jMfVo @ 00:04:06).
action_checklist: Run the mirror-in, equity-out spread: on a $100,000 house with an $80,000 first at 4 percent, sell at $105,000 at about six and a quarter percent to earn that rate on the $25,000 equity and two and a quarter percent on the underlying [kris haskins — kM__5b36grI @ 00:13:23].
Attach the wraparound addendum to the standard purchase contract and mark whether the deal is a mirror wrap or an equity wrap [kris haskins — kM__5b36grI @ 00:15:56].

Collect the underlying-loan control package before buying any wrap note: power of attorney, authorization form, mortgage statement, seller contact details, SSN, date of birth, and online password [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — ZLt_A_LBSu0 @ 00:03:16].

Set up a third-party payee so the buyer's payment hits the first mortgage first and only the remainder goes to the seller [REISkills.com - Where you learn Real Estate Investing — 9rVA292DHlY @ 00:02:06].

In Texas, deliver the underlying lien disclosure and finance disclosure notices to the buyer in both Spanish and English at bare minimum [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — VDXOvtqzbZk @ 00:06:45].
Model the deal as two linked notes on the same property address, flagging the wrap note so amortization, cash flow, and NPV track side by side [Note Unlimited — gUg3ObEfMB0 @ 00:02:07].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I explain and close a subject-to deal with a seller, their agent, and their mortgage company, especially on pre-foreclosures?
chapters.title: Buying Subject-To: Pitching Sellers, Agents, and Lenders
chapters.subtitle: Step-by-step subject-to timeline, live seller and agent phone scripts, in-person appointments, subject-to vs. assumption vs. seller finance, talking to the seller's mortgage company, and buying pre-foreclosures before auction
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners buying subject-to converge on one pitch: the asset being bought is the existing low-rate loan, not the house. Pace Morby, Lex Levinrad and Flipping Mastery TV all frame the seller's alternative as a retail sale that eats roughly 10% in commissions and closing costs, then offer to take over payments, cover arrears or commission, and hand the seller a small check. Street numbers include Morby's 80% equity-deferral rate, Flipping Mastery's 16% entry fee scored against a 25% ceiling, and kris haskins' roughly $50,000 reinstatement on a Virginia Beach preforeclosure. Disagreements center on due-on-sale risk, where Robert Crager reports zero calls in 25 years and Morby reports multiple; on interest, where Ben Jensen never mentions it; and on balloons, which Maximilian Dier hates.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus: You Are Buying the Loan, Not the House
paragraphs: Every speaker who defines the play draws the same line: subject-to is for encumbered property, seller finance is for free-and-clear property. Pace Morby put it to an Instagram follower who asked about doing a paid-off house subject-to in four words, debt versus no debt, and answered that a free-and-clear asset is seller finance by definition [ajwU62m3ADk @ 00:00:54]. In his shorter breakdown he lists the four terms every creative deal turns on, price, down payment, rate and length, and notes that on a subject-to deal those terms are already fixed by the existing loan, so the buyer is inheriting a structure rather than negotiating one [Kk_nfIhy2LY @ 00:02:27]. Ben Jensen uses the same split from the preforeclosure side: sub-to means taking over the existing mortgage while getting on the deed, seller finance usually means a paid-off house where the buyer pays a down payment and the seller acts as the bank, and a wrap is selling owner-finance on top of an existing mortgage [t96wzMUDN58 @ 00:01:17]. Morby's Nevada deal shows the mechanics in plain terms: the $290k Wells Fargo deed of trust stays in the seller's name, Morby logs into the seller's account and makes the payment, and the deed moves through title and escrow [ajwU62m3ADk @ 00:02:09].

The second point of agreement is the pitch: the seller is handing over a mortgage, and the alternative is a retail sale that costs them money. Meeting a seller in person who owed about $350,000, Morby stacked the fees at 3% plus 3% plus about 4%, roughly 10%, which puts a listing at about $35,000 out of pocket [1GjR0GDWoyo @ 00:03:48]. He then told the seller the value was "the mortgage," not the house, offered to make the May and June payments, and set move-out for the end of June. Lex Levinrad runs identical math on his zero-down case: a 6% commission plus 3–4% closing means the seller nets $153,000 against a $170,000 loan, so a retail sale leaves them writing a check to get out [NKTKZd6UIHg @ 00:05:39]. Flipping Mastery TV turns the same logic on listing agents, anchoring with a low cash offer and then pivoting to taking over payments, handing the seller $5,000, and paying the closing costs and commission [rYMNGajRMfo @ 00:01:12]. kris haskins packages it for distressed owners as "our D program": closing happens at the attorney's office and the payments resume, pitched to a seller who fell behind after the birth of their child and whose PCS was expiring [X4XzY55e_n4 @ 00:15:13].

The baseline prerequisites are just as consistent: the loan has to be cheap and the payment has to sit well under rent. Levinrad's intake questions are the filter, whether the seller is current, the balance, term left, rate, payment, and whether that payment includes taxes and insurance [NKTKZd6UIHg @ 00:01:03]. His 2023 thesis names the target: owners who bought in 2021–22 and sit 10–15% underwater on 2.75–3% loans [NKTKZd6UIHg @ 00:01:29]. His longer walkthrough prefers fixed rates, less term remaining and lower rates, using a $150,000 loan at 2.875% with 25 years left, a $1,500 payment against $2,200 rent, for +$700 a month [YY7F8y8K0cU @ 00:02:34]. Flipping Mastery TV scores the rate below 4–5% and wants a spread like $2,000 rent against $1,200 PITI, or $800 a month [rYMNGajRMfo @ 00:04:46]. Morby's collaborated VA deal at 3% cash flowed on day one, with the agent paid $2,000, the seller paid $0, and a private money lender covering costs and furnishings, which is the deal he points to when he says "Equity comes and Equity goes but the cash will always flow Real Estate Investors buy cash flow" [Ou7n95pTZFE @ 00:20:19].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: Scripts, Equity Deferral, Escrow and the Servicer
paragraphs: On agent calls the script is built around the commission. Flipping Mastery TV treats an agent's 5% commission objection as the signal that a sub-2 conversation is on the table [rYMNGajRMfo @ 00:00:18], and Morby's go-to line is to ask, on the spot, whether the seller would let him take over payments if he could get the agent's commission paid [Ou7n95pTZFE @ 00:42:25]. On a live call with agent Victoria, whose North Carolina buyer had fallen out, Morby opened by refusing to touch price: "I will never negotiate with you on price" at $340K, close in 24 hours on a warranty deed, commissions paid by him, against a retail net of about $320K and a cash buyer at $260–270K [bKMcgnoYXfQ @ 00:02:27]. The loan sat at 3.75% with roughly $180–200K owed. Maximilian Dier, testing Richard Taylor's seller-finance version on realtors, opens with investor vocabulary, a 1031 exchange, cash flow, a pre-approval letter, asks the agent for rent, then lays the checkmate: a lender demands 20% down and at high rates the payment exceeds rent, while a cash buyer's poor cash-on-cash return means a lowball. He then asks how they expect to sell it and stays silent for 3–10 seconds [GqiH4Kh8eaQ @ 00:03:50].

Sellers who want equity get it deferred, not paid. Morby says 80% of his sellers defer equity 3–4 years; his offer on the North Carolina deal was $20K down with the remainder paid within about 24 months through a refinance, adding, "I would be an idiot to refinance right now" [bKMcgnoYXfQ @ 00:06:58]. His TC writes refinance conditions into the paperwork, such as a 2.5% rate trigger, and he raises objections before the seller does [bKMcgnoYXfQ @ 00:27:23]. Levinrad handles the same ask smaller: if a seller wants $15,000–20,000, offer $5,000 down plus installments [NKTKZd6UIHg @ 00:03:36]. Ben Jensen's version, on his seller-finance-to-wrap deal in Carrollton, is to reverse-engineer the seller's desired monthly payment and price and never mention interest; he took a $150K price off the seller's Zillow number, $5K down, $800 a month at 0%, shortened the amortization to 15 years because 30 years produced only about $400 a month, and set a 7-year balloon, his floor [t96wzMUDN58 @ 00:06:18]. On free-and-clear rentals Morby lets the seller build the terms: the 86-year-old Las Vegas seller and spouse set their own down payment and monthly figure that night, wanting payments "close to the rent" [vJ6uGVFs4M4 @ 00:04:13].

Once a seller says yes, the work moves to escrow and the lender. Morby's TC Molly sends the agreement, he opens escrow with a $5K EMD from a gator, runs each deal in its own Slack channel, and only underwrites after escrow opens because he "will go and comp and underwrite a 100 houses to get one under contract" [X94W660WDh8 @ 00:22:00]. On 3932 W Myrtle the gator funded arrears, EMD, the attorney, the TC, two months of buffer payments, and $15K to Morby upfront. kris haskins works the servicer directly: a reinstatement on his Virginia Beach preforeclosure required an authorization to release form, and the $46,000 figure, with about $10,000–11,000 of it principal, put the entry near $50,000 [DhOoZcypJCM @ 00:07:25]. To talk to the seller's mortgage company he gathers the seller's SSN (last four or full), an authorization to release, and a notarized limited POA; PNC verified those documents on file [FybFcuS9T7s @ 00:06:23]. Levinrad says insurance "trips up 90%": keep the existing policy and add the trust as additional insured [YY7F8y8K0cU @ 00:08:36]. Robert Crager's standing rule is to always pay the bank directly and send the seller proof [q1drqFk-FH4 @ 00:10:01].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over interest and balloon structure on seller-financed paper. Ben Jensen reverse-engineers the seller’s target monthly payment and price and will “never mention interest.” His Carrollton deal closed at $150K, $5K down, $800/mo, 0% interest, while a peer of his opens sellers at 2–4% [t96wzMUDN58 @ 00:07:57]. When a seller digs in on 4%, Jensen trades rate for price, dropping a 300 number to 250 [t96wzMUDN58 @ 00:08:59]. On balloons the camps diverge again. Richard Taylor’s script, as Maximilian Dier runs it, pays 10–15% over asking with a 5–7 year balloon. Dier says he hates balloons, and his own deal was 30 years at 0% with no balloon at all [GqiH4Kh8eaQ @ 00:06:07]. Jensen sits between them with a hard floor of never shorter than 7 years. The pricing formulas also clash. Taylor goes 15% over ask, 10% down, and sets the payment at 40% of rent, a structure Dier says he had never heard anyone use. Dier’s own method is 10% over ask with the price divided by 360, shown on a $380,000 Cleveland example [GqiH4Kh8eaQ @ 00:08:06]. Operators choosing a lane are really choosing which number they let the seller win.

Practitioners do not agree on how real the due-on-sale threat is. Robert Crager says that in 25 years a lender has “never one time” called a loan due on him [q1drqFk-FH4 @ 00:08:16]. Pace Morby says the opposite happened to him “multiple times.” He insists the correct term is the acceleration clause and points students to roughly 5 hours of training on it [Ou7n95pTZFE @ 00:09:12]. Lex Levinrad treats it as a structuring problem. He says the loan can come due in 30 days and lists USDA, federal savings bank, and VA loans as exempt. He also walks the 1982 Garn-St Germain exceptions for divorce, death, and the inter vivos land trust. In that setup the seller is trustee and beneficiary, the buyer is successor trustee, and the seller then resigns, a setup he says courses sell for “$10,000” [YY7F8y8K0cU @ 00:04:41]. The assumption-versus-subject-to debate splits the same way. Crager argues that assuming costs full qualification with tax returns and that banks “simply will say no,” so subject-to wins on speed, rate, and seasoning [q1drqFk-FH4 @ 00:03:16]. Levinrad counters with a Port St. Lucie file where the bank let the buyer assume without points. One camp shrugs off the clause, one camp papers around it, and Morby trains on it as a known event.

The exit is the third fault line. Pace Morby says wholesaling “takes money out of the seller’s pocket.” He pushes students to “skip the line” and buy, citing the Tangs closing 24 deals in 12 months [X94W660WDh8 @ 00:15:30]. Flipping Mastery TV builds a $15,000 wholesale fee straight into its subject-to entry math. The fee sits next to an $8,000 commission, $4,000 for the TC and closing, and $5,000 to the seller, for $32,000 out of $192,000. That is a 16% entry fee, which still scores under its 25% ceiling [rYMNGajRMfo @ 00:02:27]. Lex Levinrad lists rental and assignment-fee wholesale as equal exits. Hold versus wrap is the second exit split. Ben Jensen says a wrap pays you three times but surrenders appreciation and cost segregation. So he holds in appreciating areas like McKinney and wraps older houses under about $300K [t96wzMUDN58 @ 00:15:28]. Morby’s hold case runs the other way on paper. His five-year math shows roughly $30K of cash flow, $340K growing to $475K at 7% appreciation, about $40K of loan paydown, depreciation, and a tax-free cash-out refinance [bKMcgnoYXfQ @ 00:35:56]. He even pays full retail, a move he calls “a very stupid thing to do,” when the debt takeover is $0 down. Pick the exit before the pitch, because it decides what you can concede.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Most subject-to deals break after the handshake, not on the call. Pace Morby’s 3932 W Myrtle file looked clean until title came back with two lawsuits, a lien, two wholesaler memorandums, and an illegal quitclaim. Clearing it took 2 months, an attorney, and another $5K from the gator. He says 99% of the title reports he sees show issues [X94W660WDh8 @ 00:27:19]. In his words, once you open escrow “this is where the challenges start” [X94W660WDh8 @ 00:27:35]. That is why he refuses to underwrite before escrow opens: he will comp and underwrite 100 houses to get one under contract. Ben Jensen hit the contract-side version on his subject-to wrap. He self-listed at $350K and drew a full-price, day-one offer with $100K down. He then caught the realtor trying to sneak in terms, so his rule is “read your contracts” [t96wzMUDN58 @ 00:21:13]. Lex Levinrad flags insurance as the quiet killer and says it “trips up 90%” of buyers. His fix is to keep the seller’s existing policy in force and add the trust as additional insured [YY7F8y8K0cU @ 00:08:36]. Budget time and gator money for the back end before you promise a seller a move-out date, because the paperwork, not the pitch, is where these deals stall.

Servicing is where cash leaks. kris haskins needed the seller’s SSN, an authorization to release, and a notarized limited power of attorney before PNC would talk to him. Once he was inside, he found the payment had moved from $1,229 to $1,077 because of an escrow re-analysis triggered by an insurance change [FybFcuS9T7s @ 00:13:01]. Worse, a separate $342 principal check landed in unapplied funds instead of reducing the balance. His fix is to send one larger check or to pay principal by phone, which carries no fee; he made a $1,551 principal payment that way [FybFcuS9T7s @ 00:16:43]. On the Virginia Beach pre-foreclosure he shows that the number you see is not the number you pay. Arrears ran about $37,000–38,000, yet the reinstatement came back at $46,000. With principal added, that was roughly $50,000 to get in, and the figures were only good until June 1st [DhOoZcypJCM @ 00:07:25]. Robert Crager’s rule closes the gap on the seller side: you have no control over the loan terms, so always pay the bank directly and send the seller proof [q1drqFk-FH4 @ 00:10:01]. Pace Morby runs the same discipline by logging into the seller’s Wells Fargo account himself. If you are not reading the statement monthly, the lender will rewrite your spread for you.

The final checks are economic. Ben Jensen warns that on a wrap you must vet buyers or face foreclosure and taking the house back. He adds that a single AC failure runs about $6K and that the buyer pool thins out above roughly $300,000 [t96wzMUDN58 @ 00:15:28]. His second deal shows another trap. The Airbnb figure was about $4K against long-term rent near $2,500, but the city made Airbnb difficult, and the wrap he sold instead spreads about $400/mo. Pace Morby opens one in-person video by calling arbitrage a “trash model.” He then works through a seller whose $2,138 payment sits above a $1,800 US average rent. He floats PadSplit at about $125/week, around $750/mo, before landing on a traditional rental [1GjR0GDWoyo @ 00:14:30]. Maximilian Dier’s live test exposed the agent-side trap. The agent said seller financing was possible but only “shortterm,” with a refi out within 12 months, at a time Dier cited 7–8% rates [GqiH4Kh8eaQ @ 00:10:50]. kris haskins adds the honesty check that keeps zero-equity, high-payment wraps alive: “Be honest” and do not pull a switcheroo on the seller [X4XzY55e_n4 @ 00:18:42]. He also reminds operators that real estate is not passive. Run rent against payment before the second call, not after.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I turn a seller's low-rate mortgage into monthly spread income by wrapping it to an end buyer, and when should I wrap versus simply hold subject-to?
chapters.title: Wrap Arbitrage: Selling on a Wrap for Spread, Down Payment, and Cash Flow
chapters.subtitle: Subject-to wraparounds, $1,000/month wrap case studies, low-equity owner-finance wraps, mirror wrap vs. sub-to, wrap vs. lease option vs. contract for deed, underwriting spreadsheets, private-lender recycling, and wrapping buyers banks turn down
chapters.executive_summary: Wrap arbitrage practitioners agree the money is in the spread: buy or hold a low-rate underlying loan, then sell to a non-bankable buyer at a higher price and rate. Dom Inglese wraps a 2.75% Tampa sub-to at 7% for $400,000, banking $10,000 at entry on a $50,000 down payment; Grant Kemp turns $20,000 of equity into $142,377 of total collections; Nick Disney carries notes around 10.9% on private money. Operators structure the payment first, sell the monthly number instead of the rate, and prefer principal over interest. They split on servicing, with Horne Real Estate Law always using a servicer while Nick Disney pays lenders directly, and on exit, with Creative Finance Playbook declining to sell on wraps at all and preferring lease options for depreciation.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus — Spread, Non-Bankable Buyers, and Seller Security
paragraphs: The money in this play is the spread, and the practitioners say it plainly. Vena Jones Cox tells her class that most of the money made in long-term real estate investing is made on spread, and she traces wraps back to her father using them in the 1960s [jeHouEguhhE @ 00:32:32]. Grant Kemp of Propelio TV defines a wraparound as any time you finance someone a subordinate lien at a higher price or payment than the underlying lien, which means the operator profits from both a price markup and a rate markup [pCK7ihJF_-Q @ 00:00:34]. Dom Inglese runs the same logic on his Tampa portfolio: he holds the underlying mortgage at 3%, sells to a non-qualifying buyer at 8% with 10% down, and keeps the difference between 8 and 3% as cash flow [VRUDR8FXNo0 @ 00:05:03]. On a separate Tampa sub-to locked at 2.75% almost three years ago, he wraps the buyer at 7%, frames the rate as in line or even a little lower than bank rates, and notes his low-rate loan amortizes faster so the equity spread keeps widening every month [Lv34MZLHg1I @ 00:04:32]. Three income streams stack in every deal: the down payment, the monthly spread, and the back-end principal.

Every practitioner selling on a wrap is hunting the same buyer: someone who can carry a monthly payment but cannot or will not get through a bank. Dom Inglese calls them penalty box buyers, ITIN holders and people paid in cash who are simply not bankable, and he sells his Seminole Heights block house as-is to that pool [StKrDLiCONM @ 00:04:00]. In his homeownership pitch he widens the net to buyers with cash-heavy income, a recent missed payment, or no way to bring the 40% a bank wants, while still vetting each one for affordability before he sells [VRUDR8FXNo0 @ 00:01:38]. Philip Louden of WrapAcademy targets first-generation Americans, a buyer pool he credits with a trillion dollars in spending power, along with 1099 earners [oGD3QKECaGk @ 00:03:04]. Nick Disney, fifteen years into the business out of San Antonio, sells at or under $200,000, runs credit through an RMLO, and reports scores that often come back NA [DAhcIhHIoI0 @ 00:05:24]. The consensus is blunt: the wrap buyer is defined by bank rejection, not by inability to pay, which is exactly why the operator can charge a rate well above the underlying loan and still close fast. The pool is deep precisely because banks keep saying no.

The practitioners also agree on why the wrap beats a naked subject-to when the operator sits in the middle. Ron LeGrand, with 40 years buying, says he always takes the wrap, that the document type makes no difference even in a mortgage state like Florida, and that the wrap payment matches the underlying so total debt stays $275,000 rather than doubling [-3xVEOBXFzc @ 00:03:38]. Mr No FluFF reduces the difference to remedy: under subject-to the seller can only sue, while a wrap pledges the property through a deed of trust so the seller can get an attorney and foreclose, which he calls very fast and very economic [RPbZyS3NPFI @ 00:00:17]. Caleb Christopher frames the same split as court versus process, warning that neither party wins 100% in court, whereas a right to foreclose lets you bring the hammer down and just follow process [UBngwrCrCxM @ 00:09:54]. Jen and Joe of Creative Finance Playbook add that the recorded note lets the seller foreclose and, together with the HUD statement, proves to future lenders who is actually paying the underlying loan [u3lV-kVx-LU @ 00:12:09]. Mr No FluFF's summary holds across the group: a wrap is a little more complex, but it gives the seller more security.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers — Pricing, Payment Design, and Deal Math
paragraphs: Dom Inglese's Tampa wrap is the cleanest unit-economics template. His mortgage balance was $290,000 and he had $40,000 in, for $330,000 all-in; he priced the wrap at $400,000, took $50,000 down from his buyer Tom, and carried a $350,000 note, which put him positive $10,000 before the first spread payment ever landed [Lv34MZLHg1I @ 00:02:59]. His Johnny's-house example runs the same formula: buy subject-to at $300,000 on a $280,000 balance at 3% with $20,000 of his own cash, resell at the typical 10 to 15% markup for $330,000 with $33,000 down, and wrap at 7 to 8% for $13,000 net at entry plus the rate spread, both loans 30-year fixed [VRUDR8FXNo0 @ 00:03:11]. On the Seminole Heights block house he carries about $250,000 of debt at 3.125% with roughly $40,000 in, for about $290,000 all-in, and targets a buyer rate of 7.5 to 8% to clear about $1,000 a month net, with a rental fallback at $2,300 to $2,500 for $600 to $800 gross [StKrDLiCONM @ 00:10:41]. Nick Disney buys at 75 cents or less, often 70, averaging $120,000 purchases with 85 to 90 cents all-in [DAhcIhHIoI0 @ 00:15:10]. The entry profit is the down payment minus cash in; everything after is spread.

Payment design is where the operators control the spread. Ron LeGrand sets the outgoing wrap payment first, $2,700 in his example and as high as you want it, strips out taxes and insurance such as $400 to reach $2,300, then matches principal and interest from the amortization schedule; on the contract he writes the $450,000 seller carryback in paragraph 2B as $2,700 including taxes and insurance with principal and interest left to be determined [qGlXYUEjyr8 @ 00:00:59]. Ron uses a five-year example term on the schedule. Caleb Christopher runs it through his Creative Underwriter Spreadsheet: a $155,000 underlying at 4.75% over 30 years pays 808, while the same balance at 7.5% pays 1,083 for a $275 spread, and pricing the house at 250 with 30 down adds another 65,000 at 7.5% worth $454, for $729 a month total [UOyoE5Fc7VE @ 00:01:03]. He tells operators not to talk about interest rate at all and to sell the monthly payment instead [UOyoE5Fc7VE @ 00:02:24]. Grant Kemp pushes operators to prefer principal over interest, because $90,000 at 6% over 30 years produces $539.60 a month, the same payment as $64,000 at 9%, and any sale, refinance or note sale pays off principal only [pCK7ihJF_-Q @ 00:18:50].

Grant Kemp's resale case shows how all three income streams compound. He sells a $100,000 house with 10%, or $10,000, down, carries a $90,000 note at 9.5% over 30 years at $756 a month, and nets $7,000 from the down payment after a $3,000 agent fee; the spread is $245 a month for 22 years, about $65,000, then the full $756 for the last 8 years, about $73,000, for $142,377 total on $20,000 of equity, which he discounts by a third to a half for time value of money [pCK7ihJF_-Q @ 00:15:27]. Nick Disney layers private money underneath: a $50,000 private loan at 10% interest-only costs about $400, while the buyer's $100,000 at 11% pays about $900, leaving a roughly $500 spread [DAhcIhHIoI0 @ 00:25:42]. Scott Horne's firm reports Andrew Webb wrapping a 3% loan at 5.99% for underwater sellers, against roughly 7% from banks, pushing price to 410 to 415 on a $400,000 house with $25,000 down [00RujvVfDRc @ 00:08:37]. The firm layers balloons at 5, 7 or 10 years or step-ups to 7% in year 3 and 8% in year 5, and notes that note buyers want a higher rate and more equity [00RujvVfDRc @ 00:12:48].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is which side of the wrap you sit on. Grant Kemp at Propelio TV draws a hard line: buy subject-to, sell on a wrap, because buying with a wraparound wastes money and selling subject-to leaves money on the table [pCK7ihJF_-Q @ 00:04:06]. Dom Inglese runs that sell-side play in Tampa, holding a 2.75% subject-to loan and wrapping a buyer named Tom at 7% on a $400,000 price; Tom's $50,000 down against Dom's $40,000 in put Dom $10,000 ahead before the first spread payment [Lv34MZLHg1I @ 00:03:24]. Jen and Joe at Creative Finance Playbook run the mirror image. They do not sell on wraps; they buy on wraps to keep depreciation and appreciation for themselves, then sell through lease options or rent-to-own rather than carrying paper as the lender [u3lV-kVx-LU @ 00:15:17]. Ron LeGrand also wraps on the buy side: the land trust gives the seller a wrap for exactly what is owed, the wrap payment matches the underlying payment, and total debt stays at the $275k loan balance rather than doubling [-3xVEOBXFzc @ 00:04:37]. That leaves operators choosing between two income models: collect spread and down payment as the lender on the sell side, or keep the ownership benefits and exit through leasing on the buy side.

Payment plumbing splits the room. Scott Horne's firm always routes wraps through a loan servicer, framing it as protection against seller fraud on deals the firm and First Option Title close out of DFW and San Antonio [00RujvVfDRc @ 00:04:43]. Nick Disney, who funds San Antonio deals with interest-only private money, often from self-directed IRAs, pays that private lender directly with no servicer sitting in the middle [DAhcIhHIoI0 @ 00:25:14]. Caleb Christopher takes a third lane: never let the seller act as a pass-through for the buyer's money, and either pay the original lender directly or run funds through a servicing clearing house that sends receipts, so every party can prove the underlying loan is being paid [UBngwrCrCxM @ 00:05:36]. Jen and Joe skip servicing companies on their own wraps, yet flip the rule for the other structure, telling anyone buying subject-to that a servicing company is required [u3lV-kVx-LU @ 00:45:19]. The disagreement comes down to control and proof. Horne treats a third party as standard protection on every single file, Disney keeps a direct line to a lender relationship built on recycled capital, and Caleb's priority is a paper trail that keeps the seller's credit protected while the buyer pays.

Pricing philosophy diverges just as hard. Caleb Christopher tells operators not to talk about interest rate at all; sell the monthly payment, benchmark it against local rent, and leave enough room in the down payment for rehab [UOyoE5Fc7VE @ 00:02:24]. Grant Kemp argues for weighting the note toward principal: $90k at 6% over 30 years produces $539.60 a month, the same payment as $64k at 9%, and because a sale, refinance or note sale only pays off principal, the bigger balance wins at exit [pCK7ihJF_-Q @ 00:18:50]. Andrew Webb's underwater-seller play, presented by Scott Horne's firm, deliberately prices below the bank, wrapping a 3% loan at 5.99% when banks are quoting roughly 7%, so the buyer gets a cheaper payment on a low-equity house [00RujvVfDRc @ 00:06:52]. Inside Vena Jones Cox's class the hosts disagree with each other: Bill Cook avoids 0% seller notes, while Vena does almost nothing but zero percent seller-held mortgages, offering terms like $100,000 at $1,000 a month for 100 months [jeHouEguhhE @ 01:31:36]. Underneath all four positions sits the same lever: the spread can come from rate, from price, or from principal, and each practitioner picks the one the buyer and seller will accept.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is pricing a wrap the market will not carry. Jen and Joe walked away from a Sarasota deal where the wrap payment would run $5,500 a month at 6.75% against $3,400 rents, and they watch other investors wrap at 8% for $6,000 a month in $3,500 rent areas, deals that simply sit [u3lV-kVx-LU @ 00:18:26]. Their Cape Coral case failed the same check from the expense side: taxes and insurance ate $2,500 of a $4,800 payment, leaving no cash flow despite $450,000 of equity and a 2.99% loan [u3lV-kVx-LU @ 00:20:25]. Dom Inglese keeps a rental fallback on the Seminole Heights house: if the wrap buyer never materializes, the house rents at $2,300 to $2,500 for $600 to $800 in gross cash flow against a roughly $1,700 payment [StKrDLiCONM @ 00:11:20]. Grant Kemp's check runs on the back end: a $100,000 sale with $10,000 down totals $142,377 in payments on $20,000 of equity, but Grant discounts that by a third to a half for time value of money, and the $10,000 down nets only $7,000 after a $3,000 agent fee [pCK7ihJF_-Q @ 00:16:10]. Headline spread totals overstate what an operator actually banks, so every number gets stress-tested against rent, carrying costs and timing before the deal is signed.

Default handling is where naked subject-to bites hardest. Mr No FluFF warns that on a subject-to deal the only way a seller can take the collateral back is by suing, while a wrap's deed of trust lets the seller foreclose in 30 or 60 days or whatever the terms allow [oHV9AiZdwro @ 00:00:43]. Caleb Christopher spells out how those lawsuits end: neither party wins 100% in court, there is generally some sort of compromise, whereas a holder with the right to foreclose can bring the hammer down and just follow process [UBngwrCrCxM @ 00:09:39]. Ron LeGrand flags the damage that lands on the seller under subject-to: the loan stays on the seller's debt ratio and blocks new loans the seller may want later [-3xVEOBXFzc @ 00:05:22]. Scott Horne's Texas timeline shows what a clean foreclosure costs in time: a 20-day cure notice, then posting 21 days before the first Tuesday, about 43 days total with title back in roughly 60 [00RujvVfDRc @ 00:22:59]. The pattern across all four: subject-to saves paperwork up front but leaves the seller with a lawsuit and a damaged debt ratio, while the wrap's recorded note and deed of trust turn a default into a defined, calendar-driven process the note holder controls.

The remaining traps are operational. Jen and Joe list the mistakes that sink first wraps: going DIY, leaning on a transaction coordinator, using any title company that will take the file, and taking the deed outside a land trust [u3lV-kVx-LU @ 00:47:33]. Ross Badri at Make Your Money Multiply, working a $1,249,000 Ventura County example, lays out the risk stack sellers inherit: the original lender can call the loan due when title transfers even if payments stay current, the seller stays liable, California deals carry DRE disclosures and title or escrow hurdles, and the structure is wrong for unsophisticated sellers [upiVxcM_yIM @ 00:01:40]. Scott Horne puts the due-on-sale fear in hard numbers: 13 cases across 10,000 deals closed [00RujvVfDRc @ 00:19:04]. Philip Louden warns that a contract for deed keeps insurance and code problems on the investor's books, can turn into a contested eviction once a buyer has put around $30,000 down, and violates DSCR loans, a conflict Louden ties to the Jackie strategy and its 65-plus deals [oGD3QKECaGk @ 00:08:23]. Every one of these traps sits outside the spread math, so the paperwork, title partner and holding entity have to be chosen before the first payment is ever collected.

chapters.question_prompt: What is seller financing, how do sellers benefit, and how do practitioners pitch and paper it on houses, businesses, and vehicles?
chapters.title: Seller Finance Fundamentals: Making the Seller the Bank
chapters.subtitle: Seller finance vs. bank loans, seller motivations and benefits, seller finance paperwork, Texas owner-finance steps, off-market 0% marketplaces, and seller-financing businesses, trucks, and an Escalade
chapters.executive_summary: Pace Morby, Key & Capital and Greg Schwartz agree that seller finance turns a free-and-clear owner into the bank, negotiated on four terms: price, down payment, interest rate and length. Pace pays the seller's number in exchange for terms: Susan's mobile home closed at $110K, principal-only, $10K down split into two $5K installments, $375/mo, while the best cash offer was $57K. Mario's 30-unit building traded at $3M, $0 down, 4%, 50 years, no balloon, against a $1.9M cash offer. Pace prices assignment fees at $2K per $100/mo net cash flow and targets 30%+ cash-on-cash. Key & Capital counters that a 0% seller note is not clever, models 6-9% rates with 5-7 year balloons, and flags due-on-sale and seasoning traps. Greg Schwartz demands credit and background checks; Pace verifies income only.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator here frames seller finance the same way: the owner stops being a landlord and becomes the bank, and the deal is built on four levers, not one. Pace Morby lists them as purchase price, down payment, interest rate and length of time, first proving it with an iPhone demo where the market offer was $550 and he bought at $800 as $80/mo for 10 months [_M0q3Da-vxU @ 00:26:22]. Greg Schwartz in Bryan-College Station runs the identical checklist, telling operators to start with the down payment at 20, 10 or 5% before touching rate, amortization or monthly payment, then choose between a 3, 5 or 7 year balloon for liquidity or a 5, 7 or 10 year prepayment penalty for steady income [_xN91ltYUa0 @ 00:01:43]. The consensus on seller psychology is equally tight. Pace separates Sub2 sellers, driven by pain such as divorce or no equity, from seller-finance sellers, driven by gain: they want more than the market will bear, often after pulling the house off the market [8VNf8TfmufA @ 00:00:00]. The target list follows directly. Roughly 30% of properties are owned free and clear, Sub2 lists filter for 60%+ equity, and seller-finance lists should aim at 100% equity [MeNrueZIYeE @ 00:31:09].

The second pillar is that terms beat price. Pace's line is that the value of a property is never the purchase price but what you can do with it, and he taught it to Susan through his F-150 story: a truck Kelley Blue Book valued at $5K sat on Craigslist at $10K for 3 months with no calls until he added 'will take payments,' then sold for $12.5K with $1K down and $350/mo [6FXApQ1y2KE @ 00:10:17]. The same logic drives his claim that creative finance pays the seller more money every time; he says he has never seen a creative transaction that was not a win for the seller, the buyer and any agent involved, while in a cash deal only the buyer wins [8VNf8TfmufA @ 00:01:26]. On the masterclass, Pace puts the contrast in numbers: on a $200K ARV, wholesalers pay $110-130K and only about 5% of sellers accept, while creative finance pays 80-100 cents on the dollar [-E2cCPmM_Q0 @ 00:03:49]. His Leilani case shows why distressed owners say yes: a zero-down VA loan, a husband who died 30 days after closing, an 11% commission hit if she listed, so Pace took the $1,800 payment subject-to and now rents it for $2,800 [Teh6C2LGk8g @ 00:05:56].

Protection is the third point of agreement, and every speaker lands on the same paper trail. Pace says the deal structure is how you protect the seller and that the main protection is the buyer's profit; on top of that he hires a servicing company such as Westar, Evergreen or Del Toro at about $100 setup and $17 per payment drafted 5 days early, writes a new insurance policy listing the seller as additional insured, and records both the 1-1.5 page promissory note and the 80-90 page deed of trust [w1wq3uZtNx8 @ 01:06:54]. In his paperwork Q&A he draws the line on public record: the purchase and sale agreement is never recorded, but the deed, deed of trust and note are [IdhS21bvT_o @ 00:29:24]. Greg Schwartz mirrors it for Texas: a promissory note plus a recorded deed of trust, lower closing costs, a local attorney, and payments made direct or through a servicer at $30-40 [_xN91ltYUa0 @ 00:06:17]. Key & Capital adds title insurance and a recorded deed of trust to the checklist and tells sellers to use a licensed originator before carrying paper [dzuLMB2Szxc @ 00:11:14]. Where they agree most is the order: structure first, so the buyer cash flows, then the paperwork locks it.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The call script is codified. Pace records every appointment, then pivots with one line: 'I would be willing to come up to your price if you would give me terms,' followed by the F-150 story and a reframe that he will upgrade the seller from landlord to the bank [MeNrueZIYeE @ 00:04:27]. When the conversation turns to buyer risk, he says 'abducted by aliens' instead of 'hit by a bus.' He never sends the first offer. The seller names terms, and when Susan asked for $20K down at 8%, he answered that he was probably not her buyer and stepped back [MeNrueZIYeE @ 00:12:32]. The rebuilt structure on her mobile home: $110K, principal-only, $10K down paid as $5K now and $5K after six months, seller-paid closing costs, inherited tenants at about $1,650 rent throwing off roughly $1K/mo net that funds the down payment, and a $375/mo note matching her RV spot cost [6FXApQ1y2KE @ 00:14:14]. The vocabulary matters. Pace says he never writes 'zero percent seller finance' in any offer; every offer says principal-only payments [IdhS21bvT_o @ 01:02:52]. On the masterclass version the term runs 20 years, the best cash offer was $57K, and the house is now worth about $233K, roughly $120K of appreciation in 3 years.

The unit economics are just as specific. Pace's deal test: the terms must beat a bank asking 30-40% down, then the cash-on-cash return has to clear the bar; investors want a 12% minimum, he wants 30%+, because the lower the down payment, the higher the return [MeNrueZIYeE @ 00:23:58]. Wholesalers get paid off a cash-flow formula: $2K of assignment fee per $100/mo of net cash flow, or $5K per $100 at 0% interest, which with average cash flow above $500/mo puts the average fee above $10K [MeNrueZIYeE @ 00:25:18]. The ceiling is the biggest assignment fee of his life: $210K, paid as the buyer, on 30 Texas units at $3M, no money down, 4%, 50 years, no balloon, about 10x the $21K/mo cash flow, when the wholesaler's cash number was $1.7M [-E2cCPmM_Q0 @ 00:07:45]. Only 20-30% of opportunities need no money; the rest get funded by partners or private lenders sitting in second position at 8-12%, where $10K at 10% costs about $80/mo. Pace calls it financing your financing, and on a Chandler flip the interest sat in escrow. His all-in entry cost, down payment and closing costs together, averages about 8%, against the 30-35% down a bank demands, roughly $80-100K on a $300K house [_M0q3Da-vxU @ 00:43:32].

Term length and balloon mechanics are where Pace protects his downside and the seller's number. His default is a payment based on 30 years with a 10-year balloon, backed by a balloon-extension clause that automatically renews for 5 years if the property doesn't appraise at the purchase price [MeNrueZIYeE @ 00:34:02]. The Jillian deal in Atlanta shows the full stack: $1.1M, $0 down, no payments for 6 months, then about $6K/mo at 3% on a 30-year amortization with a 10-year balloon, plus a clause requiring her to buy him a steak dinner; five years later Airbnb was outlawed, he sold at $1.5M and rolled the $400K gain into an RV park [w1wq3uZtNx8 @ 00:35:23]. Key & Capital benchmarks what conventional seller-carry looks like: 5-20% down with a 10% median, 6-9% rates or 3-8% for investors, balloons at 3-10 years and usually 5-7, closing in 7-21 days against 30-45 for a bank, with no prepayment penalty [dzuLMB2Szxc @ 00:07:34]. Greg Schwartz closes the loop on collections: the buyer pays the seller directly or through a servicer at $30-40, and the note ends by refinance, sale, buyout, the balloon coming due, or foreclosure, which he calls easier than you would think in Texas [_xN91ltYUa0 @ 00:07:28].

callout.title: Script Lines and Structure Moves That Close Terms Deals
callout.body: The small word choices and sequencing moves the practitioners use to get sellers to carry paper on their terms.
items: Say 'principal only payments,' never 'zero percent,' in every written offer and on every seller call [Pace Morby — IdhS21bvT_o @ 01:02:52].

sop_steps.action: Pull owners with 100% equity and source seller-finance listings from Landwatch, the MLS and owner-finance aggregator sites.
sop_steps.detail: Roughly 30% of properties are free and clear; seller-finance lists target 100% equity versus 60%+ for Sub2, and Landwatch showed 25-30 seller-finance listings in Kalispell alone [Flipping Mastery TV — MeNrueZIYeE @ 00:31:09].

sop_steps.title: Run the pivot call
sop_steps.action: Record the appointment, deliver the terms line, tell the F-150 story, and reframe the seller from landlord to bank.

sop_steps.title: Structure the four terms
sop_steps.action: Give the seller price, then win down payment, rate and a long enough term; anchor on 30-year amortization with a 10-year balloon and an extension clause.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in seller-finance pricing is the interest rate. Pace Morby writes principal-only paper and refuses to say zero percent out loud: "I don't ever say zero percent seller finance in any of my offers we always say principal only payments" [IdhS21bvT_o @ 01:02:52]. His logic is that a seller charging 4% simply gets a lower price, Pace's illustration being $60K instead of $90K, and that a refinance would wipe out the interest they expected anyway, so 0% locks the seller's number [8VNf8TfmufA @ 00:04:37]. To back the tax side, he cites a CPA who has sold more than 40 properties at 0% for 1.25 times retail value, while admitting he is unsure of the IRS guideline he quotes for notes over $150K [IdhS21bvT_o @ 01:01:44]. Key & Capital runs the opposite playbook. Their Dallas duplex math puts the seller at 6% against a 7.32% bank loan, saving the buyer $210 a month, and they quote typical seller rates of 6-9%, or 3-8% for investors. They flag the mid-term AFR at 4.35% and land the counterpunch bluntly: "So, a 0% seller note is not clever" [dzuLMB2Szxc @ 00:11:35]. Same deal shape, two completely different answers to where the seller actually gets paid.

Term length is the second fault line. Pace pushes amortization as long as the seller will tolerate: the Mario deal ran $3M at 4% over 50 years with no balloon, the seller himself proposing 50 after Pace pitched 40, and Pace calls a 3-year payoff too short for the buyer to win [w1wq3uZtNx8 @ 01:55:13] [8VNf8TfmufA @ 00:06:31]. His default fallback is a 30-year amortization with a 10-year balloon plus a balloon-extension clause that auto-renews five years if the property won't appraise at the purchase price. Key & Capital treats the balloon as the first of three traps and describes market norms of balloons at 3-10 years, usually 5-7, with the duplex example coming due at five years with roughly $223K still owed [dzuLMB2Szxc @ 00:05:35]. Their defenses overlap with Pace's (an extension clause, a longer balloon, a refinance plan, or a fully amortizing note) but their floor is far lower: never accept a balloon shorter than 12 months. Greg Schwartz frames the choice as a menu rather than a rule: a 3, 5 or 7-year balloon suits buyers who need liquidity or plan a BRRRR refinance, while a 5, 7 or 10-year prepayment penalty suits sellers who want steady income [_xN91ltYUa0 @ 00:01:43].

Risk tolerance on the underlying loan and the paperwork splits the camp again. Pace says the due-on-sale clause has been called 10 times in roughly 40,000 deals, calls it "really easy to overcome," and keeps a deed-back plus a pre-signed lease option as the remedy [EO9EtMTTjm4 @ 01:25:45]. Key & Capital lists due-on-sale under Garn-St Germain as trap number two, alongside Fannie Mae's 12-month seasoning on refinances that pay off a seller note [dzuLMB2Szxc @ 00:08:31]. On recording, Pace records the promissory note and deed of trust on standard seller-finance closes, yet on a building carrying an SBA 504 loan he used a contract for deed with the deed left unrecorded in a safety deposit box so nobody would know ownership had transferred [p0ukMOdzoAc @ 00:11:34]. Key & Capital calls for title insurance and a recorded deed of trust; Greg Schwartz likewise records the deed of trust. Buyer vetting diverges just as hard: on vehicles Pace runs "verification of income" only, no credit check, with bankruptcies and divorces acceptable, while Greg Schwartz sets income, credit and a background check as the minimum and notes full Dodd-Frank underwriting costs over $1,000 [_xN91ltYUa0 @ 00:05:11]. Pace's view is that the buyer's profit, not the paperwork, is the seller's main protection.
