sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Pace's own origin story is the first failure mode on the table. As a renovation contractor for Opendoor, Offerpad and Zillow, he financed a flipper's rehabs, putting up $100K and getting roughly $105K back at sale; over four years the unpaid balances ran into the millions [_M0q3Da-vxU @ 00:01:30]. He then liquidated his rentals to pour another $700K in, and the flipper filed bankruptcy owing about $16M. His lawsuit rule from his seller-finance teaching is blunt: "The number one deterrent for lawsuits is making sure you're not the one that writes the first check" [w1wq3uZtNx8 @ 01:28:46]. Lease options, a structure he says he is obsessed with, burned him once when heirs contested the contract and it cost $7K to sue. Shena's Mesa duplex shows the investor-side version of the trap: bought in 2021 with 30% down, one unit vacant for months, listed by an agent for about four months without a sale, until a Sub2 student offered back the 30% plus payments in exchange for 0% interest [8VNf8TfmufA @ 00:13:52]. Pace frames that as the norm rather than the exception, claiming 50% of investors throw the house back on the market within a year [8VNf8TfmufA @ 00:14:52].

The seller side carries its own set of traps. Pace names the biggest downfall in seller finance as sellers wanting a very high price, and his workaround is to let the seller state terms first and walk when they are wrong: Susan opened at $20K down and 8%, and Pace answered "probably not your buyer" and stepped back [MeNrueZIYeE @ 00:12:32]. Sellers who try to stay landlords instead face his Arizona eviction clock: late in month one, eviction filed in month two, tenant out by months three or four, repairs in five and six, marketing in seven, a new tenant in month eight, roughly seven months of payments with no rent [8VNf8TfmufA @ 00:09:13]. Key & Capital adds the regulatory and tax drag that sellers routinely miss. Dodd-Frank tiers allow one property a year, up to three with a fully amortizing note, and more than five makes the seller a creditor; §453(i) depreciation recapture is taxed in year one even under installment treatment [dzuLMB2Szxc @ 00:11:14]. On the 1031 path, Pace warns that the 90-day pressure of a strict exchange lets replacement-property sellers exploit the clock, and he prefers a delayed 1031 with cost segregation [w1wq3uZtNx8 @ 00:44:10].

Vehicles and businesses add operational failure points that real estate doesn't. On the Escalade, Grant's balance exceeded market value and a Facebook Marketplace listing at payoff drew zero responses; attorney Sean Sinclair spent about $3,000 of research to find a vehicle cannot be bought subject-to in North Carolina, forcing a $0-down lease option instead [o3cjfzx5Ykk @ 00:11:15]. Turo cash flow cut both ways: Angelo's Turo projection showed about $2,000 a month on a roughly $1,000 payment, but Grant stopped renting after a Denali renter smoked weed in the car and Pace rejected Turo as not worth the risk [o3cjfzx5Ykk @ 00:08:40]. Pace also flags that a stolen-vehicle history can trigger a salvage title or make the car uninsurable, killing Turo use, so Carfax gets pulled first [B5EMtjV6RJM @ 00:18:40]. On businesses, brokers who refuse to submit offers get waited out, and Pace warns that buying a business is not passive until people are hired in place and the operation is automated; the Alaska carpet cleaner ran roughly $6.5K weekly payroll and 15 interviews a day in peak season [p0ukMOdzoAc @ 00:01:24]. And on institutional sellers, his verdict is short: don't waste time sending Opendoor creative offers.

callout.title: Kill-Switch Checks Before You Carry or Take a Note
callout.body: Four hard stops pulled from losses and near-misses the practitioners reported firsthand. Clear every one before signing.
items: Never be the party that writes the first check into a seller-finance deal; Pace calls that the number one deterrent for lawsuits [Pace Morby — w1wq3uZtNx8 @ 01:28:46].
Pull Carfax before carrying any vehicle note; a stolen-vehicle history can mean a salvage title or an uninsurable car that cannot go on Turo [Pace Morby — B5EMtjV6RJM @ 00:18:40].
Confirm state vehicle law before structuring subject-to on a car; North Carolina blocked it and forced a lease option after roughly $3,000 of attorney research [Pace Morby — o3cjfzx5Ykk @ 00:11:15].
Refuse any balloon shorter than 12 months and build in an extension clause, refinance plan, or fully amortizing note [Key & Capital — dzuLMB2Szxc @ 00:10:38].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I structure and underwrite creative deals, including sub-to/seller-finance hybrids, so they cash flow and hold up on paper?
chapters.title: Structuring and Underwriting Creative Deals: Hybrids and the Morby Method
chapters.subtitle: Sub-to + seller-finance hybrids, no-money-down structures, the Morby Method, multifamily creative finance, judging whether terms are good, underwriting wraps and sub-to, wrap drafting for consumer buyers, deed of trust vs. contract for deed, and a first-deal cost lesson
chapters.executive_summary: Pace Morby, James Heller, Kevin Cho and the Flipping Mastery crew run the hybrid the same way: take the existing low-rate loan subject-to, then carry the seller's equity on a separate 0% or near-0% seller note, with private money in third position to fund the entry fee. Street numbers anchor it: Heller's Colorado Springs townhouse at 146,000 on 1.5% with $400/month and a 10-year balloon; Kevin's 381,000 duplex at 4.25% sub-to plus 0% equity; Pace's $100k note at $375 for 240 months netting $925/month. The Morby Method swaps seller carryback for seller ownership in the buyer's LLC when the seller's cash-down demand cannot be negotiated away. Disagreement centers on wraps and balloons: Pace says acquire on hybrid and dispo on wrap, Fusion Notes demands Dodd-Frank underwriting and avoids balloons, and Landlord Dropout warns the underlying payment never stops.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The hybrid is a two-layer buy: the existing loan stays in place subject-to, and the seller's equity gets carried back on a separate seller-finance note. Pace Morby lays out a Georgia example with roughly 150 taken subject-to plus roughly 120 seller-financed, $0 down, 0% interest, at $300 a month [-IIDN2AQQsg @ 00:00:13], and on Flipping Mastery TV he puts hybrids at about 15% of his creative deals [6Bdxz-HKeFI @ 00:02:31]. The decision rule is equity-driven. Pace says flatly that if the seller has no equity, the deal is a sub-to [pvgEqb4r4gw @ 00:06:01]. The hybrid lives in the middle, where a cheap existing loan is worth preserving but the seller still holds real equity they want paid. James Heller's Colorado Springs townhouse fits that pocket exactly: a 360,000 ask against a 194 mortgage at 2.99%, leaving 166,000 of equity that he refused to hand over in cash because it made no sense for the deal [nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:03:31]. His answer was to keep the 2.99% loan in place and finance the gap with the sellers on a slow, low-rate note. The townhouse had sat about 60 days on the MLS and cash offers came in under the sellers' number, which is the exact friction a hybrid is built to dissolve.

Every operator here opens the seller conversation the same way: find out what the money is actually for, then trade price for terms. Pace teaches to always start with cash, never with creative finance, and to ask every seller why they haven't sold yet [pvgEqb4r4gw @ 00:02:35]; his Janie Munson lesson, find the bunnies, means locating the seller's real problem before structuring anything. Heller's key question was what the sellers planned to do with the proceeds, and the answer was savings or a CD, which made a 0%-to-low-rate note an easy swap for money that would have sat idle [nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:01:13]. Pace runs the same trade on a straight seller-finance rental: he paid Susan full retail at $100k when wholesalers were sitting at $60-70k, and told her that if she gave him terms he would give her the 100,000 she wanted [Ke0nzzYXEfk @ 00:01:23]. Transparency closes it. Heller told his sellers he was making the property a rental and would lose money every month if he paid more, then showed them the math [nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:08:01]. The pattern holds across all of them: full or near-full price satisfies the seller's number, while the payment, rate, and timing are engineered around the rent.

The paper underneath the hybrid follows a consensus too. Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network lists the acquisition routes side by side: a seller-financed note and deed of trust, a wrap of the seller's first lien, subject-to with a second lien back to the seller, or third-party second and third liens, and he insists the note and deed of trust both describe the underlying debt so any future title or mortgage company knows its lien position [it6vSh38OhY @ 00:00:54]. The Real Estate Lawyer frames the deed of trust as a three-party security instrument, borrower, lender, and a lender-designated trustee, summed up as if you don't pay you don't stay [2PWuaqjQVgc @ 00:01:07]. Pace's lien education on Flipping Mastery TV adds the ordering rule: priority follows the recorded date, taxes supersede all liens, and you don't want to sit in second unless something is in it for you and you understand the higher risk [pvgEqb4r4gw @ 00:25:10]. On the Kevin Cho duplex, the private lender sits in third behind the sub-to and the seller carry, and the pitch is the same safety net used with sellers: if the buyer defaults, they can take over the whole asset, equity and cash flow included [Yw9I--p2Ef8 @ 00:05:24].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Heller's negotiation is the cleanest worked example of the hybrid math. He opened at 0%, principal-only, and offered $400 a month; the sellers wanted more, floated annual payments of 4,800, and then asked for at least 1.5% so they could sell the note later [nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:04:48]. The final terms: the sellers knocked 20k off, the seller note landed at 146,000 at 1.5%, $400 a month on roughly a 40-year amortization, with a 10-year balloon [nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:05:26]. Against the 1,138 PITI on the 2.99% loan and about 1,900 in rent, he reports roughly $150 a month of cash flow, likely eaten by operating expenses, but on a zero-down, no-repair, rent-ready townhouse [nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:06:23]. Kevin Cho's duplex runs the same skeleton across two units: a 381,000 price, the existing loan taken sub-to at 4.25%, and the seller's equity financed at 0% with no balloon [Yw9I--p2Ef8 @ 00:02:06]. PITI of about 1,733 plus roughly 250 of seller carry puts the debt stack near $2,000, and the plan is midterm rentals for travel nurses on three-month stays, with the 3/1 front unit at 2,400 to 2,500 covering the full foundational cost so the back unit becomes the profit.

Funding the entry fee is where the third lien comes in. Pace defines the entry fee as all the cash a deal needs and says about 70% of his deals require private money, with the other 30% closing without it [pvgEqb4r4gw @ 00:32:52]. On Kevin's duplex that meant about $30k of private money and none of his own: Maricella lent $40k at 12% for 24 months in third position at $400 a month, leaving roughly $10k for the first payment and cleanup, and pushing the foundational monthly cost to $2,400 [Yw9I--p2Ef8 @ 00:06:04]. On the Flipping Mastery hybrid masterclass, the scripted offer is take over 100k at 3%, add a 100k second note with no payments for 24 months, and source the down payment from a private money lender [6Bdxz-HKeFI @ 00:06:47]. When the seller needs more money down than can be negotiated away, Pace switches to the Morby Method: get the seller's yes before the inspection period ends, sign a purchase agreement with a 30- or 60-day close, pull the lender's term sheet for down payment, rate, and payment, then go back and finalize, with the seller retaining part ownership of the buyer's LLC under a separate partnership agreement instead of a carryback [11lUs1njQMw @ 00:02:27].

Pace's straight seller-finance rental shows how to defer the down payment entirely. He took over tenants paying $1,650 a month and structured a $100k note at 0%, $375 a month for 240 months, explicitly not sub-to [Ke0nzzYXEfk @ 00:00:27]. Susan's original ask was $20k down, 8% carry, and a 10-year balloon; he pushed back, closed escrow March 31, 2020, and set the down payment as $5k at month six and another $5k at month twelve [Ke0nzzYXEfk @ 00:01:58]. The cash-flow table carries it: $1,650 rent minus $375 seller payment, $150 taxes and insurance, and a $200 vacancy and repair reserve nets $925 a month, so six months of net covers each $5k installment from tenant cash. He also sets a hard line on the Morby Method: if there's not active income coming in on the deal, he will not do one [rQCg4GFRLAI @ 00:05:44]. His Maricopa VA underwriting shows the same discipline on cash flow. Payments of 1313 plus 165 solar plus 325 on the seller note total 1803 against 2,200 rent, and his recalculated cost of $1,818 against $2,200 leaves $382 before the private money lender is paid, which he labels a non-cash flowing deal [t7aFESM6V_k @ 00:11:06].

callout.title: Street-level moves for structuring the hybrid stack
callout.body: Four moves the operators use to keep the acquisition clean, get past seller-side resistance, and find the deals in the first place.
items: Don't buy on a wrap and keep the sub-to note clean; acquire on hybrid and dispo on wrap, where a 6% wrap over a 3% loan is the arbitrage [Flipping Mastery TV — 6Bdxz-HKeFI @ 00:05:33].

When a seller's attorney kills a straight sub-to over the deed-and-mortgage split, switch to an agreement for sale: the seller keeps the deed and mortgage, seller-finances for about 5 years, and you refinance once there is enough equity [Pace Morby — 11lUs1njQMw @ 00:01:22].
The title company is not the bank: expect the arrears figure to be off by about $5,000 in legal fees and build that into the entry fee [Pace Morby — t7aFESM6V_k @ 00:05:54].

Send offers before calling: the LOI Blaster pairs a roughly 50-cents-on-the-dollar cash offer with a full-price creative offer asking for terms, about 30 seconds per batch, because agents don't check email [Pace Morby — IHTKcj3dVN0 @ 02:31:35].

sop_steps.title: Sort the lead by equity
sop_steps.action: Classify every lead as free-and-clear, high equity, or low equity before writing any offer.
sop_steps.detail: Free-and-clear and high-equity owners get seller finance; low-equity owners get sub-to or lease option; a cheap existing loan sitting under real equity is hybrid territory [Pace Morby — IHTKcj3dVN0 @ 00:45:01].

sop_steps.title: Open with cash and find the bunnies
sop_steps.action: Lead with a cash number, ask why the house hasn't sold, and ask what the seller plans to do with the proceeds.
sop_steps.detail: Always start with cash, never creative finance, then locate the seller's real problem; Heller's sellers only planned savings or a CD, which opened the door to a low-rate note [Flipping Mastery TV — pvgEqb4r4gw @ 00:02:35].

sop_steps.title: Underwrite backwards from the rent
sop_steps.action: Start from the existing mortgage payment and market rent, find the margin, then set the maximum seller payment.
sop_steps.detail: Open the seller note at 0% principal-only, factor repairs and down payment, and leave margin for PM, utilities, and repairs before agreeing to any rate [James Heller -- Hellerman Industries — nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:08:34].

sop_steps.title: Fund the entry fee and paper the stack
sop_steps.action: Layer private money behind the sub-to and seller note, then document every underlying lien.
sop_steps.detail: Kevin's lender put $40k at 12% for 24 months in third position, pitched on taking the whole asset on default [Pace Morby — Yw9I--p2Ef8 @ 00:05:24]; the note and deed of trust must describe each underlying debt [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — it6vSh38OhY @ 00:00:54].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether to buy on a wrap at all. Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network treats the wrap as a standard acquisition lane next to seller notes and subject-to with a second lien back to the seller. It comes with one hard floor: the wrap balance must be at least equal to all underlying debt, and you can budget for PMI or MIP but cannot charge the buyer for insurance you are not providing [it6vSh38OhY @ 00:04:30]. Pace Morby, teaching on Flipping Mastery TV, says don't buy on a wrap. Keep the subject-to note clean, treat a wrap at 6% over a 3% loan as arbitrage, and run the rule acquire on hybrid, dispo on wrap [6Bdxz-HKeFI @ 00:17:20]. The Landlord Dropout ran that disposition play on a former rental, selling for $140k with $4k down and $136k carried at $1,350 a month over 30 years on top of roughly a $90k underlying balance. That turned about $250 of net rental income into a $650 spread, with the buyer handling maintenance [hIflx_8aWVI @ 00:02:24]. Fusion Notes splits the difference: wraps can be sold, but they need stronger underwriting than straight notes, and most traditional note buyers pay off the underlying loan when they buy one [JAyoDBTIEIE @ 00:55:11].

Seller-note pricing is the second fault line. Pace Morby says 'the majority of the deals we do are 0% seller finance' [t7aFESM6V_k @ 00:12:31]. On the Poyer rental, the seller opened at $20k down, 8% carry and a 10-year balloon. Pace paid full retail at $100k, traded price for terms, and landed $375 a month for 240 months at 0%, with the down payment deferred into two $5k installments [Ke0nzzYXEfk @ 00:01:39]. James Heller -- Hellerman Industries also opens every negotiation at 0% principal-only. On a Colorado Springs townhouse, though, the sellers wanted at least 1.5% so they could sell the note later, and Heller conceded: $20k knocked off, $146,000 at 1.5%, $400 a month on roughly a 40-year amortization, and a 10-year balloon [nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:05:26]. Fusion Notes pushes against both styles from the note-buyer side. Avoid balloons, rising rates and rising payments because they also confuse servicers, and on owner-occupied loans any balloon has to sit at least 60 months out. The speaker is unsure whether rate adjustments follow the same rule and advises against both [JAyoDBTIEIE @ 00:53:22]. Heller's 1.5% coupon was driven by the sellers wanting a note they could sell, which is the same convertability Fusion Notes underwrites every loan toward.

The third split is how to paper a deal when the seller's side pushes back. A seller's attorney shut down a straight subject-to on a $1M house with $750K owed plus $50K in HOA dues. Pace Morby's fix was an agreement for sale to appease the attorney: the seller keeps the deed and the mortgage, seller-finances for about five years, and the buyer refinances once there is enough equity [11lUs1njQMw @ 00:01:22]. When the seller needs more money down and it cannot be negotiated away, the Morby Method gets a yes before the inspection period ends and signs a purchase agreement with probably a 60-day close. It then pulls the lender's term sheet and gives the seller part ownership of the buyer's LLC under a separate partnership agreement instead of a carryback [11lUs1njQMw @ 00:02:27]. Pace caps that same tool hard: no Morby Method without active income on the deal, because people take $400k and then bail on the payments, and a novation is the alternative offered [rQCg4GFRLAI @ 00:05:44]. TerraFunded shows why instrument choice matters in Texas. An unconverted contract for deed lets the seller keep everything, while a deed of trust forces a trustee sale that hands roughly $27,500 back to the buyer at a $130k sale after 36 payments [Q9c1Be5WnWI @ 00:06:20].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The recurring firsthand loss is that the underlying debt never stops. The Landlord Dropout moved into creative finance after a roof, a driveway and HVAC across three rentals cost over $25k in 90 days, more than eight years of one property's $250 monthly cash flow [hIflx_8aWVI @ 00:00:23]. On the resulting wrap sale, the same operator lists the exposures that remain. The underlying payment stays due if the buyer stops paying, maintenance is not guaranteed, servicing and default costs still apply, and 30 years of payments have not actually been collected yet [hIflx_8aWVI @ 00:04:26]. Fusion Notes reports the note-side version: when a wrap defaults you still pay the underlying, taxes, insurance and legal fees. The speaker has four to five foreclosures active, and borrowers often file bankruptcy the day before the sheriff's sale, most recently about six weeks earlier [JAyoDBTIEIE @ 00:41:03]. Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network flags the slow-motion version on double wraps. One stack seen in the field had three modification liens on top of down-payment assistance and a first lien. HUD liens carrying 0% interest and no payments make it easy to lose track of balances and end up upside down unless every balance is tracked [it6vSh38OhY @ 00:05:25].

Pace Morby's own live underwriting shows how quickly a creative deal stops cash flowing. On a Maricopa VA loan, the stack ran $1,313 on the first, $165 for solar and $325 on a $90k seller second with a five-year balloon, totaling $1,803 against $2,200 rent. The $45k raise for the deal added about $350 a month, pushing it to roughly $400 negative [t7aFESM6V_k @ 00:01:01]. To save it, the seller payout was ground down to $26k plus $9,500 in arrears for a $35k entry, and the assignment fee was cut from $10k to $5k and deferred until a second deal [t7aFESM6V_k @ 00:04:18]. Even then, the final $1,818 monthly cost against $2,200 left $382 before the private money lender got paid, and Pace labeled it a non-cash flowing deal [t7aFESM6V_k @ 00:11:06]. James Heller -- Hellerman Industries closed a zero-down, no-repair townhouse at about $150 a month and admits that probably gets eaten up by operating expenses. Heller is counting on equity paydown and depreciation of 20 to 30 thousand or more instead. The margin capped the seller at $400 a month, and Heller told them that paying more meant losing money every month [nO_A1GtSlaA @ 00:06:23].

Closing and exit risk kills deals after the numbers already work. Pace Morby lists child-support and IRS liens as deal killers and has a Kermit, Texas RV park stuck under contract for two years over a title error [IHTKcj3dVN0 @ 02:42:07]. On another acquisition, Claude AI surfaced 15 of 45 homeowners suing the builder over uncompacted dirt during diligence, a defect that would never show up in the payment math [IHTKcj3dVN0 @ 02:43:10]. On the back end, Fusion Notes warns that cashing out paper is slow: several weeks, and sometimes over a month even at banks with established processes. Institutional buyers pay more than retail buyers because of lower cost of capital, and retail buyers are flaky. Without the underwriting package and TRID disclosures, some buyers, such as First National Acceptance in Michigan, will not even make an offer [JAyoDBTIEIE @ 00:32:05]. A big check at closing does not rescue the paper either. A 25 to 30% down payment with no documented income cannot be made compliant, cannot be sold to a bank, and may be viewed as predatory, which leaves the note holder carrying 30 years of payments with no exit [JAyoDBTIEIE @ 00:35:22].

chapters.question_prompt: What does the due-on-sale clause actually allow lenders to do, what exceptions exist, and how do operators structure around it?
chapters.title: The Due-on-Sale Clause: Law, Exceptions, and Practitioner Workarounds
chapters.subtitle: Loan acceleration mechanics, Garn-St. Germain exceptions, land trusts and LLC transfers, deed-back and lease-option fallbacks, myth-busting live sessions, and what happens when a lender invokes the clause
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree the due-on-sale clause is a lender right that is rarely exercised. Pace Morby puts calls at roughly one in 500 houses, the Investor Army Podcast guest reports fewer than ten across fifteen thousand owner-financed mortgages, and William Tingle reports 24 plus years without one. The real triggers are operational, not the recorded deed: botched insurance, missed payments, bad paperwork, a deed moved too fast after a foreclosure reinstatement, small local banks, and angry sellers or ex-spouses. Street mechanics include a 10 to 15 day post-reinstatement wait, Westar servicing at $27 a month, due-on-sale insurance near 1% of price, and a deed-back-plus-agreement-for-sale cure inside a 30 to 35 day letter window. The sharpest split is land trusts: Clint Coons builds subject-to deals around them, while Morby says a land trust does not stop the clause.

key_metrics.context: Morby's estimate of how often the clause gets called on subject-to deals, including deals using land trusts and other strategies.

key_metrics.value: About 1% of purchase price ($4,000 on a $400,000 home)
key_metrics.context: Coverage whose provider will fix a called clause or refinance the house out with its own money; many operators skip it because of cost.

key_metrics.context: Wait after catching up a foreclosure before closing escrow; transferring the deed 3 days into reinstatement is Morby's most common cause of a call.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus: Rare Calls, Known Triggers, Clean Cures
paragraphs: Every operator here agrees on the baseline: the due-on-sale clause is real, it lives in the note or deed of trust, and it gives the lender a right, not an obligation, to accelerate the loan when ownership moves. Pace Morby states flatly that he has had it called on him multiple times and that anyone claiming it never happens has not been doing subject-to long enough, yet he pegs the rate at roughly one out of every 500 houses [cOTyo3LTDPk @ 00:00:12]. Ken McElroy frames it as a right but not the obligation and traces its origin to the 1980s, when rates near 18% sat against 4% loans and wraps were everywhere [ulx_sqYnYVA @ 00:00:00]. The Investor Army Podcast guest says subject-to triggers the clause rather than violates it, notes it sits in about 98 percent of deeds of trust, and reports fewer than ten calls across fifteen thousand owner-financed mortgages and 75 million originated [WFGzQCgPP54 @ 00:02:26]. William Tingle adds 24 plus years without a single loan called, conditioned on on-time payments and proper insurance [ccfeK6C6SeI @ 00:01:15]. The consensus is not that the risk is zero; it is that the risk is small, predictable, and driven by operator sloppiness.

The second point of agreement is what actually wakes a lender up, and it is almost never the recorded deed itself. Morby says that most of the time the bank never notices, that even when it notices it does not care, and that the real triggers are transferring insurance incorrectly or stopping payments [cOTyo3LTDPk @ 00:01:35]. Clint Coons lands in the same place from the asset-protection side: unpaid taxes, missed payments, or no insurance are what draw the lender's eye, and red flags like an out-of-state address or an uninsured property should be avoided [nS_9Os_42MQ @ 00:06:30]. In his longer breakdown, Morby ranks the top five ways banks find out: a small local bank plus redeeming a foreclosure at the wrong time, improper insurance, a missed payment, incorrect paperwork, and an angry seller or ex-spouse [KXUHeABJyeY @ 00:42:38]. The Investor Army guest names wrong insurance as the main cause behind their handful of calls and flags small banks such as Colonial Savings, which called five houses, as riskier than Wells Fargo or Bank of America [WFGzQCgPP54 @ 00:10:11]. Morby also stresses that banks are not notified when the county recorder records a deed, because they bundle and sell loans rather than watch titles.

The third consensus is that a called clause is a paperwork problem with a long fuse, not a seizure. Coons says there is no credit damage and no jail, and that the lender's ask is either refinance, pay off, or put title back into the borrower's name [nS_9Os_42MQ @ 00:07:02]. The In Rem Podcast reviewer says every clause they have read, across private, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, and VA paper, carries a notice of acceleration with 30 days to pay the full balance, and that lenders usually also offer the option to put title back in the seller's name within 30 days [d9fjKwIC-VE @ 00:01:43]. Morby's demand letter gives 35 days, carries no fine, and when the buyer calls the bank the issue is resolved 90%+ of the time, with the servicing simply synced [W60Ytz4Wb5U @ 00:16:54]. Even when a lender pushes past the letter, Morby says acceleration runs through foreclosure, which takes three to 12 months depending on the state, and a judicial foreclosure costs a bank $30,000 to $50,000 and dents its ratings and warehouse lines [dMDfltvY39k @ 00:36:23]. Karla Kyte adds the statutory floor: in death and divorce, lenders have to honor the transfer.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The first mechanic every Morby student learns is timing around a foreclosure reinstatement, because that is where most of his own calls came from. The typical case: the seller is in foreclosure, he catches up the payments, the deed transfers three days later during reinstatement, and the bank calls the clause; the fix is to wait 10 to 15 days after the loan is reinstated before closing escrow [cOTyo3LTDPk @ 00:03:27]. On the Lost Dutchman deal, where the deed moved a day after redemption with a small local bank, he tightened that into a cooling-off period of at least five to ten days while holding the physical warranty deed for about 30 days before recording [KXUHeABJyeY @ 00:43:27]. Insurance is the second build. Morby gets a second policy a week before close with the seller as loss payee, and a broker notifies the bank about 30 days after close [dMDfltvY39k @ 00:33:30]. The Investor Army guest gives the exact stack: on a rental, the investor is named insured, the seller additional insured, and the lender mortgagee; on a wrap, the end buyer is named insured, the seller additional insured, the lender primary mortgagee, and the investor secondary mortgagee [WFGzQCgPP54 @ 00:04:00].

Payments and paperwork are the third and fourth triggers, and Morby automates both. He routes payments through Westar servicing at $27 a month, which makes five payments covering principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and seller equity [dMDfltvY39k @ 00:31:29]. His sub2 purchase agreement carries about 19 disclosures, including continued liability and a due-on-sale plan, followed by a TC plus escrow or a closing attorney; the deed is one page and costs $17, and skipping title insurance is called lazy and irresponsible [W60Ytz4Wb5U @ 00:11:42]. For a backstop, due-on-sale insurance runs about 1% of purchase price, roughly $4,000 on a $400,000 home, and the provider will fix it or refinance the house out with its own money [cOTyo3LTDPk @ 00:01:54]. Many operators skip the coverage because of cost. Morby is also part-owner of Equity Assurance, which negotiates with the bank and, if that fails, refinances with the exact same terms and earns the interest [4krb0pqCMC8 @ 00:00:57]. The seller contract also includes a $50,000 fine if the seller goes to the bank, aimed at the angry-seller trigger, and Morby's team says it spent $40,000 to $50,000 over six to seven years drafting documents it revises every three to six months.

When the letter lands, the execution sequence is consistent. Step one is the phone: per Morby, the buyer calls the bank and more than 90% of the time it is perfectly fine; otherwise the fallback is an executory contract and/or a lease option or land lease [W60Ytz4Wb5U @ 00:17:25]. At Johnston Johnson Bank he reached the president, the founder's son, who suggested deeding the property back to the owner and buying on an agreement for sale; Morby then wrote an Arizona agreement for sale, recorded it at the county recorder, and says all five times the paperwork was simply rearranged [cOTyo3LTDPk @ 00:04:24]. The In Rem Podcast lays out the same restructure: a warranty deed from buyer back to seller, then either an agreement for sale where payments mirror the existing loan and the buyer holds equitable interest and possession, or a long-term lease with option to purchase, with Garn-St. Germain allowing leases up to three years [d9fjKwIC-VE @ 00:05:12]. Option two is selling to a third party within 30 days; option three is a refinance, caveated by current rates. Morby holds the executory-contract deed unrecorded in a safety deposit box that needs both parties to sign off, with a three-day notice on breach [dMDfltvY39k @ 00:40:40].

callout.title: What the operators do that most subject-to buyers miss
callout.body: Four moves that keep the lender asleep or turn a called clause into a routine paperwork swap.
items: Never notify the bank: there is no due-on-sale department, phone support is mostly overseas virtual assistants, and on the Whitman deal Morby spent a 4-hour round trip calling the bank trying to get the clause called and could not [Pace Morby — dMDfltvY39k @ 01:56:03]

On LLC transfers, match LLC ownership and percentages to the deed; Fannie Mae exempts transfers to a borrower-controlled LLC on loans from June 1st, 2016 onward, and Freddie Mac requires the original borrower to be managing member [Ken McElroy — ulx_sqYnYVA @ 00:04:01]

When the lender mails a letter asking you to verify ownership, answer it with the LLC operating agreement or the land trust agreement rather than ignoring it [Clint Coons Esq. | Real Estate Asset Protection — nS_9Os_42MQ @ 00:04:29]

In a divorce, the spouse awarded the home should send the lender the separation agreement and lock in full account access; the lender cannot call the loan or force a refinance because in death and divorce they have to honor it [My Divorce Mortgage Planning with Karla Kyte, CDLP — DANV_9GW0PU @ 00:05:49]

sop_steps.action: Raise the due-on-sale clause proactively and paper it in the purchase agreement.

sop_steps.title: Time the deed and stack the insurance
sop_steps.action: Hold the deed transfer until the reinstated loan cools off and set insurance before close.
sop_steps.detail: Wait 10 to 15 days after reinstatement before closing, and get a second policy a week before close with the seller as loss payee so a broker can notify the bank about 30 days after close [Pace Morby — dMDfltvY39k @ 00:26:41]

sop_steps.title: Automate payments and close clean
sop_steps.action: Route the loan through a servicer and buy title insurance on every deal.

sop_steps.action: Call the bank first, then restructure, sell, or refinance inside the 30-day window.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split on the street is whether a land trust shields a subject-to deal. Clint Coons now structures acquisitions through a land trust with the investor's LLC as beneficiary, puts the seller on title as initial trustee so the record reads 'Tom as trustee,' then has Tom resign so the buyer steps in as undisclosed successor trustee, arguing that nobody sees the trustee because the trust is not a public document [0hSERgZotJM @ 00:05:06]. Pace Morby calls that theory a myth: a land trust hides who the new owner is but does not change the fact that the deed moved to a new entity, beneficiaries stay visible in Arizona, and half of the called loans Morby hears about were bought in land trusts [KXUHeABJyeY @ 00:29:41]. The Garn-St Germain camp narrows the argument further: Brooke and Dan read the 1982 act as protecting a transfer into a revocable inter vivos trust only when the property is under five units and the borrower stays beneficiary [l81_UM-dG9Y @ 00:02:38], while Joe Seagull says that exception is gone once the property is out of the borrower's name and the borrower has moved out, and flatly refuses to extend it to second homes or investment property [yd3L18YPXDU @ 00:02:04].

Practitioners also split on how often the clause actually fires and how hard it bites. Pace Morby's own numbers drift across appearances, from roughly one in 500 deals to four out of about 700 to ten calls with one active, and the takeaway Morby pushes is that the clause is a boogeyman that is easy to solve [dMDfltvY39k @ 00:15:02]. William Tingle goes further, reporting 24-plus years with no loan called as long as payments land on time and insurance is set up properly [ccfeK6C6SeI @ 00:01:15]. Joe Seagull runs the opposite read: legacy loans at 2 to 3 percent sitting against 6 to 7 percent money give lenders a reason to call notes and relend, and while judges may stall out of sympathy, the lender ultimately gets its non-monetary foreclosure [yd3L18YPXDU @ 00:02:24]. UpCounsel frames the consequence as immediate full repayment or foreclosure, whereas Morby counters that acceleration runs through a foreclosure process that takes three to 12 months depending on the state, which is the cure window operators actually work inside [KXUHeABJyeY @ 00:16:41]. Morby's own answer to whether an operator should worry is a flat yes, with the worry dial pinned at level 10 only for the uninformed.

The LLC question and the fallback-clause question draw a third line. Ken McElroy tells investors not to fear moving property into an LLC, citing Fannie Mae's exemption for transfers to a borrower-controlled LLC on loans from June 1st, 2016, Freddie Mac's requirement that the original borrower be managing member, and the tactic of matching LLC ownership and percentages to the deed [ulx_sqYnYVA @ 00:04:01]. Clint Coons has moved the other way on subject-to deals, no longer deeding to an LLC because it reads as a red flag if the lender pulls title, a reversal Coons ties directly to higher interest rates [0hSERgZotJM @ 00:01:46]. Pace Morby goes the opposite direction from silence on paperwork, loading a sub2 purchase agreement with about 19 disclosures that spell out continued liability and a due-on-sale plan, and Morby insists the clause is something to bring up with the seller even when the seller does not care [W60Ytz4Wb5U @ 00:08:09]. William Tingle refuses to write a deed-back or lease-option fallback clause into the contract at all, because it unsettles sellers who want certainty [ccfeK6C6SeI @ 00:00:04]. The In Rem Podcast lands closer to Morby, laying out restructure, sale, or refinance as the three paths once a 30-day acceleration notice arrives.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated firsthand failure is closing too fast after curing a foreclosure. Pace Morby's typical call came when a seller was in foreclosure, the payments were caught up, and the deed transferred three days later during reinstatement, which tripped the clause; the fix Morby now runs is to wait 10 to 15 days after the loan is reinstated before closing escrow [cOTyo3LTDPk @ 00:03:13]. On the Lost Dutchman deal the deed moved a day after redemption at a small local bank, and the corrected sequence is to redeem, sit through a cooling-off period of at least five to ten days, and hold the physical warranty deed for about 30 days before recording [KXUHeABJyeY @ 00:42:38]. Bank size is the second trap. Morby's line that banks are way too big to care breaks down at the small end, where very small banks may notice transfers on their own, and the Investor Army guest names Colonial Savings with five houses called while rating Wells Fargo and Bank of America fine [WFGzQCgPP54 @ 00:10:11]. When Morby reached the president of a small bank, the founder's son, the cure was to deed the property back and re-buy on a recorded Arizona agreement for sale [cOTyo3LTDPk @ 00:04:24].

Insurance is the trigger every camp names. The Investor Army guest, with fifteen thousand owner-financed mortgages and fewer than ten called, pins the main cause on wrong insurance and spells out the fix: on a rental the investor is named insured, the seller additional insured, and the lender mortgagee, while on a wrap the end buyer becomes named insured and the investor slides to secondary mortgagee [WFGzQCgPP54 @ 00:04:00]. Pace Morby's version is a second policy bound a week before close with the seller as loss payee, then a broker notifies the bank about 30 days after closing [dMDfltvY39k @ 00:33:30]. Missed payments are the next landmine, and Morby pays Westar $27 a month to push five separate payments covering principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and seller equity so nothing slips. Clint Coons lists unpaid taxes, missed payments, and no insurance as the real triggers, and recounts a borrower who moved 14 rentals into 14 LLCs, got caught by the insurer's spot check, and was told to retitle with an ability to cure [nS_9Os_42MQ @ 00:07:47]. Morby adds incorrect paperwork to the list, including roughly 10 setup steps such as redirecting the lender's mail [KXUHeABJyeY @ 00:55:00].

The last class of failures comes from people, not paperwork. Pace Morby's fifth trigger is an angry seller or ex-spouse: on a Chandler deal of roughly $350,000, the ex-wife was still on the mortgage while the husband held the deed alone, her attorney threatened, and attorney Sean Sinclair had to resolve it, and Morby's seller contract now carries a $50,000 fine if the seller goes to the bank [KXUHeABJyeY @ 00:51:27]. Karla Kyte sees the divorce trap from the other side, with a client paying the mortgage without account access because the ex-husband never granted it, and pushes access terms into the separation agreement [DANV_9GW0PU @ 00:03:54]. The affidavit trap is sharper. Clint Coons has an active client being asked to attest the seller still resides in a property titled in an LLC, and Joe Seagull warns that a false affidavit is wire fraud if emailed and bank fraud because it goes to a federally regulated lender [yd3L18YPXDU @ 00:03:48]. Run the economics before signing anything: due-on-sale insurance runs about 1 percent of price, roughly $4,000 on a $400,000 home, and the refinance exit carries today's rates, which is the caveat the In Rem Podcast attaches to its third option [d9fjKwIC-VE @ 00:07:27].

callout.title: Pre-Close Kill Switch
callout.body: Every item below is a trigger that practitioners watched fire on live deals. Clear all four before the deed moves.
items: Reinstatement timing cleared: no deed transfer until 10 to 15 days after the loan is reinstated, with the physical warranty deed held about 30 days on small-bank loans [Pace Morby — cOTyo3LTDPk @ 00:03:27].

Insurance structure verified: investor named insured, seller additional insured, lender mortgagee, and on wraps the end buyer named insured with the investor as secondary mortgagee [Investor Army Podcast — WFGzQCgPP54 @ 00:04:00].
No false paperwork to the lender: a false affidavit emailed to a federally regulated lender is wire fraud and bank fraud [TrustThisTV — yd3L18YPXDU @ 00:03:48].
Seller and ex-spouse risk mapped: confirm who is on the mortgage versus the deed, because an angry ex-spouse on the loan is a top-five trigger [Pace Morby — KXUHeABJyeY @ 00:51:27].

Set insurance with the investor as named insured, the seller as additional insured, and the lender as mortgagee before close [Investor Army Podcast — WFGzQCgPP54 @ 00:04:00].
Route payments through Westar servicing at $27 a month so principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and seller equity never slip [Pace Morby — dMDfltvY39k @ 00:31:29].
When the demand letter lands, have the buyer call the bank first, which is perfectly fine 90-plus percent of the time once servicing syncs [Pace Morby — W60Ytz4Wb5U @ 00:16:54].

chapters.question_prompt: Beyond due-on-sale, what goes wrong in subject-to and wrap deals, and how do I protect myself and the seller?
chapters.title: Sub-To and Wrap Failure Modes: When Deals Go Sideways
chapters.subtitle: Real due-on-sale call stories, seller bankruptcy after closing, homeowners insurance and mortgagee clauses, HOA foreclosure, deed in lieu, buyer/seller risk warnings, agent 'scam' critiques, and attorney views on legality
chapters.executive_summary: Attorneys, lenders, agents, and active sub-to operators agree on the structure: title moves while the seller's loan and credit exposure stay put. Due-on-sale enforcement is reported as rare but real. Eddie Speed pins 90% of trips on the hazard insurance, and Evan Ragsdale survived a PennyMac call by deeding back and restructuring as a contract for deed. A seller bankruptcy inside 90 days lets a trustee unwind the deal. To guard against that, operators wrap the loan with a secured note, add a reaffirmation clause and a notarized affidavit of solvency, and screen for judgments, tax liens, and evictions. Wrap spreads run from 3.5% underlying to 4.5%-6%. Practitioners split sharply on legality. Some call the play a legal breach of contract, while one broker calls it a scam bordering on mortgage fraud.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: Title Moves, Debt Stays, and the Deal Breaks in Predictable Places
paragraphs: Every attorney and operator here describes the same core structure: the seller deeds the property to the buyer, the seller's mortgage is not paid off, and the buyer takes over the payments. Attorney Patrick McQueen on Kelly Zitlow's channel draws a hard line between this and an assumption. An assumption means getting the lender's permission and putting a new qualified borrower on the loan. In a subject-to deal, 'you hope that the lender never finds out' [pYujIjfIOkE @ 00:03:01]. Bramlett Partners puts it in one sentence for sellers and agents: the buyer takes title, the mortgage stays in the seller's name, and the buyer agrees to make the payments [dge6WTAROFI @ 00:00:37]. Eddie Speed, a seller-finance note buyer since 1980, adds a key point about the buyer's position. The sub-to buyer is not technically legally liable for the debt, but they know they lose their interest in the property if they stop paying [coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:03:24]. That split is the root of every failure mode that follows. The seller keeps the debt on their credit with no ownership. The buyer holds title without liability. The lender holds a covenant it may or may not enforce. Tim Harrison of Straight Up Mortgage Talk frames the seller exposure bluntly: how that buyer pays your mortgage will reflect on your credit score [Qnk52S1LXHI @ 00:00:15].

On the due-on-sale clause, the consensus is that enforcement is rare but not zero, and the triggers are specific. Bramlett Partners says the clause sits in dang near 100% of conforming, FHA, and VA loans and lets the bank demand the full balance once title passes. They also concede the clauses 'are very rarely ever enforced' and that the promoters are 'mostly right' [dge6WTAROFI @ 00:05:03]. Jeff Hampton of Real Estate Law Guys agrees that due-on-sale clauses are very rarely exercised. Hampton then warns that a lender sitting on a 3.2% fixed loan while rates run 7% has a financial incentive to call it [nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:05:44]. Eddie Speed says servicers are not out running title hunting for these deals. Something trips the switch, the servicer then has a duty to investigate, and 90% of the time that switch is the insurance [coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:13:07]. Evan Ragsdale actually had the clause called on a PennyMac-serviced deal. Ragsdale lists the same short set of triggers: missed payments, mishandled insurance, or a smaller in-house servicer that watches files closely. In their case the payments were current, so they blame the insurance the end investor ignored guidance on [m8scT0nPuzY @ 00:01:16].

The second consensus risk is a seller bankruptcy, and the lawyers agree on the 90-day line. Jeff Hampton cites section 547 of the Federal Bankruptcy Code. If the seller files within 90 days of the transaction, the trustee can treat it as an avoidable preference and unwind the whole deal. The buyer loses title and possibly the money sunk into improvements [nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:01:00]. The In Rem Podcast attorney gives the same window. After 90 days, they add, the trustee generally cannot set aside a straight arm's-length deal unless there was insider dealing, fraud, or impropriety [2ZZq6UibGDE @ 00:02:29]. Kelly Zitlow asked what happens to a buyer's $100,000 cash in a seller bankruptcy. Patrick McQueen's answer is 'probably gone,' because that money may need to go to the seller's creditors, and the buyer will be dragged into the case either way [pYujIjfIOkE @ 00:07:38]. The shared prescription is having the capacity to absorb a blowup. Speed says the savvy operators doing sub-to can write a check and pay off the underlying mortgage if something goes wrong. Speed also says a first deal probably should not be a sub-to [coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:04:59]. McQueen likewise steers buyers toward a short time frame and a fix-and-flip exit, with enough runway to finish the flip if the lender calls the loan.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The paperwork fix the attorneys push is to stop doing naked sub-to and wrap it. Patrick McQueen lays out the math. A seller holding a 3.5% loan should carry the wrap at 5.5% or 6% to earn the spread. On a $500,000 sale against a $400,000 balance, the $100,000 gap is covered with cash, a wrap mortgage, or a junior note secured by a second deed of trust [pYujIjfIOkE @ 00:05:59]. Bramlett Partners gives sellers a slimmer version: 3.5% underlying and 4.5% or 5% to the buyer. They tell sellers to weigh down payment size, buyer credit, and the rate spread, and to have an attorney draft every document [dge6WTAROFI @ 00:06:45]. The In Rem Podcast attorney says to always do a wrap on sub-to, even if it is a promissory note 'only for performance,' secured by a mortgage or deed of trust. That way the seller becomes a lender, and the note, not the house, becomes the bankruptcy estate asset [2ZZq6UibGDE @ 00:03:02]. Jeff Hampton reports the same effect. The seller becomes a secured creditor, the trustee can collect payments or sell the note but cannot sell the house, and the buyer keeps possession. Hampton contrasts that with buyers just Venmoing payments with no contract, which Hampton calls gambling [nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:03:53].

The seller-side diligence is concrete. William Tingle, 26 years into the business, asks every seller directly whether they are in bankruptcy or considering it. Tingle then adds a notarized affidavit of solvency to the closing package. It states that the seller is not considering bankruptcy, can meet all financial obligations, and did not obtain any funds involved through illegal means. Tingle also produces a HUD even on a kitchen-table closing [D8NZHrMYpSE @ 00:08:12]. Jeff Hampton's red-flag scan during due diligence covers multiple judgments, tax liens, and collections or pending evictions. Hampton calls any hit a ticking time bomb ready to explode [nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:02:49]. The In Rem Podcast attorney writes a reaffirmation into their subject-to addendum, so the seller agrees to reaffirm the existing loan and keep it from being impacted by a bankruptcy filing [2ZZq6UibGDE @ 00:05:08]. Caleb Christopher warns that title companies and attorneys will not hand over paperwork that survives closing. The buyer needs a power of attorney among a pile of other documents. Disclosures and acknowledgments that the credit stays in the seller's name must be signed up front, because springing the sub-to addendum at close of escrow drops a bomb on a seller who already has moving trucks booked [369aexLYPNM @ 00:05:28].

Insurance is where operators get most specific, because it is the most cited trigger. James Bealer has the seller convert the owner-occupant homeowner policy to a landlord policy. The investor is added as additionally insured, and so is any wrap buyer. Bealer also holds a limited power of attorney for insurance matters. Bealer used to have wrap buyers buy their own policy but stopped, because it could trip the due-on-sale clause on the underlying loan [Y7CyY8gLd3U @ 00:03:10]. Eddie Speed rejects the street fix of keeping the seller's policy and stacking a second policy that names the buyer. Speed asks who pays the claim if the house burns down and reports that their legal counsel says that is definitely not how to fix it [coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:15:06]. On transaction costs, Caleb Christopher's creative TC team charges $150 to $350 for front-end contract work, depending on timeline and whether a seller walkthrough is needed. Transaction management starts at $1,000, with half upfront and the rest at close. The fee is written in as a closing cost reimbursed by the end buyer on assignments [369aexLYPNM @ 00:12:01]. Hans of Sub2Investor reports roughly $1,000 in closing costs on a deal where the seller received zero cash, including a $125 mobile notary fee [WxPHAXmQ-j4 @ 00:05:39].

callout.title: How Operators Keep a Sideways Sub-To Deal Alive
callout.body: These are field-tested moves from operators who had a due-on-sale scare, insurance confusion, or trust-structure questions land on their desk.
items: When the due-on-sale clause was called on a PennyMac loan with current payments, Evan Ragsdale's team deeded the property back to the original borrower to resolve the lender's concern. They then restructured as a contract for deed, keeping control, cash flow, and upside on the same economics [Evan Ragsdale — m8scT0nPuzY @ 00:02:08].

Hans's mobile notary mailed the full closing packet to Freedom Mortgage instead of the title company: deed, settlement statement, trust documents, and the title exception sheet. Nothing happened, and the loan modification still went through. Hans's mentor's read was that there is no due-on-sale department at the mortgage company [Sub2Investor — WxPHAXmQ-j4 @ 00:09:36].

Get the seller to switch to a landlord policy early in the conversation, right at closing. Keep the relationship with the seller clean, because you may need their help on insurance later [James Bealer — Y7CyY8gLd3U @ 00:05:47].

The trust provision only lets the borrower move the property into their own trust, not the buyer's trust. A trust with an LLC as beneficiary is a way to paper it, but it does not sidestep the covenant [On The Market — coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:08:06].

sop_steps.title: Screen the Seller for Bankruptcy Risk
sop_steps.action: Ask the seller directly about current or planned bankruptcy, then run a red-flag scan on public records.
sop_steps.detail: Ask whether the seller is in bankruptcy or considering it, since a seller already in bankruptcy cannot sell [William Tingle — D8NZHrMYpSE @ 00:06:02]. Then check for multiple judgments, tax liens, and collections or pending evictions [Real Estate Law Guys I Asset Protection — nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:02:49].

sop_steps.title: Paper the Deal Before the Closing Table
sop_steps.action: Get the full sub-to addendum, disclosures, wrap note, and reaffirmation language signed with the purchase contract.
sop_steps.detail: Secure the deal with a promissory note and a mortgage or deed of trust, even if the note is only for performance. Include a seller reaffirmation of the existing loan in the addendum [In Rem Podcast — 2ZZq6UibGDE @ 00:05:08]. Get credit-stays-in-your-name acknowledgments signed up front, not at close of escrow [Caleb Christopher — 369aexLYPNM @ 00:05:28].

sop_steps.title: Close, Record, and Control the Document Trail
sop_steps.action: Record the deed immediately, collect the affidavit of solvency, and confirm the signed packet reaches the title company.
sop_steps.detail: Record the deed immediately and keep 91-plus days distance from any known distress [Real Estate Law Guys I Asset Protection — nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:06:46]. Track the notary's return envelope, because Hans's packet went to the lender instead of title [Sub2Investor — WxPHAXmQ-j4 @ 00:05:08].

sop_steps.title: Fix Insurance and Fund a Plan B
sop_steps.action: Convert the seller's policy to a landlord policy with additional insureds, and hold capital to answer a called note.
sop_steps.detail: Have the seller switch to a landlord policy and add the investor and any wrap buyer as additionally insured [James Bealer — Y7CyY8gLd3U @ 00:03:35]. Be positioned to write a check and pay off the underlying mortgage if the lender calls it [On The Market — coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:04:59].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over how much weight the due-on-sale clause deserves. William Tingle [D8NZHrMYpSE @ 00:12:59] reports that across hundreds and hundreds of houses the team has never dealt with a due-on-sale issue, and ranks the clause a lesser worry than seller bankruptcy. Hans of Sub2Investor [WxPHAXmQ-j4 @ 00:08:54] ran what Hans calls a true test case: a mobile notary shipped the warranty deed, settlement statement, title exception letter and trust agreement straight to Freedom Mortgage, and zero happened; the mentor's advice was that there is no due-on-sale department at the mortgage company, so keep quiet and give it time. Evan Ragsdale [m8scT0nPuzY @ 00:00:13] reports the opposite outcome on a loan serviced by one of the largest mortgage servicers in the country, with payments current, which proves the call is an option the lender can exercise rather than a myth. Eddie Speed on On The Market [coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:11:27] reframes the whole debate: servicers are not out running title hunting for subject-to deals; something trips a switch, and only then are they under a fiduciary responsibility to investigate. The operator read is that the clause rarely fires by itself. Specific, avoidable events fire it, so the real fight is over controlling those triggers rather than arguing about whether lenders care in the abstract.

Practitioners also split on what the strategy even is. Chuck Vosberg of Florida Real Estate Scene [9fmPGWpE4qo @ 00:02:47] calls it an illegal assumption and mortgage fraud worked through loopholes, says legal does not mean it is not a scam, and refuses to represent clients who enter these agreements. Attorney Michael Gross on Mamadou Diallo's channel [UpPEu5m2V4Y @ 00:04:41] takes the other side: the seller breaches a contract with the lender, a breach of contract is not a violation of law, and if the lender does not care, nothing is inappropriate about the deal. Eddie Speed [coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:10:10] lands with Gross, saying it is not illegal but you are breaking a covenant in the security document, and admitting openly that it is a legal maneuver the servicer is not totally cool with. The insurance playbook is contested too. James Bealer [Y7CyY8gLd3U @ 00:04:19] once had end buyers on wraps carry their own homeowners policy, then stopped because it could trip the due-on-sale clause; Bealer now has the seller convert to a landlord policy and add the investor, and owner-finance buyers, as additional insureds. Speed rejects the popular patch of keeping the seller's policy and stacking a second policy where the investor is insured, asking who pays the claim if the house burns down.

On seller bankruptcy, the defensive playbooks diverge. Jeff Hampton of Real Estate Law Guys [nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:03:37] and the In Rem Podcast attorney [2ZZq6UibGDE @ 00:03:02] both push a wraparound note secured by a mortgage or deed of trust, even a performance-only note, so the seller becomes a secured creditor and the note, not the house, lands in the estate. They disagree on the downside inside 90 days: Hampton warns you might not get reimbursed for improvements, while In Rem describes the trustee returning whatever funds the buyer put in and restoring the status quo. Caleb Christopher [369aexLYPNM @ 00:06:49] argues the deal should be excluded from the bankruptcy outright, because the seller no longer owns the asset and the mortgage is current and someone else is responsible for it. William Tingle [D8NZHrMYpSE @ 00:08:12] relies on paper and economics instead: an affidavit of solvency in every closing package, plus a Central Georgia trustee's rule of thumb of no claw back without a clear $50,000-plus in real equity. Hampton adds the opposite caution: short-term rental subject-to deals carry higher value that attracts trustee scrutiny, and a deal is not done just because the deed is recorded. Past 90 days, Hampton still flags three traps: an unrecorded deed, insider dealing with a related seller, and a fraudulent-conveyance challenge.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most vivid firsthand failure is operational, not legal. Hans of Sub2Investor [WxPHAXmQ-j4 @ 00:05:08] closed a remote deal through a mobile notary, roughly $1,000 in closing costs including a $125 notary fee, and the executed packet went by FedEx to Freedom Mortgage instead of the title company, mid loan modification; Hans spent about three months on edge before the portal showed the modification booked. Evan Ragsdale [m8scT0nPuzY @ 00:01:16] traces the called loan to insurance: payments were current, but the end investor ignored the insurance guidance and raised visibility with the servicer. Ragsdale's fix was to deed the property back to the original borrower, which immediately resolved the call, then restructure as a contract for deed so record title never changed while the team kept the cash flow and upside. Eddie Speed [coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:13:07] puts the insurance trigger at 90% of the time: a clerk processing the annual declarations page sees the insured is no longer the borrower and kicks it to a supervisor. Speed also lists human triggers: a seller who panics 60 days later and calls the lender, or a divorced spouse who applies for a new mortgage two years on and asks, what mortgage. Weak paperwork, not the clause, is what keeps blowing these deals up.

Bankruptcy is where the money actually disappears. Kelly Zitlow's guest, attorney Patrick McQueen [pYujIjfIOkE @ 00:07:38], walks a buyer who put $100,000 down on a wrap into a seller bankruptcy and answers flatly that the money is probably gone, because it may belong to the seller's creditors, and the buyer will be dragged into the case with no way out. Jeff Hampton [nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:02:02] lists the 90-day clawback damage: lost title, unreimbursed improvements, and short-term rental bookings that must be cancelled because it is not your property anymore; Hampton has seen buyers just Venmo mortgage payments with no contract and calls that gambling. William Tingle [D8NZHrMYpSE @ 00:09:26] has had several sellers file after closing across 26 years, and the full extent was a phone call from the trustee or the seller's bankruptcy attorney, answered with a HUD the team produces even on kitchen-table closings. In Rem Podcast [2ZZq6UibGDE @ 00:04:19] flags the residual trap past 90 days: the trustee may sell the note to somebody else, and the lender gets notice of the filing because the debtor is still the borrower, which can invoke the due-on-sale clause. Their subject-to addendum has the seller reaffirm the existing loan for that reason.

The economics check runs both directions. Tim Harrison of Straight Up Mortgage Talk [Qnk52S1LXHI @ 00:01:37] notes the seller's mortgage stays in their name, so a lender can hold it against a seller's next purchase until 12 months of proof that someone else is paying, and a buyer's foreclosure lands on the seller's credit unless the seller brings the loan current. Bramlett Partners [dge6WTAROFI @ 00:04:31] prices the buyer-default scenario: the seller must foreclose to get the house back, a process of six months or so during which the seller keeps paying to protect credit, which is why Bramlett screens on down payment size, credit, and a wrap spread such as a 3.5% underlying rate re-lent at 4.5% or 5%. Eddie Speed [coT9sTaZqQg @ 00:17:09] warns that about 50% of states have delinquent-borrower protection laws that can make a behind-on-payments seller a protected class and put the buyer in a fiduciary role, a fact investors often discover after closing. Ted Thomas [FeymZ_67wns @ 00:03:20] shows why the alternative exit is no rescue: a deed in lieu still leaves a foreclosure on the borrower's record for three to seven years, judgment and tax liens can kill the deal, and in the eyes of the IRS forgiven debt becomes income.

callout.title: Four Kill-Switches Before You Fund a Subject-To or Wrap
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, a scare, or a called loan the practitioners lived through. If any gate fails, the deal does not fund until it is fixed.
items: Ask the seller point-blank whether they are in or considering bankruptcy, and scan for multiple judgments, tax liens, collections or pending evictions before closing [William Tingle — D8NZHrMYpSE @ 00:06:02].

Lock down insurance at closing: seller switches to a landlord policy with the investor added as additional insured, because the declarations page is the trigger 90% of the time [James Bealer — Y7CyY8gLd3U @ 00:03:10].

Route the executed closing packet only to the title company and track the envelope, since a misdirected FedEx put the deed and trust documents on the lender's desk [Sub2Investor — WxPHAXmQ-j4 @ 00:05:08].
Hold a plan B for a called note: the borrower gets roughly 30 days after a notice of default, so be ready to pay off, refinance, or deed back and restructure [KELLY ZITLOW — pYujIjfIOkE @ 00:15:12].

chapters.pull_quote: Deals don't fall apart because of clauses. They fall apart because of panic and bad advice. — Evan Ragsdale (m8scT0nPuzY @ 00:02:47).
action_checklist: Add a notarized affidavit of solvency to every subject-to closing package stating the seller is not considering bankruptcy and can meet all obligations [William Tingle — D8NZHrMYpSE @ 00:08:12].
Paper every subject-to as a wrap: give the seller a promissory note, even performance-only, secured by a mortgage or deed of trust [In Rem Podcast — 2ZZq6UibGDE @ 00:03:02].
Check for bankruptcy flags, record the deed immediately, and keep 91-plus days distance from any known seller distress [Real Estate Law Guys I Asset Protection — nAfkFrw2mTU @ 00:06:46].
Have the seller change the homeowner's policy to a landlord policy and add you as additionally insured right at closing [James Bealer — Y7CyY8gLd3U @ 00:03:10].
Put the full subject-to addendum and disclosures into the purchase contract up front so the paperwork survives close of escrow [Caleb Christopher — 369aexLYPNM @ 00:05:28].
If the due-on-sale clause is called, deed the property back to the original borrower and restructure the position as a contract for deed [Evan Ragsdale — m8scT0nPuzY @ 00:02:08].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I close sub-to and wrap transactions cleanly, and how are seller-financed and wrapped sales taxed?
chapters.title: Closing, Title, and Taxing Creative Sales
chapters.subtitle: Title company vs. law firm closings, title-company questions for creative files, Texas wrap rules and seller disclosures, IRC Section 453 installment sales, Form 6252 reporting, AFR minimum interest, monetized and structured installment sales, 1031 with seller financing, and wrap seller taxation
chapters.executive_summary: Creative-finance closers agree the wrap and subject-to deal lives or dies at the closing table and on Form 6252. Attorney Hamilton Rucker and Scott Horne push files to attorney-run closing offices because escrow officers cannot draft notes or deeds and Texas demands a 7-day underlying-lien disclosure, while Caleb Christopher got turned away cold by a Wisconsin title office. Hans Goldstein shows Professional Equities lets a wrap seller keep the wrapped loan inside the contract price, taxing only cash received, and walks a $1,200,000 sale to a 0.6067 gross profit percentage. Mark J Kohler bars dealers from installment treatment, Patrick Moore models an 8% note netting $10.9 million versus $7.652 million lump sum, and practitioners split over intermediary structures, 1031 note handling, and monetized installment sales flagged on the IRS dirty dozen list.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Attorney Hamilton Rucker frames the wrap as a big box: the seller's existing $100,000 bank loan stays in place as the wrapped note while the buyer signs a new $150,000 note with the seller, so the seller becomes the lender [4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:01:10]. Money flows one way: the buyer sends one $1,500 payment, the seller pays the $1,000 bank installment, and the remaining $500 is the seller's spread, with the seller legally responsible for keeping the underlying loan current [4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:01:50]. The buyer takes a warranty deed at closing, not a lease or rent-to-own, while the property stays subject to the existing lien rather than formally assumed. Hans Goldstein lays out why that structure matters at tax time: under IRS Publication 537, when a buyer assumes or takes subject to a mortgage, the mortgage reduces the contract price and any portion above adjusted basis becomes a year-one payment, handing a low-basis owner with a big loan a large tax bill with little cash [v8iQSeRjmR8 @ 00:00:00]. The wrap escapes that trap because the full Tax Court, in Professional Equities Inc. versus Commissioner, 89 TC 165 decided in 1987, struck down the 1981 temporary regulation that deemed wrapped debt taken subject to, reviving the older Stonecrest method [v8iQSeRjmR8 @ 00:00:38].

On where to close, the practitioners line up hard against the default retail title desk. Rucker states Texas law requires a wrap to close at a title company or an attorney's office to be valid, and that standard contract forms are not enough; the deal needs a custom wrap addendum drafted by a lawyer [4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:06:18]. Scott Horne adds the division of labor: escrow officers have no authority to prepare the note, deed of trust, or warranty deed, so a title company closing without issuing title insurance is really running the file through an affiliated law firm in the background [fNubolIgxnE @ 00:01:05]. Caleb Christopher put this to a live test, calling a Wisconsin title company about a residential subject-to purchase where the seller's mortgage stays in place and there may be no cash to seller; after checking with the owner, the office said it would pass [BBTWC2u7edM @ 00:02:20]. Stephanie at Music City TC treats that refusal as the norm to screen for: on a normal sale almost any title company can close, but an existing loan staying in place, seller notes, arrears, a power of attorney, or an entity buyer will slow down or blow up an inexperienced office, sometimes the week of closing [-AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:00:31].

The tax side agrees on one core mechanic: carry the paper and you pay tax as the money arrives. Mark J Kohler draws the line plainly: take cash or run a 1031 exchange and the installment sale does not apply, but take a note back and carry a first or second trust deed and you have one, with each payment split into capital gain, depreciation recapture, interest, and return of basis [jThMHTcyEdY @ 00:00:21]. Jason D. Knott runs the cleanest version: a $125,000 vacation home with a $105,000 basis produces $20,000 of gain, a 16% gross profit percentage, and $4,000 of reportable gain on each $25,000 annual payment across five years [ifqWkX-3DBI @ 00:03:15]. Jeff Jinks puts scale on it: a $1,000,000 building with a $200,000 adjusted basis carries $800,000 of long-term gain and roughly $200,000 of combined federal, state, and 3.8% Affordable Care Act tax at a rough 25%, which Section 453 can defer for up to 30 years [TZPUpsL8ecI @ 00:02:27]. Kohler flags the baseline prerequisite every flipper must clear: dealers and real estate professionals running fix-and-flips and rehabs do not get installment treatment and owe all the tax now [jThMHTcyEdY @ 00:01:27].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Hans Goldstein walks Form 6252 line by line on a rental building sold for $1,200,000 with a $240,000 down payment and a $960,000 note at 6.5%. Line 5 is the $1,200,000 selling price, line 6 assumed mortgages is $0, line 8 basis is $550,000, line 9 depreciation is $150,000 for a $400,000 adjusted basis, and line 11 selling expenses are $72,000 [mIvRRP_DEd0 @ 00:00:20]. Line 12 recapture stays at $0 because straight-line building depreciation is unrecaptured Section 1250 gain that rides inside the gain and comes out first as payments arrive. Line 19 gross profit percentage is $728,000 divided by $1,200,000, or 0.6067, rounded to at least four digits; year-one line 21 payments of $250,730 produce $152,118 of taxable gain, while the $62,084 of interest skips the form and lands on Schedule B. Year two is plug-and-play: $11,449 of principal times 0.6067 equals $6,946 [mIvRRP_DEd0 @ 00:02:06]. Mark Barnes of Potential CPE adds the recordkeeping discipline: the seller keeps a loan amortization schedule to split interest from principal [mGwBpI_LQw0 @ 00:06:30], and tracks 1250 gain twice, in tax software and in Excel, as audit evidence over a multi-year contract, telling preparers not to be afraid to charge for it [mGwBpI_LQw0 @ 00:08:19].

Pricing the note starts at a floor. Goldstein states installment sale interest must be at least the applicable federal rate, tested at the lowest AFR for the note's term class across the three months ending with the month the binding written contract is signed, under Section 1274(d)(2), and stresses the AFR is a tax minimum rather than a market rate for a private note [-0WdI-B7uuM @ 00:00:00]. Under Revenue Ruling 2026-19, October 2026 monthly-compounding rates were 4.17% short term, 4.52% mid term, and 5.10% long term, and an October contract can borrow the lower August rates. Goldstein's example, a $960,000 note at 6.5% on a 30-year amortization with a 7-year balloon, produces $417,696 of interest over seven years, $62,084 of it in year one, generating $17,259 of year-one tax and $100,329 in total [-0WdI-B7uuM @ 00:01:14]. Patrick Moore of Ironclad Wealth Management warns that pricing below market turns the discount into a gift to the buyer [48sBi3Y9sgE @ 00:06:34], and shows the payoff of charging a risk premium: on $9.5 million of gain, a lump sum nets $7.652 million, a 0% note nets $8.1 million, and an 8% note nets $10.9 million despite about $4 million in tax [48sBi3Y9sgE @ 00:05:01].

Stephanie at Music City TC scripts the title intake. To open the file, get the full list in writing: the signed purchase agreement and every addendum, the seller's most recent mortgage statement, a signed authorization letting the title company talk to the seller's lender, and for an LLC buyer the articles, operating agreement, and proof of good standing [-AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:02:16]. On the settlement statement, the existing loan should not appear as a payoff; demand a draft early and read it line by line for how the loan balance, past-due catch-up, and the seller's escrow balance are shown, then get the exact reinstatement figure in writing from the lender with funds sent straight to the lender at closing [-AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:03:42]. Scott Horne notes Texas subject-to and wrap purchases trigger an underlying lien disclosure notice and an insurance disclosure notice the seller is mandated to give the buyer, paperwork most escrow officers simply never handle [fNubolIgxnE @ 00:03:56]. Rucker covers insurance: never let the seller cancel the old policy, because a bank that sees required coverage dropped may move toward foreclosure; carry double coverage, the original policy for the lender plus a new buyer policy [4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:04:32].
