callout.title: Closer and Tax-Desk Moves the Pros Actually Run
callout.body: Field-tested moves from the closing table and the Form 6252 desk that keep creative files funded and the tax bill tied to cash actually received.
items: Flippers who cannot use installment treatment should still carry paper, but back into a down payment big enough to net the full tax on the gain at closing, so every later payment is after-tax money taxed only on interest [Mark J Kohler — jThMHTcyEdY @ 00:01:40].

Put the carryback note in the qualified intermediary's name: if the seller of the replacement property will not take it, the note is not paid within 180 days, and nobody buys it, the intermediary simply assigns it back and the seller falls back to installment treatment [Asset Preservation, Inc. — uBB6B7Fz6Xc @ 00:09:27].

On wiring, the good answer from a title company is that it will never change wiring instructions by email and you should always call back at a number you already know to confirm [Music City TC — -AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:05:06].

Close creative files at a law-firm closing office that can still order title evidence and issue a title policy anywhere it is needed, so you get both attorney-level answers for buyer and seller and the insurance [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — fNubolIgxnE @ 00:07:13].

sop_steps.title: Interview the closer before sending the file
sop_steps.action: Run the 12 questions across experience, documents, closing handling, and logistics before the contract goes to title.
sop_steps.detail: Ask how many subject-to, seller-finance, or wrap closings the office did in the last year, who handles the file by name, what the underwriter requires, and who drafts the deed, note, and deed of trust; walk away if they have never closed one but will figure it out [Music City TC — -AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:01:05].

sop_steps.title: Serve the disclosures on the calendar
sop_steps.action: Deliver the Texas underlying-loan notice at least 7 days before closing and a complete seller's disclosure notice even as a non-occupant investor.
sop_steps.detail: The notice must list all existing loans and warn of due-on-sale and insurance risk or the buyer can cancel and recover earnest money [Attorney Hamilton Rucker — 4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:05:06]; investors who never lived in the house still fill out the seller's disclosure in detail, including repairs and unpermitted work [Andrea Saavedra, Realtor — VhziKmSIpLQ @ 00:01:57].

sop_steps.title: Price the note above the AFR floor
sop_steps.action: Set stated interest at or above the lowest applicable federal rate in the three-month look-back, then add a private-buyer risk premium.
sop_steps.detail: The AFR is a tax minimum tested in the three months ending with the binding contract month, not a market rate for a private note [Hans Goldstein: Tax & Exit Planning — -0WdI-B7uuM @ 00:00:00]; below-market rates are treated as a gift to the buyer [Ironclad Wealth Management — 48sBi3Y9sgE @ 00:06:34].

sop_steps.title: Elect and report on Form 6252 every year
sop_steps.action: File Form 6252 in the year of sale and complete Part 2 every following year, keeping an amortization schedule alongside.
sop_steps.detail: Part 2 repeats yearly, multiplying principal received by the gross profit percentage while interest goes to Schedule B [Hans Goldstein: Tax & Exit Planning — mIvRRP_DEd0 @ 00:01:46]; skip the form and the full tax balance comes due in year one while payments trickle in over ten years [Ironclad Wealth Management — 48sBi3Y9sgE @ 00:01:49].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Closing venue is the sharpest split. Scott Horne runs his creative files through a law-firm closing office that can still order title evidence nationally. His argument is that escrow officers have no authority to prepare the note, deed of trust, or warranty deed, and the departments of insurance bar them from discussing document provisions with nervous sellers [fNubolIgxnE @ 00:02:09]. His blunt read: if a title company is closing a sub-to without issuing title insurance, you are really closing with an affiliated law firm behind the scenes [fNubolIgxnE @ 00:01:05]. Stephanie at Music City TC keeps the deal inside a title company but interviews it first. She asks how many subject-to, seller-finance, or wrap closings it did in the last year, who the named closer is, and whether the underwriter will insure the structure [-AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:01:05]. Her test is speed and specificity: 'We do a few of those every month' beats 'I'd have to check.' Attorney Hamilton Rucker sets the Texas floor. He says the deal must close at a title company or an attorney's office to be valid, never at the kitchen table, with a lawyer drafting a custom wrap addendum because standard contract forms are not enough [4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:06:18].

On the tax side, the wrap itself has two competing readings. Hans Goldstein lays out the Treasury position. Temporary Treasury Regulation 15A.453-1B3II, issued in 1981, deems the wrapped debt taken subject to even though the seller still owes it. Under that reading the wrap is taxed like an assumption, and mortgage above basis becomes a year-one payment [v8iQSeRjmR8 @ 00:00:17]. Against that, the full Tax Court in Professional Equities Inc. v. Commissioner, 89TC165, decided in 1987, held the regulation invalid and applied the older Stonecrest method. Under that method the contract price includes the full wrap note, the gross profit percentage drops, and year one taxes only the down payment and principal received [v8iQSeRjmR8 @ 00:00:38]. Whether a seller gets installment treatment at all is the second split. Mark Kohler draws a hard line: dealers and real estate professionals doing fix-and-flips and rehabs do not get the installment sale and pay all the tax now. They can still carry paper, provided the down payment covers the tax on the overall gain [jThMHTcyEdY @ 00:01:27]. Jason D. Knott notes the opposite election for eligible sellers: you are allowed to record all of the gain in the year of sale without the cash. His example taxpayer John chose to recognize gain only as the cash arrived [ifqWkX-3DBI @ 00:05:21].

For taking buyer risk off the table, the playbooks diverge hard. Patrick Moore at Ironclad Wealth Management models a plain installment note at 8% interest, because selling to a private buyer is a risky purchase. For the Daniels' $9.5 million gain, that produces $10.9 million in net proceeds versus $7.652 million on a lump sum [48sBi3Y9sgE @ 00:05:01]. His structured version parks the buyer's money with a qualified intermediary, typically a large insurance company, which pays the seller over 10 years at about 5%. That nets roughly $9.9 million and kills default risk, swapping it for intermediary risk [wCs54NX0Oe8 @ 00:04:09]. Jeff Jinks pushes further into monetized installment sales, where the seller takes a loan against the installment income stream for liquidity. The structure sits on the IRS dirty dozen list. He defends it by focusing on the word improper and by ordering an outside-counsel opinion letter on the actual documents before committing [93T1nghQfhs @ 00:04:10]. Asset Preservation, Inc. offers the 1031 route with several exits. The seller can keep the note for Section 453 treatment or assign it to the replacement-property seller. Other options are to have it paid off inside 180 days, buy it back with outside cash, or sell it to a note buyer at a 25% to 40% discount [uBB6B7Fz6Xc @ 00:07:59].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The closing desk is where creative files die first. Caleb Christopher recorded a cold call to a title company in Wisconsin, a state where he had not worked yet. The escrow staffer asked whether the deal was ultimately a cash transaction. Caleb explained there might be no cash to the seller and that it was not an assumption, only continued payment on behalf of the mortgagor. After checking with the owner, the answer was 'we're gonna pass' [BBTWC2u7edM @ 00:02:20]. Scott Horne sees the same reflex everywhere. New investors default to the title company they know, and title company ABC looks at the sub-to and says 'Yeah, we can't do this' [fNubolIgxnE @ 00:08:58]. He adds that many title companies claim to understand creative deals and really do not. By his count only three or four closing outfits in Texas have a working knowledge of this business [fNubolIgxnE @ 00:08:06]. Stephanie at Music City TC says a title company that does not close these regularly will slow you down, ask for things at the last minute, or back out the week of closing. Her red flags: they have never closed a subject-to but will figure it out, cannot state underwriter requirements, will not send a draft settlement statement before closing day, or cannot name who handles the file [-AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:05:23].

The wrap carries traps that detonate after closing. Rucker warns that the due-on-sale clause gives the bank a technical right to call the note. Banks usually do not act while payments arrive on time, but they absolutely can, so the buyer must be ready to refinance and pay off the underlying loan [4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:03:56]. He flags a self-inflicted wound as well. Sellers who cancel the old insurance policy to save money can make the old bank panic and move toward foreclosure. His fix is double coverage: the original policy stays in place and the buyer buys a new one [4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:04:32]. Rucker adds that under Texas law, a missed 7-day underlying-lien notice hands the buyer a right to cancel and recover earnest money. Horne confirms that on sub-to and wrap buys, the seller is mandated to deliver both the underlying lien disclosure and the insurance disclosure [fNubolIgxnE @ 00:03:56]. Andrea Saavedra, Realtor hits investors from another angle. The line 'I never lived in the property' does not exempt an investor from the Texas seller's disclosure notice. The disclosure is a legal representation subject to liability if a buyer reasonably relies on it. A buyer can also terminate for any reason up to seven days after receiving a late notice [VhziKmSIpLQ @ 00:01:57].

The tax math punishes sellers who skip the economics check. Goldstein shows that a low-basis owner with a big loan who takes the assumption route can face a large year-one tax bill with little cash. The gross profit percentage hits 100%, so every later dollar is gain [v8iQSeRjmR8 @ 00:01:45]. He also warns that Section 1245 and 1250 recapture under IRC 453(i) is taxed in full in the year of sale, even if the seller receives nothing that year [mIvRRP_DEd0 @ 00:03:10]. Ironclad's Patrick Moore lists the rest of the damage. The biggest risk is a buyer who cannot pay, forcing a repossession while hoping the asset still runs, and personal guarantees often fall short of the balance. Other income of $500,000 to $600,000 erases the bracket savings. Deferring more than $5 million triggers 453A interest penalties, and below-market interest is treated as a gift to the buyer [48sBi3Y9sgE @ 00:07:10]. Mark Barnes at Potential CPE adds the record-keeping trap. The seller must maintain a loan amortization schedule and track Section 1250 gain twice, in software and in Excel. That worksheet is the evidence in an audit, and the income runs for several years. He also tells preparers not to be afraid to charge for this service [mGwBpI_LQw0 @ 00:08:19].

callout.title: Kill the file before it reaches the closing table
callout.body: Run these four checks before a creative file goes to title, because each one maps to a deal that practitioners watched stall, cancel, or produce a tax bill with no cash behind it [Music City TC — -AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:05:37].
items: Before you send the file, confirm the title company names one closer and states its underwriter requirements. It must also deliver a draft settlement statement that does not show the existing loan as a payoff [Music City TC — -AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:03:25].

In Texas, deliver the list of all existing loans with the due-on-sale and insurance warnings at least 7 days before closing. Otherwise the buyer can cancel and take the earnest money back [Attorney Hamilton Rucker — 4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:05:06].

Keep the seller's original insurance policy in force to satisfy the old bank, and bind a separate buyer policy so the wrap never triggers a foreclosure panic [Attorney Hamilton Rucker — 4coBBRVrtIA @ 00:04:48].

Model year-one tax before signing. Include recapture taxed in full in the sale year and any mortgage above basis on an assumption-style structure, so the seller is not left with a big bill and little cash [Hans Goldstein: Tax & Exit Planning — mIvRRP_DEd0 @ 00:03:10].

chapters.pull_quote: "Trained monkeys guys can draft the closing package, the note, the deed of trust, the warranty deed. It's the other side of the equation, the 90%, the disclosures." — Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network (fNubolIgxnE @ 00:08:25)
action_checklist: Interview the title company with 12 questions in four groups (experience, documents, the closing itself, logistics) before the file is sent [Music City TC — -AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:01:05].

Get the open-file list in writing: signed purchase agreement and every addendum, the seller's latest mortgage statement, a signed lender authorization, and LLC articles, operating agreement, and good-standing proof [Music City TC — -AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:02:16].
Pull the exact reinstatement figure in writing from the lender and have title send it straight to the lender at closing with confirmation afterward [Music City TC — -AAdJ4WwUuM @ 00:03:57].
Use a simple spreadsheet to back into the required down payment so the seller nets the full tax on the gain after closing costs [Mark J Kohler — jThMHTcyEdY @ 00:01:58].

Test stated note interest against the lowest applicable federal rate for the term class in the three months ending with the month of the binding written contract [Hans Goldstein: Tax & Exit Planning — -0WdI-B7uuM @ 00:00:00].

Complete Form 6252 Part 2 every year: gross profit percentage rounded to at least four digits, principal on line 21, interest routed to Schedule B [Hans Goldstein: Tax & Exit Planning — mIvRRP_DEd0 @ 00:01:46].

chapters.question_prompt: How do Dodd-Frank and the SAFE Act apply to seller financing and wraps, and which exemptions and ability-to-repay rules must I follow?
chapters.title: Dodd-Frank and Seller Financing: Exemptions and Ability-to-Repay
chapters.subtitle: One-property and three-property seller exemptions, ATR/QM reasonable determination, when an RMLO is required, SAFE Act/RESPA for owner carry, tax-sale owner financing, and underwriter traps
chapters.executive_summary: Operators selling on owner carry agree Dodd-Frank only bites when a seller carries paper for a buyer who will live in the house, and that land contracts and contracts for deed count too. Outside two lanes, one free pass a year for a natural person, estate, or trust, and three deals in any 12 months, a licensed originator must run the eight-factor ability-to-repay file. Five-year fixed rates, no negative amortization, and 2%-per-year, 6%-lifetime adjustment caps apply, and the three-deal lane bans balloons. Street numbers: $400 to $500 per originator file, a 43% back-end DTI line versus Call the Underwriter's 57% compliance ceiling, and three-year damages exposure that survives as a foreclosure defense. The fights are over stacking LLCs, whether the free pass needs qualifying, and whether compliance pays on cheap houses.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator here draws the same trigger line: Dodd-Frank bites when the buyer will live in the house. Randy Rodenhouse pins it to seller-financed notes originated on or after January 10, 2014 where the buyer occupies the property as a primary residence; a note bought that was originated before that date needs no Dodd-Frank structuring check, and commercial deals, rentals, fix-and-flips, and land sit outside the rules entirely [BjTl8XnBotM @ 00:01:13]. William Bronchick, who reports more than a thousand owner-finance closings as principal, attorney, and title company owner, narrows it the same way: the law reaches the sale of a residential property, mobile homes included, to an owner-occupant, and does not touch an investor buying with seller carry, subject-to, a wraparound, or a lease option, nor a sale to an investor or a commercial buyer [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:07:41]. Ed Billheimer shuts down the obvious workaround: claiming to be an investor while the house is really for your sister 'is not going to fly' [z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:02:24]. Scott Horne, an RMLO, adds that investor purchases stay outside the consumer world, yet when a seller asks to have the investor-buyer processed anyway, the answer is simply to go get it done [1WQyfpf7efQ @ 00:03:57].

The second point of agreement: renaming the paper changes nothing. Billheimer tells sellers that contract for deed, land contract, trust deed, and land trust structures all fall under Dodd-Frank, warning them to be careful what kind of paperwork they use if the plan is to sidestep the rules [z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:07:37]. Dan Deppen of Call the Underwriter says the CFPB issued a statement that every consumer rule applying to mortgages and deeds of trust also applies to land contracts; only the takeback process differs in forfeiture states, while the disclosures and fee limits carry straight over, and Deppen was struck by how many investors believed otherwise after taking over Call the Underwriter [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:43:38]. Bronchick gives the same answer to a webinar attendee who holds title until payoff: an installment land contract is a financing tool and sits inside Dodd-Frank [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:38:24]. Within that scope, ability-to-repay is the center of gravity. Horne calls the ATR rule 'really the number one rule for Dodd-Frank for us people,' paired with staying inside the APR rules, and frames the whole point of pulling buyer information as confirming the buyer can actually repay the note being created [1WQyfpf7efQ @ 00:03:06].

The exemption map is also shared, even where the details later split. Brian Gibbons lays out two lanes: one property in any 12-month period, or three properties in any 12-month period, with a natural person eligible for the single lane and corporations, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and estates working the three-deal lane; every other scenario requires a mortgage loan originator who specializes in seller financing [Ee0wPpu_LNc @ 00:01:13]. Rodenhouse lists the guardrails that ride along with the exemptions: the rate fixed for the first five years, no negative amortization, any adjustment capped at two percent per year and six percent over the life of the loan, the seller cannot be a builder, and the seller must have owned the property [BjTl8XnBotM @ 00:04:46]. Bronchick calls the single lane the 'one free pass' a year for a natural person, estate, or trust, and stresses that an LLC holding a rental and selling it to the tenant falls outside it [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:16:48]. Even with an exemption in hand, Gibbons would still run every deal through an originator, because it kills the buyer's excuse, protects the seller, and denies the buyer a defense in court if the seller is hauled in over the ability-to-repay rule [Ee0wPpu_LNc @ 00:00:49].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The ability-to-repay file is built on eight factors that trainers and practitioners recite almost identically. My Mortgage Trainer lists them: current or reasonably expected income or assets other than the property itself, current employment status, the monthly payment on this loan calculated at the introductory or fully indexed rate whichever is higher, payments on any simultaneous loan on the same property, taxes, insurance and costs like HOA fees or ground rent, debts plus alimony and child support, the debt-to-income ratio or residual income, and credit history; the information relied on must be verified and the evidence retained for at least three years after consummation [3qzRqAVS2ZA @ 00:01:12]. Gibbons stresses that 'reasonable third-party verified information' means, for example, the employer confirming the employment status the borrower wrote on the application [r0FyiCHdxVU @ 00:01:33]. The FDIC's Surge Sen frames the two compliance routes: consider and verify those eight factors, or originate a qualified mortgage, which adds feature limits that non-QM loans do not carry [MfYdg5BCNlk @ 00:02:17]. Patrick Ritchie fills in the underwriting habit on non-employment income such as retirement, disability, or Social Security: the rule of thumb is that it should be likely to continue for at least three years [NXTK3N8EVO8 @ 00:09:17].

Hard numbers are thin, which is why operators bring their own. Bronchick says the only specific guideline in the eight-part test is a 43% back-end debt-to-income cap, and calls it no deal killer because Bronchick's personal owner-carry standard is the old three-to-one rule, roughly a 33% back-end ratio [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:19:24]. Billheimer, a working loan officer, treats 43% as a guideline rather than an absolute requirement; the point is that the ratio looks reasonable [z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:07:13]. Deppen runs a 57% debt-to-income compliance threshold but wants 50% or lower when lending personally because the math is easy to run mentally: a $1,500 payment with no other monthly debts needs $3,000 gross income, and adding a $500 car payment means the buyer needs $4,000 plus [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:23:38]. Ritchie explains why one fixed line misleads: automated approvals through Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, VA, or USDA can push past 43%, a borrower at 52% can still get approved that way, and Ritchie has watched FHA and VA approvals land in the 50% range when the file shows a high FICO score or heavy reserves [NXTK3N8EVO8 @ 00:16:01].

The execution chain is cheap and short. Bronchick literally walked down the hall to a mortgage originator in the same office building: the buyer fills out a 1003 in that office, the originator reviews the eight factors, documents them, enters them into the computer, and spits out about a dozen disclosure forms, all for $500 that gets charged to the buyer and added to closing costs [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:25:25]. In the later webinar Bronchick adds that the job took roughly 40 minutes, that sellers doing volume can charge the buyer a one-point origination fee to cover it, and that outfits in Texas, California, and other states now handle owner-finance origination for anywhere from $500 to $1,500 [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:33:08]. Billheimer maps the timeline: the seller lines up an advisor on contract and note structure plus a loan officer on buyer qualifying before the contract is written, the buyer applies online, both parties sign, the buyer delivers assets, income, and liabilities, the loan officer pulls hard copies like W-2s, title opens, and the seller reviews the loan officer's file before closing [z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:09:05]. Deppen layers on the TRID clock: loan estimate seven business days before closing and closing disclosure three business days before [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:06:10].

callout.title: Structuring Moves Operators Use Inside the Rules
callout.body: Levers the practitioners use to protect yield, qualify thin-file buyers, and keep lease-option exits clean while staying inside the owner-occupant rules.
items: Rent first, then convert: holding a year or more on a rent-to-own before switching to a wrap or contract for deed gives you a payment history to document and long-term capital gain treatment instead of a short-term gain [William Bronchick — ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:19:33].

On a free-and-clear house, throw a $1,000 mortgage on it and sell on a wraparound so the paper becomes a second lien with the 8.5% markup allowance instead of the 6.5% first-lien allowance [William Bronchick — MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:29:01].

For ITIN or blank-credit buyers who can document income, add conditions requiring examples of bills paid every month for the last year, such as utilities, phone, rent, or online subscriptions, to establish payment behavior [Sub2Investor — 1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:21:46].

Underwrite lease-option tenants up front, then pull credit again for a quick delta when they exercise, and write credit and debt-to-income conditions into the option so you are never stuck choosing between violating Dodd-Frank or the agreement [Sub2Investor — 1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:13:54].

sop_steps.title: Classify Occupancy and Exemption Lane
sop_steps.action: Confirm the buyer's intended occupancy and which exemption lane the selling person or entity sits in before structuring any terms.
sop_steps.detail: If the buyer will occupy as a primary residence, Dodd-Frank applies; a natural person, estate, or trust gets one owner-occupant deal per 12 months under the single-property exemption, and an LLC, corporation, or partnership cannot use it [Randy Rodenhouse — BjTl8XnBotM @ 00:03:46]. Any person, estate, trust, or corporate entity gets three deals a year without an originator but must qualify the buyer under the eight-part test and keep the file [William Bronchick — MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:17:40].

sop_steps.title: Pre-Screen the Buyer on DTI Math
sop_steps.action: Run quick debt-to-income math on the buyer before paying for underwriting.
sop_steps.detail: Deppen pre-screens at 50%: a $1,500 payment with no other debts needs $3,000 gross monthly income, and a $500 car payment pushes the requirement to $4,000 plus [Sub2Investor — 1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:23:57]. Bronchick screens tighter with the old three-to-one rule, about a 33% back-end ratio, well under the 43% line [William Bronchick — MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:19:44].

sop_steps.title: Engage the RMLO Before the Contract
sop_steps.action: Bring in the loan officer with your written guidelines before the contract is drafted, and make the contract contingent on loan approval.
sop_steps.detail: Billheimer has the seller contact both an advisor on note structure and a loan officer on buyer qualifying before the contract is written, then the buyer applies online and delivers income, asset, and liability data [Ed Billheimer — z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:09:05]. Bronchick has the RMLO take a 1003 after the contract, test the ratios plus any seller criteria like a minimum credit score, issue an approval, and print the disclosures the buyer signs at closing [William Bronchick — ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:31:41].

sop_steps.title: Build the Collateral File for Resale
sop_steps.action: Assemble the underwriting package, compliance certificate, disclosures, and borrower financials into a note file you retain.
sop_steps.detail: Call the Underwriter issues its own certificate stating the file was reviewed and is Dodd-Frank compliant, since no official certificate exists [Sub2Investor — 1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:26:54]. Seller Finance Consultants says a note's value is created at origination, so the full collateral file must sit in the note file for maximum resale value [Seller Finance Consultants, Inc. — SB_vfxPYuF8 @ 00:02:02], and the ATR evidence must be retained at least three years after consummation [My Mortgage Trainer, Inc. — 3qzRqAVS2ZA @ 00:01:12].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is over entity stacking. William Bronchick, an attorney who says he has closed over a thousand owner finance transactions, argues the three-deal exemption runs per person or per corporate entity, so an LLC owned by you, one owned by your spouse and one owned by your IRA could "jack this to nine deals a year" without a licensed originator [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:20:01]. In his later webinar he pulls back: affiliated entities have not been litigated much, "I don't know," and he probably would not risk it, even while sketching the you, your wife, and 50/50 LLC structure [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:18:34]. Seller Finance Consultants takes the hard opposite line: you cannot just create multiple entities, because that is a blatant attempt to evade Dodd-Frank and its intention, and the same goes for lease options, forbearances, loan modifications and parking the buyer in a title-holding land trust [SB_vfxPYuF8 @ 00:00:43]. Even the counts drift between speakers. Randy Rodenhouse and Brian Gibbons frame the investor lane as three owner-occupant sales per 12 months, while Ed Billheimer describes it as fewer than four in any rolling 12 months, looking back and forward, with the corporate seller allowed to qualify the buyer itself [z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:03:12].

The second fault line is whether to run every owner-occupant deal through an originator. Scott Horne, himself an RMLO, says every state he knows except Texas has no de minimis rule, and Texas's three-property carve-out leaves open whether skipping the first three breaks compliance on the fourth, so he processes the buyer every time [1WQyfpf7efQ @ 00:02:33]. Brian Gibbons concedes the exemptions exist but would still use an originator because it kills the buyer's ability-to-repay defense in court [Ee0wPpu_LNc @ 00:00:49]. Bronchick sits squarely on the other side: his first move with any law is to find an exemption, and he frames the rest as a risk-versus-reward calculation, asking what the odds are that a defaulting buyer can afford an attorney who knows Dodd-Frank and then wins in front of a judge [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:28:37]. He says he has seen not one reported owner-finance case and that a seller who absolutely needs balloons may choose to ignore Dodd-Frank and suffer the consequences. Seller Finance Consultants flips the logic toward resale: even the few exempt loans should get an MLO, because a note's value is created at origination and the collateral file must prove the exemption when the paper is sold [SB_vfxPYuF8 @ 00:01:41].

Lease options and balloons split the room too. Bronchick says a simple lease with option to a tenant for a year or two is not covered, but a ten-year deal with a declining balance that amortizes like a contract for deed arguably is [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:08:36]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy draws no such line, lumping the lease option in with contract-for-deed owner financing as extending credit that must follow Dodd-Frank on any primary residence [o4SYyovrZw4 @ 00:00:27]. Dan Deppen of Call the Underwriter splits the difference: it is not seller financing when signed, but it becomes seller financing on exercise, so he underwrites at the front end and pulls credit again for a quick delta when the tenant exercises [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:13:37]. Balloons draw conflicting readings as well. Rodenhouse says the single-property exemption permits one, Billheimer says a natural-person balloon cannot land until after five years, and Seller Finance Consultants claims an MLO can create the balloon a seller is forbidden to write alone. Inside the three-deal lane, where balloons are banned, Bronchick's workaround is a rate ladder: fixed for five years, then 8, 10 and a 12% cap until the buyer cries uncle and refinances or sells [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:23:32].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The failure everyone circles is the foreclosure counterclaim. Bronchick lays out the exposure: actual damages, statutory damages refunding all interest and fees, plus attorneys' fees and court costs, with a three-year limitations window that does not protect you on a counterclaim, so a buyer foreclosed ten years in can still claim an offset [MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:13:21]. He calls it rare, since a buyer who cannot pay you rarely can pay an attorney who knows Dodd-Frank, yet he still prepares as if it will come up. Gibbons describes the same private cause of action for all finance charges and fees within three years, plus a defense to foreclosure at any time during the life of the loan [r0FyiCHdxVU @ 00:02:15]. Ed Billheimer pushes the stakes higher, opening his session with civil penalties of 5,000 a day, 25,000 a day if reckless and a million a day for violations knowingly committed, along with rescission, refund of all money paid, disgorgement and public notification [z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:00:39]. Deppen frames the realistic version: a loan defaults, you start foreclosure, and the borrower claims they never had the ability to repay and never got the disclosures; without the underwriting package showing on-time disclosures, the outcome rests on judicial discretion, worst case an enforceability problem [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:33:01].

Several shortcuts blow up on contact. Deppen warns against having the borrower sign a deed in lieu at closing to skip foreclosure: the deed is effective the day it is signed, so recording it two years later can mean the loan was never valid and you owe back every payment [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:41:26]. Bronchick flags the cash-heavy buyer with no tax returns: 30% down, self-employed, nothing filed in five or ten years, and Dodd-Frank kills that sale outside the one free pass [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:39:05]. Billheimer shuts down the paper-investor dodge, saying a buyer who claims to be an investor while the house is really for a sister "is not going to fly" [z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:02:24]. Deppen also flags the lease option that promises seller financing at exercise: if the tenant buys two cars and pushes debt-to-income to 80%, the seller is stuck choosing between violating Dodd-Frank or breaching the agreement, which is why he wants credit and debt-to-income conditions written into the option and spelled out verbally [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:14:41]. Bronchick's raw-land fix belongs here too: write in a ban on any structure, camping or residence for the first year, because a buyer who moves a mobile or cabin on within a year drags the sale back under Dodd-Frank.

The economics checks cut both ways. Deppen has watched clean loans with big down payments and good credit sell at 102% of balance, while compliant-but-sketchy paper with a small down payment gets priced to a 15% yield, a huge haircut on a 9%, 30-year note [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:55:26]. Institutional buyers such as First National Acceptance will not even make an offer without the TRD disclosure. Scott Horne says processing the buyer is crucial if you want to sell the mortgage and maximize profit [1WQyfpf7efQ @ 00:04:13]. On cost, Bronchick paid a mortgage guy down the hall 500 bucks for roughly 40 minutes of paperwork, and says outfits in Texas and California charge anywhere from 500 to 1,500, which you can recover with a one-point origination fee charged to the buyer [ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:32:54]. That point counts toward APR, and APR above APOR is what trips higher-cost status at 1.5 points on a first and 3.5 on a second, and high-cost status at 6.5 and 8.5, where prepayment penalties and default rates are barred. Deppen's scale warning for volume sellers: Texas called out Colony Ridge for a default rate around 50 times the national average across thousands of loans [1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:31:21].

callout.title: Four Kill Switches Before You Carry Paper To An Owner-Occupant
callout.body: Each gate below comes straight from a trap a practitioner walked into, watched a client hit, or flagged from closing files. Clear all four before the buyer signs.
items: Occupancy purpose decides coverage, not the name on the deed: a buyer LLC, or an investor story for a house that is really for a sister, does not take a primary residence outside Dodd-Frank [William Bronchick — ZGvGq-_10yA @ 00:37:21].

Never take a deed in lieu at closing as your default remedy, because it is effective on the date signed and can void the loan and force a refund of every payment [Sub2Investor — 1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:41:26].

Keep a written file documenting your due diligence on all eight ATR factors, since considering them without documentation does not hold up when the counterclaim lands [William Bronchick — MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:18:16].
Stress-test residual income, not just DTI: a borrower with four kids in California and about 500 dollars left each month can pass the ratio and still fail [Sub2Investor — 1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:24:46].

chapters.pull_quote: "In my head, I think of it as ... the ability to repay and the willingness to repay." — Dan Deppen, Sub2Investor (1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:22:40).
action_checklist: Classify every sale first: only owner-occupied primary residences trigger the rules, while rentals, fix and flips, commercial and land sales to investors are exempt [Randy Rodenhouse — BjTl8XnBotM @ 00:01:52].
Count your owner-occupant carries per seller type on a rolling 12-month look back and look forward before promising terms [Ed Billheimer — z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:02:49].
Have the buyer complete a Fannie Mae 1003, then verify with bank statements, tax returns, W-2s, recent pay stubs, references and a pulled credit report [William Bronchick — MNznbFmtOwI @ 00:23:37].
Pre-screen with debt-to-income math: a 1,500 PITI plus a 500 car payment needs 4,000 or more in gross monthly income at a 50% line [Sub2Investor — 1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:23:57].
Send the loan estimate seven business days before closing and the closing disclosure three business days before closing [Sub2Investor — 1oenw8zc-5s @ 00:06:10].

Run the owner-carry timeline: seller calls the advisor to structure the note before the contract, loops in a loan officer, buyer applies, and the seller reviews the LO file before closing [Ed Billheimer — z2sAmk5whKo @ 00:09:05].

chapters.question_prompt: What regulatory and servicing infrastructure sits behind a note, from MLO rules to loan servicers and payment histories?
chapters.title: Compliance and Loan Servicing: The Back Office of Every Note
chapters.subtitle: Dodd-Frank origination and MLO compensation rules, RESPA/TILA/ECOA, SAFE Act exam concepts, non-QM qualification, choosing full-service vs. client-managed servicers, servicing timelines, reading payment histories and servicer portals, and why poorly documented seller-finance notes are worthless
chapters.executive_summary: Note operators and servicers converge on one rule: board every note with a licensed servicer, because the servicer is the compliance shield, the fraud preventer, and the payment record that makes paper sellable. Sohail Badruddin sees at least a couple of noncompliant notes a week and rejects or forces reclosing on the blatant ones, while the servicing desk Scott Horne and Sohail walk through runs a fixed waterfall: four-day check hold, underlying lien first, escrow into trust, fee, then remainder to the investor. Street pricing runs $15 to $35 per loan per month for performing paper, roughly $90 plus contingency for full-service collections, and $350 to $700 for attorney-reviewed closing packages. The split comes on control: FIXnotes and Rick of Paperstac keep loss mitigation in-house, while full-service shops can bill a point on UPB when a loan reperforms.

key_metrics.label: Full-Service Collections Servicing Cost
key_metrics.value: About $90 per loan per month plus a contingency fee on collected deals
key_metrics.context: FIXnotes calls this the most an investor pays for servicing and reports never finding a full-service shop at that price with satisfying results.

key_metrics.label: Standard Client-Managed Servicing Fee
key_metrics.value: $30 per loan per month standard; as low as $15 with bare-bones servicers
key_metrics.context: Benchmarked against the BSI itemized fee menu for servicers doing more than sending statements.

key_metrics.label: Attorney-Reviewed Closing Document Package
key_metrics.value: $350 to $400 for a standard note and deed of trust package; $600 to $700 for a wrapped note
key_metrics.context: Sohail Badruddin's pricing for doc prep with attorney review, usually charged to the borrower.

key_metrics.context: Servicer waits for a borrower check to clear before paying the underlying lien, escrow, fee, and investor remainder.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator in this back office starts from the same point: the servicer is not optional overhead, it is the core of the note business. Chris of 7e Investments calls the servicer the heart of the operation, the company that collects payments, keeps the investor inside state and federal rules, and through which everything flows [SZhJFIusBp4 @ 00:00:43]. JKP Holdings host Dave Putz tells every note creator to board with a servicer, because the servicer can and will reject flawed paper, not to be rude but to protect itself from audits [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:06:44]. On the Owner Finance Network walkthrough, Sohail Badruddin and Scott Horne keep the job narrow: the servicer does not modify loans and is not a hardcore collection agency; it collects payments, distributes them properly, and acts as the fraud preventer that keeps money from being pocketed in a distressed stretch instead of paying the mortgage [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:10:34]. The Loan Note Exchange breakdown calls collecting and servicing the long part of a note's life, ten to twenty years of tracking interest, principal, taxes, insurance, and late follow-ups, and rates a clean payment record among the most valuable things a holder owns, because it drives what the note is worth today [epnA26NInuc @ 00:03:37].

The second point of agreement is that the paperwork and the escrow money have to be clean before a servicer will touch them. Sohail reports that Provident Loan Servicing sees at least a couple of noncompliant notes every week; blatant ones get rejected or sent back to be reclosed on the servicer's suggestions, and lenders who refuse cannot be onboarded because a foreclosed borrower will sue everybody involved [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:07:44]. Nathan Turner's North Carolina land contract shows the pattern: a promissory note under one page when Sohail puts normal at three to four pages, a blank notary block, an unrecorded contract, and a seller collecting taxes and insurance inside the payment instead of escrowing them, which Nathan calls the borrower's money, not the lender's [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:20:37]. Horne and Sohail run escrow the same way in daily operations: where no underlying lender escrows, the servicer holds taxes and insurance in a dedicated trust account that nobody else touches, and only principal and interest move on to the investor [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:11:59]. Chris of 7e lists escrow collection as a function every investor must consciously assign, to the servicer, an internal team, or another hire, alongside workouts on non-performing paper [SZhJFIusBp4 @ 00:01:36].

Licensing trainers and servicers describe the same federal overlay, built after the 2008 crisis, sitting on top of owner-occupied paper. Ameritrain boils Dodd-Frank down to three things for an MLO: it created the CFPB, delivered the ability-to-repay rule, and strengthened protections for homeowners after closing [35EmXeZQAsY @ 00:05:13]. Shari Olefson lays out the qualified mortgage lines: no riskier adjustable or balloon structures, a term no longer than 30 years, fees capped at 3%, and monthly expenses no higher than 43% of monthly income, with QM lenders getting protection against lawsuits [g-UjM12V8m0 @ 00:02:32]. Sohail maps that directly onto seller paper: a 30-year, fully amortized, regular-payment note typically lands as QM, while balloons and prepayment penalties push it into non-QM, so the recommendation is to err toward QM because a bank buyer pays more for it, even though most note buyers ignore the distinction [uKK5_EVlvus @ 01:02:09]. SAFE Act trainer Pat O'Connor defines an MLO as someone who takes a residential application and offers or negotiates terms for compensation or gain, and flags the NMLS identifier required on the application, the note, and the mortgage or deed of trust, on top of a 20-hour prelicensing minimum and eight hours of annual continuing education [xZohXlsFnks @ 00:22:30].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The Horne and Sohail timeline starts before closing. The note holder downloads the servicer's package, fills out the investor side early, and the borrower signs their portion at the table; after closing the servicer needs the note, the deed of trust, the closing disclosure, and cancelled checks for ACH [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:01:08]. The first-payment math trips people up: close January 15 and the first payment is March 1, but interest from January 16 to month end and escrow for the stub period plus February still have to be handled, because March pays February's interest backward and March's escrow forward. Their fix is collecting the 15 days of interest and forward escrow at the closing table, or forwarding the escrow piece to the servicer's trust account so nobody chases it when taxes come due [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:02:18]. Within days of boarding, borrowers get a welcome letter and statement by email and mail, with check, Cash App, and ACH options. FIXnotes adds that onboarding is where the servicer's real work sits, uploading the CSV and Excel files, after which mailing houses handle statements [5H6jVWw2QK0 @ 00:04:57]. Loan Note Exchange's worked example shows what gets boarded: $142,000 financed at 7% over 20 years for roughly $1,100 a month [epnA26NInuc @ 00:01:37].

Once money lands, the servicing desk runs a fixed sequence. Checks sit four days to clear; then the servicer pays any underlying lien, pulls escrow into trust, deducts its fee, and forwards the remainder to the investor [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:09:56]. Sohail confirms the same three-to-four business day clearing window on the JKP show, which is why note language ordering a servicer to pay the first lien immediately cannot bind it [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:42:45]. The calendar is simple: due on the 1st, late on the 2nd, a 10-day grace period, and a late charge starting day 11. A late notice plus email, text, and call go out after the grace period; by the 20th the investor is told and urged to call the borrower, and in Texas the recommended law firm sends the initial foreclosure notice on the 20th so months of nonpayment do not pile up [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:19:19]. Escrow shortfalls against an underlying lender come out of the investor's principal and interest, overages are held until the annual analysis, and borrowers cure shortages in a lump sum or over 12 months. On the collection side, FIXnotes pairs one RESPA hello letter with one attorney letter that routes callers to a web form or straight to a cell phone [5H6jVWw2QK0 @ 00:01:11].

Pricing is where operators get nickel-and-dimed. FIXnotes puts full-service collections at about $90 per loan per month plus a contingency fee and says no servicer at that price produced satisfying results; client-managed servicing at $30 is standard, with bare-bones shops as low as $15, and the BSI itemized fee menu is the benchmark for comparing boarding, deboarding, bankruptcy, and loss mitigation charges [5H6jVWw2QK0 @ 00:04:06]. Rick of Paperstac sees performing servicing from $10 to $35, warns that $35 on a $200 payment eats nearly 25% of revenue, and flags full-service shops charging one point on UPB when a loan reperforms [kXMfkHu1Tu0 @ 00:03:17]. Chris of 7e says the $20 to $25 monthly fee balloons to $40 to $45 through add-ons, so the fee schedule must be read side by side with the servicing agreement [SZhJFIusBp4 @ 00:03:22]. Dan Deppen of Fusion Notes runs Allied at $18.50 a month because it is dirt cheap, but keeps a separate spreadsheet to find loans in Allied's unordered account list and decodes notes like S/W BORR for spoke with borrower; FCI costs more but has the cleanest portal, including a payment day variance column that showed a 217-day gap [Wt2pat2PE2w @ 00:18:17].

callout.title: Servicer-Side Edges the Pros Actually Use
callout.body: These are the moves operators run on top of the standard servicing stack to find hidden exits, speed up workouts, and keep paper boardable.
items: Read the servicing notes, not just the ledger: one Paperstac operator paid about $30,000 for a four-years-delinquent contract for deed with a $40,000 payoff because the notes said the borrower would sign a deed in lieu, and the borrower signed once a new owner replaced the rude attorney [Paperstac — VkGqESM8fdY @ 00:03:17].

Hold delegated authority and negotiate yourself: FIXnotes preps the modification the day of the borrower call, sends it with the servicer's ACH authorization form, and sees the loan modified within about 30 days [FIXnotes | Non-Performing Note Investing — 5H6jVWw2QK0 @ 00:02:02].

Patch missing material terms with a borrower-signed addendum instead of a full redo; only an incorrect interest rate or P&I amount forces redoing the documents [Note Investing & Seller Financing - JKP Holdings — uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:09:09].
Favor servicers whose call logs store borrower and lender emails, as Madison's do, so any staffer covering a vacation can follow your written instructions [Fusion Notes — Wt2pat2PE2w @ 00:15:46].

sop_steps.title: Pre-board the investor before closing
sop_steps.action: Download the servicer package, complete the investor side, and send it in ahead of the closing date.
sop_steps.detail: After closing, deliver the note, deed of trust, closing disclosure, and cancelled checks for ACH so the servicer can board immediately [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:00:50].

sop_steps.title: Settle stub interest and escrow at the table
sop_steps.action: Collect the partial-month interest and forward escrow at closing, or forward the escrow piece to the servicer's trust account.
sop_steps.detail: Sohail recommends bringing in the 15 days of interest plus forward escrows at closing so nobody chases the money at tax time [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:03:14].

sop_steps.title: Interview servicers on license, fees, and portal
sop_steps.action: Confirm state licensing, read the fee schedule against the servicing agreement, and test the online portal.
sop_steps.detail: Ask which states the servicer is licensed in first, since New York shrinks the field to one or two servicers [7e Investments — SZhJFIusBp4 @ 00:02:44]; reject any servicer without portal access to pay history and servicing notes [Paperstac — kXMfkHu1Tu0 @ 00:04:29].

sop_steps.title: Run pay history and servicing notes diligence
sop_steps.action: Pull 12 to 24 months of pay history plus the servicing notes from the seller before closing any purchase.
sop_steps.detail: Price rolling-30 payers down and treat rolling-60 as heavy risk [Paperstac — VkGqESM8fdY @ 00:05:20]; always request the servicing notes from the seller during due diligence [Fusion Notes — Wt2pat2PE2w @ 00:03:11].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over who drives the borrower once a loan is boarded. FIXnotes prices full-service collections at roughly 90 bucks a month per loan plus a contingency fee on anything collected, says no full-service shop has delivered results worth that, and calls client-managed servicing the sweet spot, where the licensed servicer handles statements and year-end tax accounting while the investor or a hired attorney runs skip tracing, letters and modification calls [5H6jVWw2QK0 @ 00:00:00]. Rick at Paperstac refuses to crown one model and matches the shop to the operator instead: FCI lets a hands-on investor set up and drive their own loss mitigation flows, while SN likes to take control for investors who would rather sit in the back seat [kXMfkHu1Tu0 @ 00:02:10]. Scott Horne's servicing desk draws the hardest line, stating the servicer does not make decisions to modify a loan and is not really the collection agent, only collecting payments, distributing them properly and acting as the fraud preventer [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:10:34]. Yet that same Texas operation has its recommended law firm send the initial foreclosure notice on the 20th of the month if the payment has not landed, specifically so investors do not sit idle while a borrower slides one, two, then three months behind [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:19:19].

Price is where the numbers split, and every practitioner quotes a different floor and ceiling. FIXnotes calls 30 bucks per loan per month pretty standard for a servicer doing more than mailing statements, and has seen bare-bones shops go as low as $15 [5H6jVWw2QK0 @ 00:04:06]. Rick at Paperstac has seen performing servicing anywhere from 10 or 15 dollars up to 35, and warns that 35 bucks against a 200-dollar payment knocks out nearly 25 percent of revenue and starts eating yield [kXMfkHu1Tu0 @ 00:02:41]. Chris at 7e Investments argues the headline rate is the wrong number to shop at all: servicers tack on monthly add-ons, so a loan you think costs 20 or 25 bucks turns into 40 or 45 very quickly, which is why the fee schedule has to be read side by side with the servicing agreement before signing [SZhJFIusBp4 @ 00:03:22]. Dan Deppen at Fusion Notes shows the trade-off from inside live portals, calling Allied definitely not easy to work with yet keeping loans there for one reason, because they are dirt cheap at 18.50 a month [Wt2pat2PE2w @ 00:18:17]. The cheap-shop camp is buying margin and paying for it in decoding time; the other camps are buying visibility and fewer surprises on the invoice.

Practitioners also split on what belongs in the paper itself. Loan Note Exchange walks a seller-financed example where payments run on a 20-year schedule but a balloon brings about $112,000 due all at once after seven years, presenting it as an ordinary term choice [epnA26NInuc @ 00:01:59]. Sohail Badruddin of Provident Loan Servicing takes the opposite line on owner-occupied paper: balloons, don't do it; interest-only, don't do it; and anything under a five-year balloon Provident will not even board [uKK5_EVlvus @ 01:01:17]. Even inside that same episode the room splits on prepayment penalties, with one host stating they are against the law on owner-occupied notes and Sohail correcting that you can do it, it is just not how you would want to, the same way balloons are frowned upon rather than illegal [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:59:48]. Dani Rudd of Legacy Mutual Mortgage pushes from the other direction on non-qualified product, noting a non-QM loan with as little as 10 percent down carries no PMI and that its rates have lately been pricing better than qualified mortgages [5VZzJLRM1kI @ 00:04:07]. The operator read: the balloon and non-QM structures one camp treats as routine, the servicing camp may refuse to board at all.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Nathan Turner's North Carolina file is the cleanest anatomy of worthless paper. On the surface the numbers looked great: roughly $200,000 of property value, a $145,000 sale price, $30,000 down, 10 percent interest on a 30-year amortization. Then the promissory note turned out to be less than a page, and Nathan knew without reading a word that this was not going to be good [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:15:41]. The signatures were there but the notary block was blank, which the hosts treat as unenforceable on its face [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:20:04]. The servicing history showed the seller collecting principal, interest, taxes and insurance as one payment and keeping the escrow, which Nathan calls a big no-no because that is the borrower's money held for them [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:20:37]. The contract for deed was never recorded, which Nathan says means it does not exist in the judicial system, so there is nothing to enforce when payments stop, and the last three months of payments had already been missed, making it a non-performing note on top of everything else. Nathan told the seller to tune it up first; the seller never fixed it, and the deal died [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:22:27].

When paper like that reaches a servicer, the reversal comes fast. Sohail sees at least a couple of non-compliant notes a week; the blatantly out-of-compliance ones get rejected or sent back for the lender to reclose with Provident's corrections, and lenders who refuse simply cannot board, because the servicer will not absorb the reputational risk of a borrower who sues everybody involved [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:07:44]. In court the downside is worse: best case the documents get corrected, worst case a judge nullifies the contract with a rescission, the lender refunds everything the borrower paid over, say, five years, and then waits for the property to be vacated; on a wrap, most of those proceeds already went to the underlying note [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:13:40]. The panel also kills the pre-signed deed in lieu and the clause making a note null and void at 30 days in arrears, because a borrower cannot be bound in advance to hand the property back without court involvement [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:48:47]. The flip side shows up at Paperstac: a four-years-delinquent contract for deed sat dead because the borrower stopped answering a rude attorney, and the Paperstac host read the servicing notes, called, and got the deed in lieu [VkGqESM8fdY @ 00:04:07].

The quieter losses are operational. Scott Horne's servicing desk explains that when the escrow being collected runs short of what the underlying lien holder charges, the shortfall cannot be short-paid and comes straight out of the lender's principal and interest payment [adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:13:11]. Dan Deppen has owned loans where the borrower kept paying while the servicer allocated every dollar to interest, late fees and lender advances, with none of it reaching principal, which is why each payment's breakdown has to be checked before it goes into the books [Wt2pat2PE2w @ 00:07:11]. Rick at Paperstac warns that a servicer's loss mitigation pricing can hide a point on the UPB when a loan reperforms, a fee that may be worth paying if the servicer did the work, but not if the investor did the outreach and the servicer collects at each hurdle [kXMfkHu1Tu0 @ 00:03:17]. Sohail flags a late charge written as 5 percent of the total payment due: charging on escrows just for being late puts the lender out of compliance and can land them in court, so the charge has to run on principal and interest only [uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:54:28]. Each leak looks small on one statement and only surfaces when the investor actually reconciles.

callout.title: Kill Or Reprice The Note Before It Boards
callout.body: Every item below comes from a file a practitioner either walked away from, got rejected on, or had to clean up after. Run all four before money moves.
items: Pull the promissory note, notary block and recording proof first; a sub-one-page note, a blank notary block or an unrecorded contract for deed means walk or force a reclose [Note Investing & Seller Financing - JKP Holdings — uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:20:04].
Read 12 to 24 months of pay history alongside the servicing notes; knock the price down for rolling 30s and price in heavy risk for rolling 60s [Paperstac — VkGqESM8fdY @ 00:06:38].

Take payoff figures only from the lender directly or that lender's servicer directly, never from a third party, because payoff fraud happens out there every day [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:16:51].
Lay the servicer's fee schedule over the servicing agreement line by line so a 20 to 25 dollar quote does not quietly become 40 to 45 [7e Investments — SZhJFIusBp4 @ 00:03:22].

chapters.pull_quote: A servicer is kind of like the placeholder in football where they hold it for the kicker; they did their job as expected, but if they screw up then it's magnified to the extreme. Attributed to 7e Investments (SZhJFIusBp4 @ 00:02:11).
action_checklist: Download and complete the investor side of the servicer's boarding package before closing, then deliver the note, deed of trust, closing disclosure and ACH paperwork right after signing [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:01:08].

Have a doc-prep attorney review every note and deed of trust instead of reusing a template, budgeting about $350 to $400 for a standard package and $600 to $700 for a wrap, usually charged to the borrower [Note Investing & Seller Financing - JKP Holdings — uKK5_EVlvus @ 00:12:47].

Interview servicers on which states they are licensed in before buying notes there, since markets like New York leave only one or two servicers to choose from [7e Investments — SZhJFIusBp4 @ 00:02:29].

Pull a servicer's published itemized fee menu covering boarding, deboarding, bankruptcy, escrow, foreclosure and loss mit so every servicer interview is priced against it [FIXnotes | Non-Performing Note Investing — 5H6jVWw2QK0 @ 00:02:56].

Pair the servicer's hello letter with one attorney letter that routes the borrower to a web form or a call to your cell, then send the modification and ACH form the same day so the loan is modified within about 30 days [FIXnotes | Non-Performing Note Investing — 5H6jVWw2QK0 @ 00:01:11].

Put every borrower workout or loan modification in writing and send it to the servicer so they can adjust terms and stop reporting the borrower late or pursuing foreclosure [Scott Horne's Owner Finance Network — adTW0EyLeRk @ 00:20:31].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I become the bank by buying performing and non-performing mortgage notes at a discount, and how do I profit from them?
chapters.title: Buying Mortgage Notes: Discounted and Non-Performing Loan Investing
chapters.subtitle: Where to source notes, buying at deep discounts, non-performing note resolutions and six exit strategies, notes vs. rentals returns, note funds vs. direct buying, first-purchase stories, and 'become the bank' breakdowns
chapters.executive_summary: Note buyers, from boutique shops to a $600-700M NPL desk, agree that non-performing mortgage paper trades cheap because banks refuse partial payments and dump defaults at 25-60% of value. They also report that most defaults trace to a life event and that many of those borrowers can be brought back to paying. The operator consensus is to buy first-position, secured, single-family collateral with deep equity. Hire a licensed servicer. Then exit through the borrower via forbearance, modification and resale rather than foreclosure. Street pricing runs from 96 cents for scratch-and-dent paper down to roughly 40 cents at notice of sale, and PPR prices off the lower of UPB or property value. Reported results include 90% reperformance, an 11.5% average yield and a 20% IRR on a 189-loan trade. Practitioners split on whether NPL foreclose-and-flip suits beginners and whether to buy notes directly or through a fund.

key_metrics.label: NPL Reperformance Rate
key_metrics.context: Lauren Wells of 7e Investments reports that about 90% of the non-performing notes the firm buys return to paying status. Under 5% are liquidated, tracked against biweekly benchmarks.

key_metrics.label: Seasoned Portfolio Average Yield
key_metrics.context: Kevin Shortle, a former commercial appraiser with 30+ years in notes, reports an 11.5% average yield with an 86% investment-to-balance ratio and investment-to-value under 60%.

key_metrics.label: 189-Loan NPL Trade IRR
key_metrics.context: PPR bought about $23M UPB against about $50M property value for about $18M. Over 50% reperformed, about 25% paid off or short-sold and about 20% foreclosed, over an 18-month weighted average hold.

key_metrics.label: DIY vs. Fund Return Spread
key_metrics.context: Rick Allen and TJ Osterman report that direct note buyers earn 12-18% and that NPLs have hit 40-50%, but that direct buyers will lose some deals. Funds spread risk at lower 8-12% returns.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator here agrees that the inventory exists because of a broken bank workflow, not broken borrowers. Lauren Wells of 7e Investments says roughly 90 to 95 percent of the non-performing notes the firm buys trace back to a life event: job loss, a death, a health crisis or COVID [nauUgmh1YZg @ 00:04:00]. 7e's fund walkthrough adds the mechanical trigger. Banks refuse partial payments, so a three-month delinquency snowballs into a twelve-month one. The firm then steps in to renegotiate so the borrower's payments become investor distributions [El1w73FgjM0 @ 00:00:11]. Larry Hoffman explains why the paper hits the street cheap. Banks dump non-performing loans to free lending capacity and satisfy regulators, at 25 to 60 percent of their actual dollar value [R_jwbBWh1LA @ 00:04:43]. FIXnotes adds that charge-off is how most loans reach the secondary market in the first place [lxjMbDIOEGw @ 00:03:33]. The consensus play follows directly. Buy the debt at a deep discount, step into the lender's shoes and fix the payment relationship the bank was too rigid to fix. The business is the spread between what the seller accepts and what the borrower ultimately pays or the collateral fetches. These operators price from that gap rather than from face value.

The second point of agreement is collateral discipline. Bill Mencarow of Paper Source tells beginners to buy first-position notes only and to stick to single-family homes or farmland. Mencarow also tells them to ask whether they would actually want to own the property, and rules out factories and shopping centers [LuxJXWLFKHI @ 00:13:54]. FIXnotes puts a number on why lien position matters. An unsecured loan is worth roughly 100 times less, about 50 basis points versus 50 cents, so checking county records for secured status and lien position comes before any bid [lxjMbDIOEGw @ 00:01:23]. Sierra Davis, a data scientist who buys and originates notes, warns that junior liens carry wipe-out risk and pushes secured paper only [UimgP_cJydU @ 00:17:39]. Institutional buyers run the same filter at scale: PPR Capital Management's NPL book is 1-to-4 unit residential and 99 percent single-family detached [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:02:11]. The equity cushion is the other half of the rule. Mencarow calls a down payment under 15 to 20 percent scary and says mobile homes with zero or $1,000 down usually default. The best collateral, per Mencarow, is an owner-occupied single-family home in a stable, diversified economy, backed by an amortized note rather than a balloon. That cushion lets an operator negotiate from strength instead of hoping the market holds.

Third, practitioners agree the money is made through the borrower, not the courthouse. PPR's Taylor Nelson says every exit decision starts with borrower intent. Nelson adds that exiting through the borrower (reperform, season, resell) is more profitable '99% of the time' [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:06:37]. Mencarow has been investing in notes since the 1980s, has never foreclosed and negotiates instead [LuxJXWLFKHI @ 00:16:46]. FIXnotes lays out six exits: full or discounted payoff, modification or structured settlement, cash for keys or deed in lieu, short sale, foreclosure, and an NPL loan sale to a local investor. It ranks foreclosure as the least favorable of the six [qxx8ymWOrGU @ 00:03:34]. Colin Whitenack describes the same posture. Close, get a servicer involved because you cannot service the mortgage yourself, then enter 'problem-solving mode,' where the borrower either reperforms or gets help exiting the property [gxiK62dzE34 @ 00:00:42]. The servicer point is near-universal. PPR outsourced servicing after Dodd-Frank, Davis insists on a licensed servicer, and FIXnotes calls skipping servicing to save $25 a false economy. A reperformed loan can then be held for cash flow or sold to performing-note buyers. That resale is the flip that turns a distressed purchase into a realized gain, with foreclosure kept as the backstop that gives negotiation its teeth.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Pricing is where the operators get specific. Lee Arnold's ladder starts from a $100,000 note at 8 percent over 30 years, about $833 a month, and walks the price down as the paper gets uglier. Arnold quotes 96 cents for scratch-and-dent paper paid past the 15-day grace period, 92 cents for 30-to-60-day slow-pay, and 80 to 84 cents once the borrower stops responding [tszcHb-Spo4 @ 00:02:25]. The price falls to 60 to 65 cents at notice of default or lis pendens and roughly 40 cents at notice of sale. At that stage, a modification that restores the note to $100,000 turns a $40,000 buy into a $60,000 profit [tszcHb-Spo4 @ 00:03:39]. PPR's Nelson prices off the lower of the loan balance or the property value. That means 80 to 90 cents of UPB on equity loans and about 70 cents of property value on upside-down ones [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:13:56]. Wells reports that 7e buys at 40 to 60 percent of value from credit unions, whole-loan traders, liquidating funds and a broker's weekly list [nauUgmh1YZg @ 00:05:54]. Sierra Davis runs the yield math backward. Take a $40,000 UPB note paying $500 a month at 8.5 percent, secured by a $100,000 property. Offering $22,000 targets a 12 to 15 percent yield and nets about $475 a month after servicing.

The diligence and closing sequence is consistent across shops. PPR prices the data tape first and submits a bid. Once awarded, it runs 30 to 60 days of diligence on collateral, the assignment chain, tax and title, and a drive-by BPO, then closes 30 to 45 days after that [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:15:09]. Davis compresses the retail version into an indicative offer followed by 14 to 21 days of diligence on the three Ps: people, property and paperwork. Davis prefers 24 to 48 months of payment seasoning, closes with an assignment and allonge, then boards the loan with a servicer [UimgP_cJydU @ 00:33:40]. Whitenack's checklist is the field version. Order a BPO, review payment history, rates, amounts paid, the last payment and anything unusual, and confirm insurance is in place and taxes are current [gxiK62dzE34 @ 00:00:16]. Sourcing feeds the front of that pipeline. Dan of Fusion Notes names Paperstac, Tradex and Watermark Exchange, plus Facebook buy/sell groups where you post your buy criteria and conferences like Note Expo, DME and IMN. Dan then points to two overlooked channels. Foreclosure attorneys have large investor networks, and loan servicers know which clients are selling portfolios or closing funds [PXDW2SqUfMA @ 00:01:19]. Davis caps exposure at or below 75 percent ITV and prices to the worst-case exit.

Once the loan is boarded, the workout script decides the return. FIXnotes says the two biggest points of loan resolution are building rapport and gathering intel, while playing good cop against an unseen 'loan committee' [lxjMbDIOEGw @ 00:05:29]. Every call runs on three questions: What happened? Where are you now? What do you want to do? [lxjMbDIOEGw @ 00:06:48]. In the FIXnotes lifecycle, a loan goes 90 days late, gets a demand letter, then moves to forbearance, modification, reinstatement or foreclosure. FIXnotes favors forbearance because it keeps the foreclosure pending and avoids modification phantom income, and writes its modifications at 9 percent and up. 7e's sequence is an attorney demand letter, then a negotiated plan, then reperformance [El1w73FgjM0 @ 00:07:24]. Wells describes the plan itself: forbearance or a trial plan for six months, then a loan modification. Arrears are wrapped to the end of the loan or paid quarterly, and the reperformed note is then resold for profit [nauUgmh1YZg @ 00:05:15]. PPR's modification toolbox adds deferring principal to a balloon and extending terms to 30 or 40 years. The FIXnotes exit menu supplies the stick: a deed in lieu, cash for keys, or a short sale where waiving the deficiency buys cooperation. 7e frames having multiple exits as the negotiating leverage itself.

callout.title: Edges the Operators Use at the Bid and the Workout
callout.body: These are the moves practitioners say widen the spread between purchase basis and realized exit, from bidding to deal structure to off-market sourcing.
items: Bid lower on loans carrying legacy 3-5% rates. Those borrowers can afford to reinstate, which kills the upside, so write your own modifications at 9% and up [FIXnotes | Non-Performing Note Investing — lxjMbDIOEGw @ 00:07:28].

In a partial, the buyer still receives a full assignment and endorsement, the purchase agreement limits the months bought, and the note is reassigned back afterward. The ideal partial makes you whole, and everything after it is gravy [Paperstac — Il6eOQ_69VM @ 00:14:44].

Create sellable paper. On a $100K lot, the most Kevin Shortle pays for a $90K or $80K note is $70K. Fix it by splitting into a $70K first, a $20K second and $10K down [Investor Fuel - Real Estate Mastermind — VrGeElvxk5E @ 00:22:01].

Work loan servicers for off-market supply. They know which clients are selling portfolios or closing funds, and foreclosure attorneys can connect you to their investor networks [Fusion Notes — PXDW2SqUfMA @ 00:01:36].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether to run your own tape or hand capital to a fund. Rick Allen and TJ Osterman of Paperstac put DIY returns at 12 to 18 percent, with non-performing loans hitting 40 to 50 percent, but they warn flatly that you will lose some deals, while fund returns sit in the 8 to 12 percent band with risk spread across the book [EdBetMgLDeQ @ 00:06:20]. Their answer is a hybrid: park $100K of $150K in funds and run the remainder through partials and hypothecation, or split $500K into $400K passive and $100K active [EdBetMgLDeQ @ 00:15:35]. 7e Investments sells the passive side directly, quoting a $5K Reg A+ minimum at 7 percent for one year or 8 percent for four years, and an accredited-only Reg D Class E5 bond paying 11 percent monthly on a $500K minimum [El1w73FgjM0 @ 00:03:15]. Kevin Shortle, running a personal book after 30-plus years, reports an 11.5 percent average yield at 86 percent investment-to-balance and under 60 percent investment-to-value [VrGeElvxk5E @ 00:17:02]. The operator read: a solo buyer who executes well matches or beats the top fund tier, but absorbs every blown deal personally instead of across 120-plus pooled assets.

Practitioners split hard on whether non-performing paper is a beginner play. Stealth Wealth pitches buying non-performing notes, foreclosing, and flipping as low risk and says it works especially well for investors who are just starting out [0m8vHNeASRY @ 00:06:24]. Bill Mencarow of Paper Source tells newcomers on Toby Mathis's channel to get a mentor and stick only with first-position notes, and adds that in notes since the 80s Bill has never foreclosed, negotiating every time instead [LuxJXWLFKHI @ 00:13:54]. FIXnotes treats the property as the outcome to avoid: set upset bids low because REOs are the opposite of why they are in the business, and buy under 60 cents so even a 70-cent recovery still pays [lxjMbDIOEGw @ 00:04:18]. Taylor Nelson at PPR Capital Management ranks exiting through the borrower as more profitable 99 percent of the time, reperforming, seasoning, and reselling rather than taking title [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:06:37]. The FIXnotes six-exit menu still keeps foreclosure live as the least favorable lever, alongside cash for keys, deed in lieu as the stick, and short sales where waiving the deficiency buys cooperation. Net: the foreclose-and-flip camp is a minority voice, and the operators with the biggest books push negotiation and treat the courthouse as leverage, not the business model.

Pricing frameworks diverge too. Lee Arnold anchors to cents on the note balance by delinquency stage: 96 for scratch-and-dent, 92 for slow-pay, 80 to 84 for non-performing with no response, 60 to 65 at notice of default, and about 40 at notice of sale [tszcHb-Spo4 @ 00:02:25]. PPR instead works off the lower of loan balance or property value, paying 80 to 90 cents of UPB on equity loans and about 70 cents of property value on upside-down loans [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:14:14]. Larry Hoffman frames bank dumps at 25 to 60 percent of actual dollar value, while Preferred Trust guest Lauren Wells of 7e buys at 40 to 60 percent [R_jwbBWh1LA @ 00:04:58]. Servicing splits the same way: PPR outsourced to a licensed servicer that executes its loss-mitigation waterfall, while FIXnotes pushes client-managed servicing and calls skipping a servicer to save $25 a false economy [lxjMbDIOEGw @ 00:09:31]. On exits, Bill Mencarow sells the next nine years of payments and keeps the tail, Tracy Rewey sells a partial that makes the seller whole so everything out in the future is gravy, and Kevin Shortle buys the next 40 of 56 payments. Pick one pricing model and one servicing model before you bid, and run every tape through the same math.
