sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Time is the silent killer of NPL returns. Taylor Nelson of PPR describes a loan underwritten for a 12-month hold that a Chapter 13 bankruptcy filing stretched to 36 months, still closing at roughly a 20 to 25 percent return but tying up capital three times longer than projected [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:20:18]. Sierra Davis flags that foreclosure timelines vary by state, with New York able to take years, and that junior liens carry wipe-out risk [UimgP_cJydU @ 00:15:35]. Kevin Shortle puts Florida foreclosure at about 18 months, warns that a contested contract for deed can be forced into foreclosure by a judge, and notes COVID-era modifications stretched some loans to 60 years before rules changed October 1, with foreclosures expected to rise from here [VrGeElvxk5E @ 00:28:24]. PPR's own 189-loan trade, roughly $23M UPB against $50M of property value bought for about $18M, still saw about 20 percent foreclose, even as it produced about $8M gross profit at a 20 percent IRR over an 18-month weighted hold [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:21:34]. The check: model the worst-case state timeline and a bankruptcy delay into every bid, because even a well-bought 189-loan book carried a one-in-five foreclosure rate and holds that can triple. Plan reserves accordingly.

Overpaying is the most repeated self-inflicted wound. FIXnotes warns that borrowers sitting on 3 to 5 percent legacy rates can simply reinstate, leaving you holding cheap debt, so the bid has to drop for those files, while their own modifications get written at 9 percent and up [lxjMbDIOEGw @ 00:07:28]. PPR confirms the resale side of that trap: low-coupon loans fetch a weaker price when you go to sell the reperformed paper [DEk2gIFHJiM @ 00:12:02]. Kevin Shortle sees the same mistake on note creation, where a seller carries a $90K or $80K note on a $100K lot and Kevin pays at most $70K for it; the fix is structuring a $70K first, a $20K second, and $10K down so the paper is sellable [VrGeElvxk5E @ 00:21:12]. Bill Mencarow adds collateral traps: a down payment under 15 to 20 percent is scary, and mobile homes sold with $0 or $1,000 down usually default, so stick to single-family homes or farmland over factories and shopping centers, and ask whether you would want to own the property [LuxJXWLFKHI @ 00:14:30]. Personal Finance for Everyone lists skipping diligence, overpaying, impatience, and thin cash reserves as the four standard ways a cheap note becomes a costly mistake.

Even the passive route has trapdoors. Rick Allen and TJ Osterman describe note investing as very passive until it is not, then very involved, and admit Reg A+ was exorbitant once you stack an attorney, accountant, controller, fund admin, and two audits, which is why they would pick Reg D in hindsight [EdBetMgLDeQ @ 00:04:08]. Lauren Wells of 7e reports the honest loss line from just under 100 loans: less than $8,000 lost across three loans in a year and a half, with about 5 percent going through full foreclosure via a partner REO firm [nauUgmh1YZg @ 00:09:18]. 7e's own fund walkthrough labels the investments speculative and illiquid and flags rising delinquencies and flattening values as the reason for stricter buying [El1w73FgjM0 @ 00:12:05]. Tracy Rewey, in the business since 1988, tells newcomers to expect that not every note pays and to learn the financial calculator [Il6eOQ_69VM @ 00:23:49]. Fusion Notes adds a sourcing trap: the best deals never really hit the street, so a buyer who fails to close inside a stated buy box never sees the good paper. The economics check is simple: budget for losses, fund overhead, and dead time before you count the yield.

callout.body: Each gate comes from a loss, delay, or pricing mistake the practitioners hit or watched others hit. If a file fails any one of them, the bid dies or the price drops.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I sell, partial out, fund, and trade notes, including notes I create from my own seller-financed or wrapped deals?
chapters.title: Note Exits and Liquidity: Partials, Sales, Funding, and Marketplaces
chapters.subtitle: Selling partials, selling a note after one payment, pricing a note for sale, buying notes with no money, five creative funding sources, hypothecation with local banks, turning a rental into a note, Paperstac listings and trading, note arbitrage, and first-deal mistakes
chapters.executive_summary: Note holders exit through three doors: a full sale, a partial sale of the next block of payments, or borrowing against the paper. Fred and Tracy Rewey, Cal Ewing, and the Paperstac operators agree the partial is the sharpest lever. It lets a holder raise cash at 10-13% investor yields while keeping the tail, and the buy-full, sell-front-partial play can recover nearly all capital. Seasoning drives price: Moxxie buys after one payment, but 6-12 months moves offers and 24+ is stronger. Bank-like paper fetches 95-98% of principal versus 90%-70% for seller-finance notes. Marketplaces bundle listing, escrow, collateral audit, timed auctions, and an AI price predictor. Disagreements center on leverage: Justin Roberts hypothecates notes with local banks at about 80%, the JKP host doubts a 10x leverage claim, and Paperstac calls partials on wraps potentially sticky.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across the Paperstac, Rewey, and Cal Ewing camps, the partial is the default liquidity lever for a performing note. Instead of dumping the whole asset, the holder sells a defined block of upcoming payments and keeps the tail. Paperstac frames it as buying, say, 100 of 360 payments. The seller steps back in if the borrower defaults, and only certain servicers are set up to handle the split [XRyBErGyKgQ @ 00:06:24]. Fred and Tracy Rewey run the classic version on an $86,900 note at 9.5%. An investor buys the next 96 of 176 payments for $47,615 at a 13.3% yield, and the seller is owed $47,249 when the note reassigns. Partial size is dictated by how much cash the seller actually needs [UwiEQOh84Y4 @ 00:17:14]. Cal Ewing used the same move on a Laredo-area mobile-home note when a private lender needed repair cash. Cal sold the next 120 payments to an IRA investor for 55,000 while keeping a 130-plus payment tail valued at 95,402 at full term [LCY-eZOK6gw @ 00:09:12]. Texas Capital Finance lists full and partial sales as the two exit types and says partials often command a higher price. That gives holders a reason to price both before letting go of the whole income stream [w4PRGbUrreA @ 00:02:30].

The exit price is set long before the sale, at origination and through seasoning. Moxxie's senior note analyst Dawn says a note can technically sell the day after it is created, and Moxxie will buy once the first payment lands. Even so, six to 12 months of consistent payments 'can make a real difference' and 24 months or more is stronger. With zero history, pricing has to lean on borrower credit, down payment and structure alone [usXnfzN3Wmc @ 00:01:02]. Cherif Medawar's buy-side checklist mirrors that: 6 months to a year of on-time payments, a real cash down payment, credit actually run, and collateral comps. Medawar's reason is that borrowers with no skin in the game walk away [bhfdMe7Dpwk @ 00:06:55]. Texas Capital Finance puts the spread in numbers. Bank-like loans sell for 95-98% of principal while seller-finance notes sell between 90% and 70%, and the closer the paper resembles a traditional bank mortgage, the higher the price [w4PRGbUrreA @ 00:08:46]. Sierra Davis adds the hard floor on paperwork: 'If the paperwork is not good, you can't forclose on it.' A broken chain of assignment or a missing promissory note kills value no matter how clean the pay history looks [XsNZ5SQXdCI @ 00:16:34].

On the full-sale side, the consensus venue is the online marketplace that bundles listing with closing. Rick Allen and Brett Berkkey of Paperstac, on Patrick Franz's show, describe the platform as 'MLS plus the title company.' Some deals sold 'in the first hour' and a pool of Colorado land notes went the same day, while listings that sit 30 days without an update expire [y6ljJ3T0eNg @ 00:33:07]. The Paperstac listing walkthrough tells sellers to pre-load files, a recent BPO and pay history, because buyers will ask for them anyway. Sellers then pick flexible, firm or make-an-offer pricing and write a description that tells the story [chL0454K1Zs @ 00:01:09]. The relaunch team warns that mispriced assets 'go to die,' and the platform now runs a price predictor retrained monthly on about 40 data points [zhg1k-uMJM0 @ 00:16:15]. Paperstac's first-deal mistakes episode drives home the back-office rule that protects every future exit: 'Record your assignments and record your deeds.' Unrecorded paper knocks buyers out of the chain of title. In their examples, one buyer surfaced three years later and tax notices arrived 18 months after a sale [MkofIE1Xq0o @ 00:14:43].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The most-repeated street play is to buy the whole note, sell a front partial that recovers the cost, and keep the tail for close to nothing. The Reweys' Dallas deal is the template. They bought a $54,000 note at 11.5% for $47,500, then sold the next 279 payments for $51,000 to an investor earning 11.7%. They netted $3,500 at closing and kept 79 payments, which paid out when the loan cleared after 18 years [UwiEQOh84Y4 @ 00:28:05]. On their base deal, selling 144 of 176 payments for the full $68,430 purchase price left 32 payments of about $800 with an 'infinite' return. Paperstac's funding episode runs the non-performing version: buy at $35,000 on a $55,000-60,000 UPB, reperform it, and sell a partial for $34,000. The buyer then sits on a $1,000 basis plus the tail. In Eddie Speed's '$100 model,' $100 stays in as the IRS 'substantial investment' [_BvWeumu2WI @ 00:02:01]. Inside a self-directed IRA the same move was described as 'bought it for 30... sold it for 30 100,' keeping $15,000-16,000 tax-free. Josh Andrews pre-sells partials before buying [XRyBErGyKgQ @ 00:13:59].

The paperwork has to spell out what happens when the stream breaks early. The Reweys' rule is that on payoff each party receives the present value of its share. That can be calculated either on yield, which they favor when selling, or as present value at the note rate, and servicing stays where it already is [UwiEQOh84Y4 @ 00:20:16]. Cal Ewing modeled three 36-month outcomes on the Laredo partial. On payoff, the investor has collected 26,217 and takes 41,900 more, for 68,000 total and a 13,017 profit, while Cal gets about 20,600 [LCY-eZOK6gw @ 00:12:50]. At a Texas non-judicial auction, a 105,000 bid less a 5,000 attorney fee against 62,500 owed produces the same 41,900 and 20,600 split, with the surplus going to the borrower. In an REO, the investor's interest converts to a present-value claim. ARV of 130,000 less 20,000 in costs nets 110,000. The investor takes 41,900 plus 10,215, described as 15% of the net, for 52,115, and Cal keeps 57,885 [LCY-eZOK6gw @ 00:19:21]. Paperstac notes that FCI is among the servicers that handle partials, and who pays servicing on default depends on the agreement [XRyBErGyKgQ @ 00:11:22].

When the holder wants cash without giving up ownership at all, Justin Roberts borrows against the paper instead. Roberts got about $80,000 against a roughly $100,000 note, plus a portfolio loan on 24 notes for about $2 million priced 'a little bit under prime.' Roberts also warns not to bank on 80% from day one [b-4NVMQ1GZ8 @ 00:20:09]. Paperstac's wrap play turns a rental into sellable paper. A property bought in 2015, owing $80,000 and worth $230,000-240,000, sells at $240,000 with $30,000 down on a $210,000 note at 8.5-9% over 30 years. After six months of seasoning the note sells for $180,000-190,000, and Paperstac pays off the $80,000 underlying lien before releasing funds [5bOm5hdSRXc @ 00:08:58]. On the closing side, 88-90% of Paperstac buyers use escrow plus collateral audit and sign a disbursement agreement only after reviewing the audit. The platform pays for FedEx two-day shipping so files land in 3-5 days, instead of a buyer wiring $50,000 and waiting 30 days [y6ljJ3T0eNg @ 00:43:47]. The relaunched site adds timed auctions of 1 to 30 days. Winning means being 'awarded' the asset, followed by a 14-day due diligence window [zhg1k-uMJM0 @ 00:04:54].

callout.title: Partial Structuring Edges From the Desk
callout.body: Small structuring moves the practitioners use to squeeze yield, protect the tail, and time the market.
items: Re-amortize a restarted loan at 360 months so payments are front-loaded with interest, and track three balances: the partial buyer's balance, the reassignment/entitlement balance, and current UPB [Paperstac — XRyBErGyKgQ @ 00:17:35].
Size the partial to your cash and yield target: on a $400 payment, 12 months equals $4,800, so paying $4,000 earns about 20% while paying $5,000 loses money [Paperstac — XRyBErGyKgQ @ 00:09:50].
Split-payment partials only work on notes paying more than $1,000/mo, and the Reweys route them through an attorney so the structure doesn't create a security [Paperstac — UwiEQOh84Y4 @ 00:32:03].
Hunt auction inventory late in the year: the relaunch team says the best deals come from 'Thanksgiving on' [Paperstac — zhg1k-uMJM0 @ 00:04:26].

sop_steps.title: Assemble the sale package
sop_steps.action: Gather the full document stack before requesting quotes.
sop_steps.detail: Pull the promissory note, deed of trust, settlement statement, insurance and tax records, and the borrower credit report, then add payment history and collateral details. A borrower score of 650+ gets the highest price [Texas Capital Finance — w4PRGbUrreA @ 00:04:25].

sop_steps.title: Get vetted and list on the marketplace
sop_steps.action: Register as a seller, pass ownership vetting, and load the asset.
sop_steps.detail: Click 'become a seller,' pass the vetting that confirms you hold the note, then list by data tape, servicer email feed, or manual entry with public/private files and pay history [Patrick Franz — y6ljJ3T0eNg @ 00:32:11]. Choose flexible, firm, or make-an-offer pricing [Paperstac — chL0454K1Zs @ 00:01:45].

sop_steps.title: Structure the partial if you are keeping the tail
sop_steps.action: Set the payment block by cash need and price it on yield.
sop_steps.detail: Let the seller's cash need set how many payments to sell, price on yield when selling, and fix the reassignment balance plus payoff treatment, where each party gets the present value of its share. Leave servicing where it is [Paperstac — UwiEQOh84Y4 @ 00:18:02].

sop_steps.title: Close through escrow and audit, then record
sop_steps.action: Fund escrow, clear the collateral audit, and record the assignment.
sop_steps.detail: Have the buyer sign the disbursement agreement after reviewing the collateral audit [Patrick Franz — y6ljJ3T0eNg @ 00:44:17], then record assignments and deeds so neither side falls out of the chain of title [Paperstac — MkofIE1Xq0o @ 00:14:43].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Partials split the room on who should sit on which side of the trade. Fred and Tracy Rewey treat buy-full, sell-partial as the cleanest exit. They sell 144 of 176 payments for the same $68,430 paid for the whole note, and the remaining 32 payments of roughly $800 carry an 'infinite' return. Their Dallas deal, bought at $47,500, sold the next 279 payments for $51,000, netting $3,500 while keeping 79 payments [UwiEQOh84Y4 @ 00:23:31]. Cal Ewing came at partials from the opposite direction, as a reluctant first-timer. Texas is Cal's favorite state and Cal did not want to sell, but the private lender on the deal needed repair cash. So an IRA investor paid 55,000 for the next 120 payments at a 10.48% IRR, while Cal kept a tail of 130-plus payments worth 95,402 at full term [LCY-eZOK6gw @ 00:09:12]. Buy-side yield expectations diverge hard. The Reweys priced their partial at 13.3%. Paperstac's hosts pitch whole-loan yields of 12 or 13 percent becoming '30 35' through partial structuring, and call the 10 to 20 percent buyers target expensive money for the seller [XRyBErGyKgQ @ 00:09:02]. The Paperstac guests on Patrick Franz's show quote partial purchases at '30 40%' yields [y6ljJ3T0eNg @ 00:13:08]. A seller reading those numbers is looking at what buyers think the lump sum is worth to them.

Pricing method is the second fault line. The Reweys run partials two ways: on yield, which they favor when selling, or at present value using the note rate. On any payoff, each party collects the present value of its share [UwiEQOh84Y4 @ 00:21:17]. Sierra Davis prices off yield and LTV together: 12% is the target, 13% is good, and nothing goes under a 10% floor. A 70% LTV cap turns roughly $85,000 to $86,000 owed on a $120,000 sale into a $75,000 offer at 11% [XsNZ5SQXdCI @ 00:41:16]. The JKP Holdings hosts push back on that mindset. They warn against pricing performing paper on yield alone and against assuming it keeps performing, and they dismiss percent-of-UPB pricing as 'an old wise sale' [b-4NVMQ1GZ8 @ 00:05:05]. Texas Capital Finance frames price from the seller's chair instead: the closer a note resembles a traditional bank mortgage, the higher the price. Bank-like paper fetches 95 to 98% of principal, while typical seller-finance notes land between 90% and 70% [w4PRGbUrreA @ 00:08:46]. These camps write very different checks on identical paper. Whoever sells a partial or a whole note has to know which lens the buyer uses: yield, LTV, or how closely the file looks like bank paper.

Leverage is where the playbooks split widest. JKP's hosts draw the line cleanly: a partial buyer owns the note for a period, while hypothecation lets the creator keep the note and borrow against it [b-4NVMQ1GZ8 @ 00:08:47]. Justin Roberts went the bank route after five or six notes drained their cash. They pulled about $80,000 against a roughly $100,000 note, plus a 24-note portfolio loan near $2 million priced a little under prime. Yet the host openly doubted 10x leverage claims and pegged fund financing at 75 to 80% advances at 4 to 5% [b-4NVMQ1GZ8 @ 00:41:50]. Justin also refuses private money at 8 to 12%, even while lending at 12% themselves. Paperstac's funding playbook runs another way. It sells a partial off a reperformed non-performer, brings in patient rather than active JV capital, or raises a Reg D fund from accredited investors. Their Reg A+ raise left them doubting they would do another, because collecting $1,000 at a time is brutal next to $100,000 to $500,000 checks [_BvWeumu2WI @ 00:06:12]. Dave Van Horn takes yet another lane: borrowing 80% of about $2 million in home equity at 4% to lend $1.6 million at 14%. Van Horn stays mixed on HELOCs, though, because undisciplined borrowers 'go to vegas' [jFBvJbcMbFA @ 00:20:36].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Most note deals that blow up do it at the closing table, not in the payment stream. Paperstac watches hundreds of closings a quarter and keeps seeing the same buyer errors. Buyers bid without an indicative bid. They show up without funds ready, so sellers suspect the loan is being shopped and block them. Their self-directed IRA custodians take weeks while the assignment sits in draft, and one deal has run three months [MkofIE1Xq0o @ 00:07:23]. Vesting mistakes on FBO wording, address, or signer are worse. Changing the PSA after the collateral is with the auditor and money is in escrow unravels the whole closing, so screenshot the vesting before anything moves [MkofIE1Xq0o @ 00:12:07]. Lowballing every listing by $20,000 gets an account frozen, and going dark mid-deal invites the seller to resell. The quietest trap hits after funding. Unrecorded assignments and deeds have knocked buyers out of the chain of title, surfacing three years later or as tax notices 18 months after a sale. Fund wind-downs then make the original seller nearly impossible to track down [MkofIE1Xq0o @ 00:14:54]. Off-platform, the Paperstac guests on Patrick Franz's show describe buyers wiring $50,000 and waiting 30 days for a collateral file. On-platform, FedEx two-day shipping lands files in three to five days [y6ljJ3T0eNg @ 00:45:12].

Collateral and paper quality kill exits further downstream. Sierra Davis's first note, bought from a mentor after seven months of study, collapsed fast. The borrower paid three times, then the roughly $75,000 house turned up empty mid-renovation. Sierra cancelled the contract and resold the property as-is on seller financing [XsNZ5SQXdCI @ 00:32:08]. Their rule since then: if the paperwork is not good, you cannot foreclose. Justin Roberts found that sloppy origination also blocks leverage. Their first dozen notes carried no RMLO and a flat $20,000 down regardless of credit, and banks rejected them as below standard [b-4NVMQ1GZ8 @ 00:16:07]. Growth then slammed into one bank's legal lending limit, forcing a pivot and a revolving door of bank contacts. Cherif Medawar flags the borrower with no skin in the game, pointing to VA loans up to $2 million with no money down where borrowers simply walk. Cherif demands a real cash down payment plus six months to a year of on-time seasoning [bhfdMe7Dpwk @ 00:06:08]. Paperstac's wrap segment adds the structural warnings. Originate through an attorney or title company, watch the due-on-sale exposure because banks are wise to subject-to deals, and never turn a great portfolio of real estate into a crappy portfolio of notes [5bOm5hdSRXc @ 00:15:37].

Run the downside math before signing any partial or note sale. Cal Ewing modeled three outcomes at month 36 on the 55,000 partial. A payoff gives the investor 68,000 total and a 13,017 profit, with roughly 20,600 to Cal. A Texas non-judicial auction at a 105,000 bid, less a 5,000 attorney fee, still pays the investor 41,900 and Cal 20,600, with the surplus going to the borrower. An REO sale at 130,000 ARV, less 20,000 in costs, pays the investor 52,115 and leaves Cal 57,885 [LCY-eZOK6gw @ 00:19:21]. Texas Capital Finance warns sellers that total future interest is not the note's value, because borrowers can prepay [w4PRGbUrreA @ 00:08:31]. Justin Roberts lived that: their first owner-financed flip paid off after two payments. Justin also reports that buyers with $20,000 to $30,000 down have dried up and four flips sit unsold. Desperate sellers are now cutting 4 to 5% 30-year notes, the kind of low-rate paper Justin says won't win 80% bank advances [b-4NVMQ1GZ8 @ 00:47:49]. Paperstac's pricing team adds the marketplace verdict: mispriced assets go to die. Their monthly-retrained price predictor runs within about 2% on sales of $30,000 or more, so an inflated ask gets exposed fast [zhg1k-uMJM0 @ 00:16:15].

callout.title: Clear These Four Gates Before Any Note Exit or Partial
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a deal that stalled, unraveled, or lost money for a named practitioner. Clear all four before signing a purchase, a partial sale, or a full note sale.
items: Lock an indicative bid off verified rate, UPB, origination date, and last pay date, and never lowball every listing by $20,000 [Paperstac — MkofIE1Xq0o @ 00:04:12].
Confirm FBO wording, address, and signer on the vesting and screenshot it before collateral goes to the auditor [Paperstac — MkofIE1Xq0o @ 00:12:07].
On a wrap, run title, disclose the underlying lien, and use partial proceeds to pay that lien off so the note moves to first position [Paperstac — 5bOm5hdSRXc @ 00:07:29].
Model payoff, auction, and REO splits between the partial investor and the tail holder before selling any partial [Cal Ewing — LCY-eZOK6gw @ 00:12:50].

chapters.pull_quote: "Record your assignments and record your deeds." — Paperstac (MkofIE1Xq0o @ 00:14:43).
action_checklist: Build the listing with photos, a recent BPO value document, pay history, and private files, because buyers will ask for the files anyway [Paperstac — chL0454K1Zs @ 00:01:24].
Choose flexible, firm, or make-an-offer pricing and write a subtitle and seller description that tell the note's story [Paperstac — chL0454K1Zs @ 00:01:45].

Assemble the sale package: promissory note, deed of trust, settlement statement, insurance and tax records, and the borrower credit report, where a 650-plus score draws the highest price [Texas Capital Finance — w4PRGbUrreA @ 00:04:25].
Size any partial to the seller's actual cash need and leave servicing where it already sits [Paperstac — UwiEQOh84Y4 @ 00:18:02].

Before pitching local banks, prepare a roughly 20-page banker package of financials, quarterly reports, and a PFS, modeled on Stinson Bland's 'banker's bible' [Note Investing & Seller Financing - JKP Holdings — b-4NVMQ1GZ8 @ 00:21:08].
Close through escrow plus a collateral audit, and sign the disbursement agreement only after reviewing that audit [Patrick Franz — y6ljJ3T0eNg @ 00:44:17].
